#8605. Start the Day Strong With This 30-Minute Workout You Can Do Right at Home

Burn every muscle of the body while revving the heart rate.

An at-home workout that requires zero equipment might sound easy—but this one will change your mind! The fun, challenging exercises (all bodyweight!) target every major muscle of the body, which means you make the most of just 30 minutes of work. Squeeze it in before you head out for the day or whenever you need a movement break today; it’s easy to fit in at any time.

Dane Miklaus, C.S.C.S., founder of WORK Training Studio in Idaho, took on the puzzle of creating this tough, no-equipment workout and pieced together a creative routine to get your muscles firing on all fronts. Consider it your go-to during a busy holiday schedule.

“I chose to focus on areas where traditional endurance athletes may have weaknesses due to underutilization,” Miklaus tells Runner’s World. Because running and most of our daily movements occur in the sagittal plane of motion—that’s forward and backward—we tend to neglect muscles used in lateral (or side-to-side) and rotational movements, causing weakness in these areas. While that not only leads to suboptimal performance, it can also increase your risk of injury, he explains.

“By implementing a lower-body routine that incorporates lateral and rotational movements, as well as upper-body and core training, runners can increase their overall athletic standards and the functional capacity of their bodies,” Miklaus says.

In addition to making you move in different planes of motion, this workout also alternates lower-body and upper-body or core exercises. That way, one muscle group gets rest as the other works, Miklaus explains, without you having to take much actual rest time.

The lower-body moves also get more difficult as you work through the seven-exercise circuit, while the upper-body ones become less intense. “This is intended to provide a balanced challenge and allow each athlete space to scale the difficulty [of the workout] to their own fitness level,” Miklaus explains.

How to do the workout: Do each exercise in order for 45 seconds. Rest for 15 seconds while also transitioning into the next move. Repeat for four total sets.

You don’t need any equipment for this workout, but an exercise mat is optional. Miklaus demonstrates each exercise in the video above so you can learn proper form.

Why it works: Target the muscles that support the hips—including the gluteus medius and minimus (the smaller backside muscles) and the piriformis (deep butt muscle)—as well as the hamstrings, adductors (inner thighs), and gluteus maximus (biggest muscle of the butt). “A more stable hip is a stronger hip, and because runners rely on their hips for every stride, exercises like these are a must,” Miklaus says.

Why it works: While you’ll hit your chest and shoulders, push-ups are also great for strengthening the deep core muscles and shoulder stabilizers, Miklaus says. The shoulder tap also adds an anti-rotation element to turn up the core-stability challenge.

Why it works: “When all you have for equipment is in your own bodyweight, adding a speed or power component is a great way to increase muscular recruitment,” Miklaus says. “So, by dropping into the squat and absorbing that force, then rebounding back out of it quickly, we turn on more of our leg muscles than if we performed a basic bodyweight squat.” The twist at the top means more fire in the rotational hip and core muscles, too.

Why it works: While runners get some biceps activation on the run during the arm swing, they often neglect their triceps, Miklaus says. This move changes that, plus it still taps into core strength.

Why it works: Build hip strength and stability with this exercise that creates a “triple extension” a.k.a. when the hip, knee, and ankle joints all get in on the action.

Plus, “just like with the drop squat, this single-leg hop variation will recruit almost every fiber in an athlete’s glutes, quads, and calves, to make them more forceful and dynamic,” Miklaus says. “What runner couldn’t stand to be a bit more explosive?”

Why it works: “When performing bodyweight exercises, it’s very difficult to stimulate the back muscles,” Miklaus says. But this move activates the latissimus dorsi (major muscle of the back), teres major, and posterior deltoid (both on the back of the shoulder). “This is important for helping to provide postural balance for athletes who only incorporate pushing movements into their upper-body routines,” he adds. Finally, the plank hold with knee drive means your abs and obliques get worked, too.

Why it works: The skater exercise forces you to slow down momentum, stabilize, and then explode again, Miklaus explains. “When moving laterally, and into a hinged position, we are able to recruit more of the deep hip muscles than is possible when only moving in the sagittal plane,” he says. In addition to strengthening muscles at the hip, it also improves ankle stability.

Mallory Creveling is an ACE-certified personal trainer and RRCA-certified run coach, who also holds certifications in kettlebell training, sports performance, and more. She has more than 15 years of experience covering fitness, health, and nutrition for a wide range of publications, and nearly 10 years of experience as a trainer and fitness instructor. Mallory stays on top of her continuing education in fitness, as well as the latest science in wellness. She has worked with some of the best experts in their medical fields, and regularly interviews researchers, trainers, athletes, and more to find the best advice for readers looking to improve their performance and well-being. As a freelance writer, Mallory's work appeared in Women's Health, Self, Men's Journal, Reader's Digest, and more. She has also held staff editorial positions at Family Circle and Shape magazines, as well as DailyBurn.com. A former New Yorker/Brooklynite, she's now based in Easton, Pennsylvania.

#8604. 8 Setup Tips to Fine-Tune Your Trap-Bar Deadlift

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Al Gerared invented the trap bar in the late 1980s, and it quickly became the deadlift tool of choice for lifters whose backs say no to the barbell.

Standing inside it improves alignment with your center of gravity, often with a more upright torso than in the conventional deadlift, which is great for a cranky lower back.

In the conventional setup, the barbell is over your midfoot, but where should your feet be inside the trap bar? Should you use the high or low handles? Where should your hips be?

Nail these details before the first pull, and your form will improve; that’s the goal of the Trap Bar setup guide.

I’ll cover everything from choosing the handle height and positioning yourself inside the trap bar to finding your ideal hip height, engaging your upper back, and building full-body tension before pulling.

Next, I’ll walk you through the trap bar deadlift setup step by step to improve your form and gains.

Before stepping into the trap bar, decide whether to use the high or low D handles. This decision affects range of motion and starting position.

High handles shorten the range of motion and let you start with a more upright torso with less hip and knee flexion. They’re great for beginners, taller lifters, or those who struggle to keep a neutral spine while hinging down.

Low handles increase the ROM, requiring more hip and knee flexion to reach the bar. This creates a deeper starting position and increases the distance you lift.

Coach’s Tip: Your choice depends on your mobility, body proportions, training goals, and your ability to create tension. If reaching the low handles requires you to round your lower back or shift your weight forward, switch to the high handles.

Where you stand inside the trap bar determines everything that follows, including your balance, hip height, and torso position. Lining up your ankles with the loading stubs puts you in a better position to lift with good form.

Internal Cue: Feel your feet on the floor.

External Cue: Line your ankles up with the stubs.

Coach’s Tip: Your ankle position sets up everything else. If the bar feels unbalanced or tilts when you begin, check your stance and adjust.

Your feet are the foundation; creating tension there gives you a stronger base to pull from, puts your lower-body joints in an optimal lifting position, and helps transfer force more effectively to the bar.

Internal Cue: Feel the tension in your hips.

External Cue: Rip the floor apart with your feet.

Coach’s Tip: If your arches collapse or your knees cave in during the first rep, you’ve lost your foundation. Reset your feet and rebuild tension.

If you start too low, your hips may shoot up before the weight moves. Start too high, and you’ll turn the exercise into more of a stiff-legged deadlift. Your sweet spot depends on your body proportions, mobility, and handle height.

Internal Cue: Feel the hamstring tension.

External Cue: Hinge back, chest up and shoulders down.

Coach’s Tip: Feeling tension in your hamstrings is key here. If you feel it excessively anywhere else, adjust your hinge.

Your grip connects you to the trap bar and creates the tension needed for proper form. The arms should act like hooks, allowing your lower body to do most of the work.

Internal Cue: Crush the handles, arms straight.

External Cue: Leave fingerprints in the handles.

Coach’s Tip: Place the handle in your palm near the base of your fingers to help prevent calluses.

Engaging your lats and upper back creates tension that stabilizes your shoulders, maintains your torso position, and transfers force more effectively from the ground up.

External Cue: Squeeze oranges in your armpits.

Coach’s Tip: If you lose your neutral spine before the first pull, you’re missing tension. Re-engage your lats before pulling.

The core acts as a bridge between the lower and upper body, and if the bridge is out, your lower back will have nasty words to say to you. A good core brace solidifies your setup before the first pull.

External Cue: Push your midsection against an imaginary lifting belt.

Coach’s Tip: If you feel your lower back rounding, reset your breath and brace.

Taking the slack out means pulling the handles until your body and the bar are loaded with tension. This prevents you from jerking the weight off the floor and losing your starting position.

Internal Cue: Full-body tension, no slack.

External Cue: Chest up, shoulders down and arms long.

Coach’s Tip: Like the conventional deadlift, you should hear the click that signals you have pulled the slack out of the bar.

Before the pull, mentally run through the list below.

The trap bar might be more forgiving than the barbell, but a poor setup can still rob you of gains. Here’s what to look for during your setup so you don’t do it again.

When you’re not centered in the trap bar, your first pull requires more work from your lower back.

The Fix: Start with your ankles roughly aligned with the loading stubs. Adjust slightly until your weight is balanced over your midfoot.

Using the low handles when you lack the mobility to maintain a strong starting position can cause your lower back to round.

The Fix: Use the high handles until you can reach the low handles without sacrificing your spinal position.

Loose lats and shrugged shoulders will cause rounding in both the upper and lower back and unnecessarily increase the range of motion.

The Fix: Squeeze the handles, engage your lats, and keep your arms straight without pinching your shoulder blades.

Gripping and ripping before pulling the slack out of the bar can put you out of position before the lift even begins.

The Fix: Root your feet, brace your core, engage your lats, and remove the slack from the bar before initiating the pull.

The trap bar deadlift is easier to learn and more forgiving than its straight-bar cousin, but that doesn’t mean you should neglect the setup. Reviewing this setup guide again shows how important setup is for good form.

At first, this checklist will take time and thought, but soon it will become automatic, and you’ll be ready to pull without overthinking every detail.

Put yourself in the best position to express your strength, and the gains will follow.

#8601. The 5 Best Outdoor Saunas for Getting Your Sweat On in 2025

Experts explain how hot and cold wellness therapies could improve health. These outdoor saunas help you get these potential benefits at home.

Written by Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Stephen Sheehan, CPT Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

Sauna bathing is an age-old Nordic tradition that can have huge benefits for your overall wellness.

There are a variety of sauna styles available, from the traditional barrels to more modern cube designs with electric heaters, infrared heaters, or wood-burning stoves. Some newer models have high-tech features like surround-sound speakers, added LED light therapy, and charging docks for your electronics. However, all you need to reap the potential benefits of your sauna experience is a high-quality product you’ll actually use.

We found six of the best outdoor saunas and included a comprehensive guide for picking the right sauna for you. We also tapped Saloni Sharma, M.D., Medhat Mikhael, M.D., and Earric Lee, a postdoctoral researcher studying exercise science and Sport and Health Sciences faculty member at the University of Jyväskylä, Finland (a.k.a., sauna central), to help us understand how sauna use can benefit athletes during training.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If you’re seeking a more technology-forward sauna experience, Sun Home’s Luminar outdoor infrared sauna is an excellent model to invest in. This five-person model uses an infrared heating system, which you can control through your phone via a mobile app. Indoor saunas often have infrared heat, but Sun Home claims its Luminar model is more than 12.5 times more powerful at 500 watts than competitors. This sauna includes Bluetooth speakers and soothing LED chromotherapy, making sitting in a hot room more enticing to beginner bathers. Yes, it’s a pricey model, but it has ample features and floor-to-ceiling windows for a panoramic view of the outdoors.

According to SweatTent, you can set up the SweatTent Outdoor Sauna in about three minutes. It is somewhat portable because it is simple to put up and take down. The material is durable, insulated, and weather-proof, so you can leave the sauna outdoors indefinitely.

A wood-fired stove heats the SweatTent and comes with 20 pounds of sauna rocks, a fire poker, and heat-resistant gloves to feed the fire safely. The SweatTent is our favorite option for a complete sauna kit. It’s easy to set up, comparatively inexpensive, portable, and works well.

The Sun Home Luminar Sauna is a cube sauna with a carbonized wood exterior and dura-glass windows built to withstand any climate conditions. Luminar has a compact footprint compared to other two-person cube saunas. It uses a combination of infrared and full-spectrum heaters positioned to maintain optimum heat regardless of exterior conditions.

The choice of grade-A carbonized red cedar wood and thick double-pane glass throughout the sauna ensures durability and insulation. With nine heaters, including three far-infrared heaters under the bench and six full-spectrum heaters surrounding the cabin, the Luminar Outdoor Sauna guarantees an efficient and effective sauna session. Sun Home places these heaters strategically to envelop the users in 3D healing wavelengths from all angles.

You can control the Luminar temperature from an app to start heating your sauna before you get home. It has Bluetooth surround-sound speakers and a panoramic view through the dura-glass windows.

The Redwood Outdoors Barrel Sauna is a traditional barrel sauna made with Thermowood. It has all the features you need with nothing extra. We appreciate that you can customize several parts of this dry sauna, from the heating mechanism (you can go the Finnish sauna route with a Harvia electric heater or a wood-burning stove) to add-ons like a weather-resistant shingled roof and even a cold plunge tub. It has a spa-like sauna scent and dry heat, and comfortably fits four to six people.

One benefit of a Thermowood sauna is its durability and resistance to the elements. Redwood Outdoors says that, when properly cared for, this sauna should have an outdoor lifespan of 20 years.

The Redwood Outdoors Thermowood Cabin Sauna is our best outdoor sauna for cold climates because of its robust, weather-resistant construction. This sauna has a traditional Scandinavian design with Scandinavian softwood treated with intense heat to provide exceptional insulation. This design enhances its longevity and contributes to its energy efficiency, ensuring even heat distribution throughout the interior.

The Thermowood Cabin Sauna package includes a Harvia electric heater, wooden heater guard, water bucket and ladle, sauna rocks, and interior seating benches, providing all the necessary components for an authentic sauna experience.

If you’ve spent quality time in the locker room sauna, you’re committed to the wellness practice, and you live somewhere with outdoor space, a sauna might be an excellent investment for your health. “Researchers have found several possible health benefits from sauna use; most importantly, they have shown to help cardiovascular diseases—particularly high blood pressure and heart diseases—as well as acute and chronic pain and neurological diseases,” Mikhael says.

Putting a sauna inside can create some logistical challenges, though, from installation to insulation and more. An outdoor sauna might be easier to install, and it gets you closer to nature, as many of them have spacious windows. “One big bonus of outdoor saunas specifically is they exist outdoors,” Sharma says. “There is a problem in our society labeled Nature Deficit Disorder, which means we aren’t spending enough time outside. There are many proven benefits of being outdoors, and these saunas allow you to combine them with the potential benefits of heat therapy.”

Depending on your model, once your outdoor sauna is installed and ready to go, you can set the temperature via a manual dial, Bluetooth-enabled app, or touchscreen. The heat comes from sauna heaters or wood-burning stoves. Some outdoor saunas allow you to set the timer up to 36 hours in advance. From there, all you need to do is open the door, climb in, and relax.

As for timing, “Two to three 15- to 25-minute sessions per week are ideal,” says Mikhael. “After 15 to 25 minutes, people can benefit the most without feeling like they’re getting dehydrated or dizzy.”

Bring a book, crank up your music, or bring a friend to sweat it out with you—and remember to stay hydrated.

“You want to ensure you’re hydrated before and after,” says Sharma. “A sauna induces a lot of sweating, so you can get dehydrated very easily.” We recommend an electrolyte powder after use if you sweat a lot.

Ideally, you should be heading to your sauna soon as part of your post-workout routine, Lee says. “We found not only is a combination of exercise and sauna bathing stronger in its effects, but many cardiovascular benefits, like lower blood pressure, were sustained for a longer period afterward.”

Most saunas use electricity to run the lights and heaters. Low-tech wood stove-heated saunas might not need any power if there are no lights. There are some solar-powered saunas, too, if you want less strain on the environment (and your electric bill). You’ll just need to make sure you have a battery as a backup.

Given their size and weight, saunas are not very portable. So we’d recommend buying an outdoor sauna once you’re living in a permanent residence rather than an apartment or rental. But even then, life happens, and sometimes you need to move. You can move a constructed outdoor sauna, but it would likely need professional equipment to hoist it into a truck bed. There are very portable tent saunas—much more affordable than the outdoor ones on our list.

The outdoor saunas we recommend cost between $1,599 and $9,799. Based on our research, the lower end of the spectrum offers plenty of heat but fewer bells and whistles. The more pricey saunas can typically seat more people, have more temperature adjustments, provide more comfortable accommodations, and are made with higher-quality materials.

Many outdoor saunas on this list offer additional accessories a la carte. While these aren’t integral to your new sauna routine, they might make it more fun, luxe, and/or comfortable. Some standard accessories we noticed are outdoor showers, cold plunge tubs such as the Plunge, and wooden recliners. Nothing’s stopping you from DIY-ing those accessories, though.

Many wellness fads are short-lived trends (and even potentially harmful). But saunas have been staples in Scandinavian life for centuries, showing significant promise in improving your well-being. Our experts say regular sauna use can improve muscle soreness and even chronic pain.

If you’ve dabbled in heat therapy in the past and want to make it more of a long-term lifestyle (and you have the budget to match), an outdoor sauna can be a valuable and beneficial tool. But, like any significant investment in your health, our experts say you should always consult your doctor before purchasing an outdoor sauna or starting a sauna routine—especially if you have severe cardiovascular or lung issues.

The cost of an outdoor sauna depends on several factors, including capacity, heat source, extra features, integrated technology, and materials. We found saunas at around $1,599 and others at up to $9,799, depending on your budget and needs.

Yes, outdoor saunas typically come with features and accessories to help weatherproof them (like shingles) and keep them dry and ventilated during winter.

When investing in an outdoor sauna, you have to consider its costs, including the electricity used by electric heaters, lighting, and more. When purchasing an outdoor sauna, look for the wattage and amount of electricity it needs to run; it doesn’t hurt to crunch the numbers to estimate your electric bill with a sauna in the mix.

#8599. 13 Best High-Tech Home Gym Products and Fitness Gear

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Home-gym gear has gotten a lot more interesting over the last few years. Smart resistance systems can replace entire cable stations, adjustable dumbbells can cover serious strength work in a small footprint, and recovery tools have become much easier to work into a normal routine. The useful stuff still comes down to one question: does the technology or design actually make training better?

We’re using “high-tech” broadly here because innovation doesn’t always need a screen or app. We personally tested every product on this list alongside plenty of other home-gym and fitness gear, and these stood out for solving real training, space, or usability problems in a meaningful way.

High-tech gear can get feature-heavy fast, so it helps to narrow your decision to what will actually improve your training and fit your space.

Start with what the product actually does once the workout begins. Useful technology should give you something you can feel or use, whether that means better resistance control or feedback that guides the session. A long feature list carries little weight if you don’t use most of it after the first few workouts.

Home-gym equipment has to live in the space long after the novelty wears off. A larger system can earn its space by replacing several other pieces of equipment, while compact gear should be easy to store or used often enough to justify keeping it around. The best designs make the setup easier to train in without creating another piece of equipment you’re constantly moving out of the way.

The Gym Monster 3 can cover enough of a strength program that it feels like the centerpiece of a home gym. During testing, the adjustable cable positions and digital resistance gave us plenty of room for compound work and accessory training without surrounding the unit with weight stacks. One-pound load changes are especially useful when a larger jump would throw off the set’s intent.

Speediance also gives you several ways to control the machine while you train. Smart Spotter monitors movement speed and can reduce resistance when a rep starts to stall, while the Bluetooth ring lets you engage or release the load without reaching for the touchscreen. Programmable cable engagement gives you more control over where resistance kicks in, which is another useful touch when you’re training alone.

Gym Nano packs a surprising amount of training capability into an 18.1-pound unit. During testing, the 16.7-foot cable gave us enough freedom to get into athletic movements beyond traditional cable exercises, while 220 pounds of digital resistance leaves room for heavier strength work. Sled Mode expands the programming options even further when you want to use the resistance for more dynamic training.

Its performance tracking is equally useful. Nano can establish baseline assessments, save individual set data, and build a training history that lets you compare sessions over time. Metrics such as power, movement speed, and rate of force development give athletes and coaches more to work with than a simple resistance readout.

The FAST Series lives up to its name when you need to change weight quickly. Magnetic pop-pins slide along the side rails to make 10-pound jumps, and you can adjust them with the dumbbell outside the cradle, which works especially well for drop sets. Included 2.5-pound microplates give you smaller loading options when a bigger jump doesn’t fit the exercise.

The weight capacity is just as impressive. These dumbbells can reach 125 pounds while measuring only 18.3 inches long at the heaviest setting, giving stronger lifters plenty of room to train without an oversized adjustable dumbbell getting in the way. The 85- and 105-pound versions can also be expanded later, and the cradles grow with them, so you aren’t locked into the weight range you originally buy.

Ab rollouts can be awkward to progress because the jump from a shortened rep to a full rollout can feel pretty big. ZeroWheel gave us much more control over that progression during testing. Motorized assistance can take some load off while you build the movement, then the resistance settings give stronger users somewhere to go once regular rollouts stop being challenging enough. The different motorized modes also open the door to exercises beyond traditional rollouts, giving the device more range than its design initially suggests.

The ZeroWheel Fitness app adds another layer that we ended up appreciating. It includes an exercise library, plus workouts and programs built around the device, so you can pull up a session and get to work without designing your own training. Tutorial videos help with unfamiliar movements, while live performance tracking gives you feedback as you go. That takes some of the planning off your plate and lets you focus on the workout.

The Strive feels different from a typical air bike because resistance isn’t tied entirely to cadence. REP’s Variable Pitch Resistance system changes the angle of the fan blades, so we could make the bike feel heavier without simply pedaling faster. That gave us more control during testing as we moved between longer conditioning work and hard intervals.

REP also addressed some of the smaller annoyances that come with air bikes. A magnetic fan cover lets you control how much air gets blown back at you, and the ratcheting seat adjustment makes position changes quicker than dealing with a traditional pull pin. Those details make the Strive easier to use when you ride it regularly.

The WB7 gives you enough adjustment to get picky about setup. During testing, the backrest and seat positions made it easy to fine-tune pressing angles, and the padding stayed comfortable across flat and incline work. The dual-slot adjustment mechanism also makes changing positions straightforward as you move through a session.

Its weight was one of the biggest practical wins. At 49.8 pounds, the WB7 is much easier to move than many heavy-duty adjustable benches, while its wide base still feels stable under load. Built-in wheels make repositioning it even easier when floor space needs to serve more than one purpose.

The 3-in-1 design gives one box several useful jobs without taking over the room. During testing, we could switch between jump heights just by changing its orientation, then use the same piece for step-ups or other exercises that needed a raised surface. That made it easy to keep in regular rotation without dedicating floor space to several different boxes.

The inner wood core provides a stable platform, and REP uses textured vinyl on the exterior for better grip. The cover is also removable, making it easier to clean or replace after enough training sessions. The smaller sizes are light enough to reposition without much trouble.

The PacerMini fits easily into a home office or small training space. During testing, the low profile and transport wheels made it easy to move when you needed the floor space for something else, and 0.1-mph adjustments gave us enough control to settle into a comfortable walking pace.

The wireless remote makes those adjustments easier when the treadmill is tucked under a desk, since you don’t have to reach down to change speed or stop the belt. The 3.0-mph top speed keeps it firmly in walking territory, while the two incline positions give you another way to change the effort.

Traditional cardio workouts can feel drab and dull. FightCamp hits different—literally—especially for anyone looking for a combat-sports conditioning program at home that brings the feel of a sweaty, old-school boxing gym to the climate-controlled comfort of your living room.

FightCamp has been around since 2018, offering reassurance that it’s an established brand when you’re investing in equipment. Its freestanding heavy bag is a good fit for both boxing and Muay Thai practitioners. The platform offers more than 3,000 on-demand workouts, led by a roster of experienced trainers. You can track every punch and kick in real time and get detailed insights into strike type, speed, and total output.

What’s also reassuring is that FightCamp continues on making improvements. Its recently launched Gen 3 trackers make it easier to monitor your progress—no console required. Up to four compact trackers—two worn in your wraps, with two optional trackers for kickboxing—pair with your phone or tablet to measure each strike in real time.

Technique workouts score punches for accuracy, while FightCamp WORK, launched in June, can now tracks sessions on any bag, anywhere, with mitts, or during shadowboxing. One of its features, Drills, allows you to run either a featured drill, or create your own, set a target for each round, and records and measures your personal bests from week to week.

The cordless setup is what immediately separates the FT-130A from more traditional compression systems. Each boot has its own controller, so there’s no separate pump or hose setup taking over the floor around you. Built-in pressure sensing also helps the system adapt compression around the shape of your legs, which takes some of the guesswork out of dialing in a session.

You still get plenty of manual control when you want it. Eleven pressure levels let you adjust how aggressive the compression feels, and the two boots can sync automatically or operate independently. That independent control also lets you use a single boot when only one leg needs attention.

The Go 3 was easy to keep in regular rotation because it doesn’t feel like another bulky recovery tool to haul around. At 1.6 pounds, it fits comfortably in a gym bag, and USB-C charging means one less proprietary charger to keep track of. Five speeds give you enough room to adjust how aggressive you want the percussion to feel.

Hyperice also includes a carrying case, and the Go 3 is TSA-friendly for carry-on travel, which fits the portable angle well. The flat and wedge attachments covered the basic areas we wanted to hit during testing, while up to four hours of battery life means it can go through several sessions before needing a charge.

The fēnix 9 Pro makes the most sense for someone whose training doesn’t stay in one lane. Strength sessions, conditioning, and outdoor activity can all feed into the same Garmin ecosystem, giving you a broader view of training load and recovery. Training Readiness and Training Status help organize that information, while newer features such as Stamina Zones and Stamina Curve add more context during longer efforts.

Garmin also makes the watch useful once you leave the gym. Multi-band GPS and onboard mapping cover navigation, while the integrated LED flashlight is surprisingly useful for early starts or nights outside. Select versions also add inReach connectivity, giving users another option if satellite communication is part of the plan.

PLAYLIST+ is what makes the TRI 2 PRO especially interesting. The headphones can record audio from a Bluetooth connection directly to their 4GB of onboard memory, letting you bring streaming music with you when your phone or an internet connection isn’t available. That also solves a major problem for swimmers, since Bluetooth won’t transmit underwater. You can load the headphones before you get in and play everything from memory once you start swimming.

The open-ear bone-conduction design also makes the TRI 2 PRO useful well beyond the pool. You can keep your ears open while running, riding, or training outdoors, and the IPX8 construction can handle full submersion down to 12 feet. The H2O Audio PRO app gives you another way to manage songs, folders, software updates, and PLAYLIST+ content from one place.

We personally tested every product in this roundup and compared each one against equipment used across home gyms, training facilities, recovery routines, and everyday fitness. The goal was to find products where the technology or design made a noticeable difference once the gear was actually being used.

We view that testing through a strength-and-conditioning lens, paying particular attention to how equipment fits into real programming. Useful innovation should give you better training options, make equipment easier to use consistently, or solve a problem that shows up in an actual home gym. Those are the products that earned a place here.

#8596. Debt And Physician Finances

Editorial Disclosure: Opinions, reviews, analyses & recommendations are the author’s alone, and have not been reviewed, endorsed, or approved by any of these entities.

Have you ever had a termite infestation? You likely didn’t realize you did until it was too late. For months or sometimes years, you go about your life without the faintest idea that something is afoot, because after all, the house looks just fine from the driveway.

By the time you notice that sagging floorboards, the structure is already compromised.

Debt is that termite infestation. You don’t realize the damage it’s doing until it’s too late. It gnaws through your income, unnoticed, until the day a job change, a market downturn or an unplanned expense reveals just how rickety the foundation has become.

More than a third of Americans earning $200,000 or more say they’re living paycheck to paycheck. Nearly a third of six-figure earners describe themselves as financially stretched, struggling, or drowning.

Physicians are not exempt from this. A high income means nothing on its own. It can open up opportunities, yes but those options feel out of reach when debt takes away the majority of your paycheck.

Student loans and a primary mortgage are fixtures of adulthood. If you’re a physician and have never had to carry these, you’re extremely lucky. Or you know something I don’t— in which case, please share your secret with the rest of us.

The median education debt for the class of 2025 was $215,000— not including undergraduate loans. Many physicians carry this into their 40s and 50s.

Nobody becomes a doctor debt-free unless family money covers the tab. In return you get to enjoy a career in medicine earning good money with plenty of lucrative options for supplementing that income.

The mortgage on a primary residence is an equally unavoidable aspect of adult finances. In return you get a place to call home and an asset that (usually) appreciates. Mortgage is debt, yes, but paying it down builds equity that would otherwise go to someone else in the form of rent.

This type of debt cannot be categorized as termites. This is the foundation you build on top of and most physicians manage it fine once attending income kicks in. There are also ways to significantly ease the burden on this type of debt.

Credit card balances, car payments beyond what a reliable car would cost, a second home bought at the top of a market, an extravagant vacation you didn’t save for but financed instead— I could go on. These are all examples of bad debt. Not because they aren’t “profitable” but also because the ROI they provide is short-lived.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Having a lake house feels great but not if you have to put up with a toxic workplace in order to pay it off. Jetting off to Switzerland feels like freedom but not if you have to skimp on your 401(k) contributions for the following years in order to pay it off.

In the second quarter of 2026, the average APR on credit card accounts that carry a balance was 22.15%, up from 21.52% in Q1. Total U.S. credit card debt reached $1.26 trillion in Q2 2026, closing in on the all-time high of $1.28 trillion set at the end of 2025. Roughly 60% of cardholders carry a balance month to month rather than paying in full.

A $15,000 balance at 22% APR costs over $3,300 a year in interest alone, money that produces nothing, builds nothing and simply vanishes. Extended across a decade of minimum payments, the total interest paid can exceed the original purchase several times over.

A 43-year-old high-earner drowning in debt posted his story on Reddit. Let’s call him Bill.

“On the outside, I probably look like a success. On the inside, I feel like I’m slowly breaking — just getting through one day at a time,” he wrote.

Him and his spouse carry close to $1 million in combined loans. Both work high-paying jobs. On paper, they look fine. In practice, their special-needs son’s therapy costs $3,000 a month. Before his diagnosis, that $3000 was the extra income they had planned to put towards paying down debt. These are the kind of curveballs life can throw at you. Out of nowhere, unannounced— thwack.

Bill tried his hand at several side businesses which failed and added more debt on top. He describes feeling trapped in a career he doesn’t enjoy with no visible exit.

Close to $1 million is debt may sound insane but in New York, D.C. or California, that number is an easy target. HCOL is no joke and Bill’s situation isn’t unique. Debt can be enticing even to the best of us.

Bill’s failure stems from the fact that he had thought nothing would ever go wrong and he would be able to pay off

the debt from the extra income. It was that years of “should be fine” income had never been forced into a written plan, so a single disruption ate the entire buffer.

That’s the sinkhole version of debt. It doesn’t look like reckless spending from the outside. It looks like a normal life that happens to be standing on ground with nothing underneath it.

Also read: Is Driving a Honda Smarter Than Flexing a Ferrari?

We love compound interest but not when it’s on the other side. Compound interest grows our savings the same way it grows balances— with indifferent efficiency.

Every month a balance carries over at 20%+ APR, that growth compounds against the borrower. Over 20 years, that comes out to 52.83x of the original number which could easily mean the difference between a paid-off house and a large credit card bill that never seems to shrink.

Every debt payment carries two costs. The first is obvious: the dollars leaving the account each month. The second almost never gets counted, because it never shows up anywhere: opportunity cost.

The cost of what you give up when your dollars go towards debt when they could’ve gone towards something profitable.

Consider a physician making aggressive payments on $215,000 in student loans during the first years as an attending.

Once the balance hits zero, that monthly cash flow can now go towards investment instead of paying a loan servicer. It can now be invested in index funds, a retirement account or a rental property that produces income instead of consuming it.

Also read: Building Wealth: Lessons In Sustainable Investment for Physicians

That’s what makes debt a double hit. Stretched across a 30-year investing timeline, missed growth frequently outweighs the interest itself, sometimes by a wide margin.

That’s why many advisors suggest building a straightforward financial foundation before reaching for anything advanced. Boring, broadly diversified investing beats clever debt-servicing strategies almost every time because it lets compounding start earlier instead of later.

The next time you sit down to fine-time your financial plan, consider the following:

Learn more: Is Diversification Finally Working Again?

After a decade of deferred spending, attending income brings much-need relief. But with it, comes the temptation to catch up all at once.

Those one-third of six-figure households that feel “stretched, struggling, or drowning” I mentioned earlier?

Their biggest downfall is precisely the fact that every income jump they are blessed with gets absorbed by a bigger house, a nicer car and a few thousand extra dollars a year in subscriptions and shopping. The brokerage accounts become the stepchildren that never get any love or attention.

Don’t be the evil stepmother. Do this instead:

Everyone takes stress as a given. As children we’re conditioned to worry about our homework and grades, as we grow older, we worry about fitting in, dating and winning the rat race.

The joys of parenthood are symbiotic with the worries of how to raise and protect our children in a world like ours. Being alive is, in essence, being stressed.

Debt adds in another layer of stress to all of that. But this is one we usually push away to the back of our minds so much so that it stops registering as stress at all.

Anyone carrying a meaningful balance knows what I’m talking about. Unexpected car repairs make us flinch. Due dates feel heavy but they arrive and we pay; then do it again the following month. Progress feels theoretical.

A systematic review of 39 U.S. studies found that debt is consistently linked to higher rates of stress and even suicide. The authors pointed to financial strain and the pressure of collection as the major drivers. Some debt, such as a mortgage, was labeled as “secure” which proves the point that not all debt is bad.

Another study reports that over-indebted consumers have lower life satisfaction and poorer health due to a diminished sense of control.

Eventually the discomfort becomes the baseline, and that’s when people take on more debt, because an actual plan to eliminate it no longer feels realistic.

Financing makes this worse by design. Nearly every major purchase now arrives with a monthly payment option built in, because a payment feels smaller than a price tag even when the total cost is higher.

47% of Buy Now, Pay Later users have been late on at least one loan in the past year. That percentage had been rising steadily, as it was 41% in 2025 and just 34% in 2024.

More alarmingly, 54% of consumers say that they wouldn’t be able to make ends meet without these loans. 29% say they use them to pay for groceries.

Financial well-being research consistently finds that experiences with debt and credit correlate directly with how secure people feel about their finances, independent of income.

So the relief once you’re on the other side? It’s exhilarating.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

A Gallup study found that among recent graduates, only 25% of those with more than $50,000 in debt were thriving financially compared to 40% of debt-free grads.

Physicians who’ve finished paying off credit cards or student loans, especially after years of aggressive payments alongside PSLF, will know what I’m talking about. The financial change is expected but the psychological weight lifting is what often catches you off guard.

If you want to experience that relief sooner rather than later, stick to aggressive repayment and steer clear of financing anything marketed by its monthly payment instead of its total cost.

Debt is sneaky like that. It can make you feel like you’re living your best life, doing better than ever— doing better than those around you. It’s a costly little dog and pony show.

Home equity products are the easiest way to explain this. A physician spends years building equity in a primary residence, then starts seeing offers to unlock that equity through a HELOC (home equity line of credit) or cash-out refinance for a kitchen remodel, debt consolidation, etc.

The homeowner is essentially being gaslit into converting equity that already belongs to them into a new long-term loan that accrues interest all over again.

These ventures can make sense in rare, high-planned situations tied to high-returns but not in cases where the motive is discretionary. Saving for a large purchase takes longer than financing it yes, but it also provides security which a new, bigger loan just cannot.

No matter how fancy it looks. Debt servicers know how to market their products well. They disguise shackles as flexibility, but really they’re coming for the wealth you’ve already built while claiming to make more for you.

Your home equity is your net worth, not spendable cash. Unless “unlocking it” funds something that generates income or measurable value.

A fee-only advisor is your best friend when it comes to dealing with offers for HELOC or cash-out refinancing. Before you decide anything, compare the total interest cost to how much you could save in 12–24 months for the same purchase before signing anything. The number might surprise you.

Debt is not a moral failing. Nobody builds a career in medicine— or anything for that matter,  without borrowing something along the way. But building wealth that lasts (preferably for generations) requires you to differentiate between good and bad debt.

Student loans, a reasonable mortgage and car payments aside, if you find yourself dreading the monthly payments you know will eat chunks out of your salary, maybe a new plan is what you’re missing.

If any of this hits close to home, you don’t have to figure it out alone. The PoF community is here to help. Drop a comment or take a look at the resources on our site made specifically for this.

And if you’ve already beaten your debt, I want to hear from you. What actually worked? What almost derailed you? Share your story in the comments. Someone reading this today is looking for proof it’s possible— you’re it.

The median for the class of 2025 was $215,000. That number doesn’t include undergraduate loans, so many physicians carry more once you add those in.

Yes. Almost nobody finishes medical school and residency debt free unless family money paid for it. The debt itself isn’t the red flag. What you do with your income once you start earning is.

Match your employer’s 401(k) contribution first, then pay off anything charging more than 6-7% interest. After that, split extra cash between debt and investing based on your rate.

Debt tied to something that produces income or builds equity. A mortgage or a loan on a rental property qualifies. A financed vacation or a car loan on something you can’t actually afford does not.

Yes, for those who qualify. Ten years of qualifying payments while working for a nonprofit or government employer wipes out the remaining balance. Confirm your employer and loan type qualify before counting on it.

As fast as possible. Average APR on carried balances sat at 22.15% in Q2 2026. At that rate, minimum payments can take over a decade and cost more in interest than the original purchase.

Absolutely. Over a third of people earning $200,000 or more report living paycheck to paycheck. Income buys options. Debt takes them away just as fast.

Rarely, unless the money goes toward something that generates income or real value. Most of the time it just converts equity you already own into a new loan with new interest.

I’m curious about your thoughts on alternative income streams outside of traditional practice—have you seen any success stories in that area? #8594. The Best Power Racks of 2025: Our Top Picks for Strength Training

Our expert shares his experience, and an Olympic lifting titleholder shares advice on choosing the best option so you get stronger with this home gym staple.

Written by Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Stephen Sheehan, CPT Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

A power rack allows you to safely perform weightlifting exercises like barbell squats and bench presses, without a spotter, in your home gym. Add-on accessories like pull-up bars, dip stations, and resistance bands can help you get the most out of your power rack, giving you the tools for a versatile full-body workout.

Whether you have limited space or are looking for a budget-friendly power rack, there are options that may work for you. We compiled a list of the best power racks for your home gym with all the details you need to find the right equipment to take your fitness routine to the next level in 2024. Shane Sevcik—a USAW-1 (USA Weightlifting) certified coach, current USA Weightlifting Foundation board member, state record holder, and Masters Pan American and World title holder—also shares his insights into what to look for in power racks.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

The REP Fitness PR-1000 Power Rack has a four-post frame made from 14-gauge steel with laser-cut holes spaced two inches apart. There are two pull-up bars—one is 1.25 inches thick, and the other is two inches thick—so you can do accessory work such as pull-ups and grip exercises without using additional space or buying a separate piece of equipment. The pull-up bars are strategically placed on the rack, spanning the front and back posts, contributing to the overall stability. There are built-in weight storage pegs on the back base for additional sturdiness. You can customize the rack using multiple accessory options such as safety straps, a dip station, and more.

Tester Brandon Lunsford, C.P.T., CF-L1, used this rack to do exercises like squats, bench press, strict press, pull-ups, and more for almost two years. He describes it as an intermediate or beginner rack and noticed movement while un-racking 350 pounds. “The rack held the weight just fine, but there was some swaying after I removed the bar. I’d recommend it to a beginner or someone who doesn’t lift to that capacity because I was happy with it otherwise.”

We like that the PR-1000 comes with chrome-coated safeties extending past the rack, offering an additional place for a barbell. The numbered uprights allow you to adjust the safeties or J-hooks quickly and never have to worry about your bar being crooked. “The J-hooks were easy to move, and the hole spacing of one inch is adequate to get the bar lined up where you need it,” Lunsford says. “I can attest to the functionality of the safeties; they worked great for me when I failed a heavy bench over 250 pounds.”

The Titan Fitness T-3 Series Power Rack is a wall-mounted power rack that folds to a closed position, which only sticks out five inches from the wall. The bolt-down uprights and side bracings keep it stable, so you feel comfortable lifting weights to 1,100 pounds. Those who want to use the dual pull-up bars for dynamic movements such as kipping pull-ups or toes-to-bar benefit from the added stability the floor attachment provides. The rear pull-up bar is two inches thick, and the front pull-up bar is the industry standard of 1.25 inches thick.

This rack is made from 11-gauge steel and features two-inch by three-inch tubing. Typically, newer racks have three-inch by three-inch steel tubing, so attachments from other brands may not work. Lunsford says, “A rack is an essential piece of fitness equipment. What sets them apart is the build, value, and accessories. A full power rack of this style with a weight capacity of 1,100 pounds for around $400 is an excellent bang for the buck.”

Lunsford says the brand uses manufacturing processes to elevate the overall quality. “The holes are laser cut instead of punched, and the brand uses robot welders instead of guides operated by humans.” This technique allows for more efficiency, precision, and consistency in enhanced craftsmanship. The laser-cut holes are two inches apart, and the bench and clean pull zone have Westside hole spacing—holes in the upright that are closer together for more precise positioning.

Free shipping is available on all Titan products, and a one-year warranty covers manufacturing defects and issues that may arise while using the product. One callout we have is the rack does not come with safety arms, which range in price from $90 to $190, depending on which type you get. The rackable weight capacity is 1,100 pounds, but the included J-cups are rated up to 1,000 pounds, so if you want to move heavier weights, you’ll need to upgrade the J-cups.

Titan offers several accessories for purchase separately, including safety bars or straps, stabilizer feet, spotter arms, pin and pipe safety set, or an extension kit to upgrade to six uprights. Other customization options include choosing from a black, red, or blue rack color, two rack depths and heights, or adding a four-pack of weight plate holders.

At only 72 inches tall (six feet), the REP PR-1050 Short Power Rack is a solution for home gyms with low ceilings, such as garages or basements. This equipment has a sturdy yet compact footprint of 58 by 48 inches and supports up to 700 pounds.

While this power rack is short, it provides a solid range of features. It comes with dual pull-up bars (supporting up to 400 pounds), numbered upright holes spaced two inches apart, rear base weight horns, chrome-coated safeties, and plastic-lined J-cups. It’s also compatible with various add-on attachments, including cannonball grips for grip strength exercises and landmine attachments for exercises including landmine presses and rows.

The Fringe Sport Retractable Power Rack is an excellent option if your garage or home gym is tight on space because it is compact and easily stored. This convenient home power rack can be retracted and folded inward or outward for storage. When retracted, it only sticks out five inches from the wall. It has a compact base and can support up to 800 pounds.

The uprights are two-by-three-inch 11-gauge steel and feature Westside spacing in the bench zone. You can set the rack’s 1.25-inch diameter pull-up bar to multiple heights. It’s 91 inches tall, which may not be ideal for low ceilings.

The unit comes with J-hooks coated with ultra-high molecular weight polyethylene (UHMW), a strong, abrasion-resistant material, to protect your barbell. Fringe Sport provides an installation video to help guide you through the installation of this power rack. It includes four mounting brackets and six detent pins to lock the rack in position.

The Sunny Health & Fitness Power Zone Strength Rack Power Cage Squat Rack has a pulley system attachment for lat pulldowns and adjustable resistance you can load with weight plates up to the 352-pound limit. You can use the lat pulldown attachment for exercises like upright rows and curls. When you aren’t using the attachment, built-in safety hook latches provide easy storage for the top long or short lever bar.

This power rack has features to help you get a well-rounded workout. The adjustable angled pull-up bar has four positions, including wide and narrow grips. The J-hooks have 18 vertical height settings, and the spotter bars with safety latches help you squat with heavier weights. There are six resistance band pins, for additional resistance against the bar.

The Rogue Fitness R-3 Power Rack is the most compact option in Rogue’s R-Series and is an excellent option for a home garage gym. This power rack comes in two height options—90.4 inches or 84.4 inches—so it works in garages and home gyms with low ceilings.

This rack is made of heavy-duty 11-gauge steel with Westside spacing (a type of spacing that allows for granular control of bar placement, such as barbells and safety bars) through the bench in a one-inch pattern and two-inch spacing above and below the bench. The unit is compatible with various Rogue Infinity Series add-on attachments, such as the Rogue Matador, fully adjustable dip handles, or a bar hanger for barbell weight storage.

The unit has a 43-inch pull-up bar, infinity J-cups, pin/pipe safeties, and four band pegs. You can customize this rack by adding a bar, bench, or plates to your purchase on the Rogue Fitness website. This unit is versatile enough for various exercises, including low rows, pull-ups, chin-ups, squats, bench presses, powerlifting, CrossFit, and Olympic lifting.

The Fitness Reality Squat Rack Power Cage has an official weight capacity of 800 pounds. This unit can help anyone hit their goals, from beginners to elite powerlifters.

Like all good squat racks, the Fitness Reality Squat Rack Power Cage has solid steel safety arms rather than hollow tubes. It features two rear stability bars. Thanks to 19 adjustable height levels, you can use the unit for various exercises besides squats, including pull-ups, chin-ups, bench presses, and overhead presses. And it’s $299, the most affordable option on our list.

It has a multi-grip pull-up bar and two 23-inch safety bars with chrome locks. While it doesn’t come with J-hooks, dip bars, or plate storage attachments, one-inch holes allow you to use this equipment with standard-sized attachments.

A power rack—or power cage—has four uprights designed to serve as a base for powerlifting, Olympic lifting, and other strength training. They are commonly used with a barbell but may have optional attachments for non-barbell exercises using cables or body weight. A full power rack allows athletes to lift inside or outside the cage. Half racks have two uprights, so athletes must lift outside the rack because there is less depth.

Research links strength training, including weightlifting, to long-term health benefits like reducing disease.

A power rack provides equipment, like safety bars, to help you lift heavy weights safely without a spotter. Some power racks come with add-on attachments, such as pull-up bars and dip bars, to help you get a well-rounded workout. Additionally, most power racks are compatible with accessories you can buy for an extra price to customize your workout for your needs.

Exercisers use a power rack for strength training, Olympic lifting, and powerlifting. Additional attachments, such as a dip station or pull-up bar, allow you to use it for bodyweight exercises. Some have pulley systems for other resistance exercises.

Correctly using a power rack can successfully enhance strength training. “It’s all about consistency,” Sevcik says. “Make sure you have some kind of progressive overload built into your programming.”

Power racks provide a safe lifting experience, which is of utmost importance, especially if you plan on training alone. The safety straps, pins, or arms—also called safeties—are a critical safety feature. “One of my biggest pet peeves is when I see people who don’t know how to set the safety arms the right way and have the pins set way too low,” Sevcik says. “The purpose of those safety arms is to give you a safe way to bail out of a lift. Otherwise, you’re just using a power rack as a big immobile squat stand.”

So, what is the correct way to set up the safety arms? “To set them up for squats, put the unloaded bar on your back and squat down to the deepest position you can get yourself into,” Sevcik says. “The safety bars should be about an inch and a half or one notch lower than your bottom position, so if you ever fail on a squat, all you do is sit your butt down to the very bottom.”

Many come with safety arms, pins, or nylon straps, but some budget options may require purchasing them separately. If you’re new to using a power rack, we recommend asking a fitness professional for guidance on different exercises and safety.

Before purchasing, measure your space and look at the rack’s total footprint. While measuring the floor and comparing it to the base is essential, ceiling height is another crucial factor. You may need a shorter option if you use your rack in a basement or a room with low ceilings.

You can retract and store a folding power rack if you’re limited in space or need room for other activities. It’s a good idea to consider your height and weight when looking at the dimensions, especially if you plan to use the pull-up bar or other attachments. You may want to leave space on each side for accessories so you can attach them on the sides if necessary. We recommend you keep the space around the rack clear of obstructions, particularly in front, so you can safely complete your lifts or bailout.

Power racks come in a variety of styles, colors, and materials. Some construction and style factors to consider include:

The power racks on this list have capacities ranging from 700 pounds to 1,100 pounds. The lower and middle weight range will likely work for you if you are a beginner or intermediate exerciser. If you are an advanced athlete, you may want to opt for a power rack with a high weight capacity and heavy-duty steel. Attachments such as safety arms, J-hooks, or pull-up bars have varying weight limits. Always stay within the recommended weight range for your safety.

How much you’re willing to spend depends on your budget and training style. Many racks on this list include a basic setup, with the option to add accessories as needed, which cuts the cost. Other racks come fully loaded with accessories, so they are incredibly versatile. However, these options cost more, so it is crucial to consider the features and whether or not they are helpful for your workout style and goals. The racks on this list range from around $299 to $965, and many brands offer free shipping.

Power racks come in various styles and features. The following sections break down Sevcik’s power rack must-haves.

Sevcik says to look for thick, heavy-duty steel such as 11-gauge. “A rack made out of thicker steel creates more leverage on the uprights. Especially when you add those attachments.”

“I think a big must-have a lot of people overlook is to make sure your J-cups, or J-hooks, have some coating on them to preserve the knurling on your bar,” Sevcik says. “If you’re doing a bench press or deadlift, [knurling] is no big deal, but if you’re an Olympic weightlifter, that’s where my snatch grip is holding onto, and I want it to be as sharp and aggressive as possible.”

“I would make sure you have enough hole patterns to make a lot of adjustments. Sometimes, they’re too spaced out, for example, in two-inch increments instead of one,” Sevcik says. “I like to have the added adjustability, especially for those heavier weights.”

Sevcik says having the option to do pull-ups is a good idea. “They’re one of the most basic, fundamental movements. Plus, if you dedicate the square footage to put the rack in there, you’ll want to get as much utility as possible because you are sacrificing some real estate.”

“It’s important to have the option to add accessories,” Sevcik says. “You might not want a dip bar right now, but down the road, you may decide to incorporate more dips in the training program, and it sure is nice to have your power rack as your one central piece of equipment.”

Many power racks come with attachments, though certain brands require you to purchase add-on attachments separately. Some of the power racks on this list come with pull-up bars (chin-up bar), safeties, and J-cups included, while others do not. It’s important to read the details of what comes with your unit to know what additional purchases you’ll need to make to achieve your desired power rack workout.

We considered the following while choosing each product on this list:

We chose budget-friendly and high-end options suitable for any fitness level and listed several compact and folding options for those with limited space. We also spoke to Shane Sevcik, a USAW-certified coach and competitive athlete, about essential add-ons and safety features.

Research suggests 30 to 60 minutes a week of muscle-strengthening exercises can benefit your health. With the help of a power rack, you can achieve a wide range of strength training fitness moves without needing a spotter. A power rack can add convenience to your workout by enabling you to get a safe weightlifting workout anytime from the comfort of your home gym.

A full power rack has four to six uprights attached by cross members, creating a cage to lift in. A squat rack—also called a squat stand—is typically two uprights and weighs less than a power rack, making it more portable. Power racks are more versatile, with the option to add accessories, while squat racks usually do not.

If you choose a freestanding power rack, anchor it following the manufacturer’s instructions to ensure it’s safe and secure.

Generally, a freestanding power rack should be a few feet from the wall so you can perform exercises comfortably and safely. Always refer to the manufacturer’s guidelines and recommendations when setting up your rack.

Common gauges are 11-gauge and 12-gauge, with lower numbers providing thicker and stronger steel; however, these tend to be more pricey options. A thinner 14-gauge steel is slightly less sturdy but likely works well for a general home gym setup. We chose racks ranging from 11-gauge to 16-gauge to suit various budgets and fitness levels.

#8593. A Top Sports Doctor Shares How Those Over 40 Can Still Train Like Elite Athletes

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

These days, many athletes play at the highest level past their late 30s and 40s. NBA icon LeBron James is still riding high at age 41, while Aaron Rogers continues to play great football at 42. Then there’s Serena and Venus Williams, who are still picking up the competitive tennis racket at 44 and 46 years respectively. In fact, there are countless examples of mature athletes who are dominating their field.

“Ah, but they have money, and coaches, and access to the best doctors,” you may argue. But would you be right? To find out, we asked a top doctor if physical longevity is reserved for the super-rich and famous. You may be surprised by what he shared.

“I think this is one of the biggest misconceptions about athletic longevity,” says Jordan D. Metzl, MD, who is a Sports Medicine Physician at Hospital for Special Surgery (HSS) in New York City. Dr. Metzl is also the bestselling author of titles including Running Strong and The Athlete’s Book of Home Remedies, not to mention being the founder of the IronStrength  fitness community, where he serves as an educator and advocate for exercise as medicine. Dr. Metzl is also pushing his own physical limits at 60. “Certainly, professional athletes have advantages that most of us don’t have, like access to personal trainers, nutritionists, physical therapists, sports scientists, physicians, and recovery specialists. They have people monitoring their training loads, sleep, nutrition, and performance. That level of support makes a difference. But the fundamental principles that allow these athletes to remain competitive are available to everyone.”

Rich or poor, famous or not, the drivers for longevity are broadly the same, shares Metzl. “The real secret is consistency,” he tells M&F. “Maintaining muscle mass, developing cardiovascular fitness, prioritizing sleep, eating well, and managing training loads are not exclusive to professional athletes. They are available to all of us.”

As we age, there are new challenges to overcome as relates to staying physically active. “I see a lot of tendon problems, particularly involving the Achilles tendon, patellar tendon, and rotator cuff,” says Metzl. “We also see plenty of knee arthritis, meniscus injuries, hamstring and calf strains, and stress injuries in bone. As people get older, the tissues that allow us to move and compete undergo biological changes. Tendons can become less tolerant of sudden increases in training load, muscle recovery may take longer, and cartilage changes can make certain activities more symptomatic. But I think it’s important to distinguish between getting older and becoming less capable. I see people in their 40s, 50s, 60s, and beyond doing extraordinary things.”

So, with all this in mind, how should we train to mitigate our maturity? “I think one of the biggest mistakes people make as they get older is assuming that they can train exactly the way they did when they were 25,” shares Metzl. “That doesn’t mean we need to stop running, playing tennis, skiing, or lifting weights. It just means we need to become smarter about preparation, progression, and recovery.”

Specifically, Metzl places a priority on the following training methods:

Metzl is also keen to point out the importance of high-quality sleep and nutrition, and making a habit of listening to what your body is telling you. “Pain that persists or progressively worsens is a signal worth investigating,” advises the medical professional. “Think about what professional athletes do. They train consistently, they work on strength and mobility, they pay attention to nutrition, and they prioritize recovery.”

“Athletes (like LeBron James) also understand that training at 40 is different from training at 20,” says Metzl. “They may modify their workloads, change their recovery schedules, and adjust their approach to competition. They are not necessarily doing more; they are doing things more intelligently. I think there is a tremendous lesson here for the public in that you don’t need LeBron’s resources to adopt his habits. You need consistency, discipline, and a willingness to adapt as your own body changes.”

If you’ve let your training lapse entirely, Metzl says that it’s never too late to make progress. “My advice is to start small and make exercise part of your daily life,” he explains. “If you haven’t exercised in years, don’t start by trying to run five miles or spend an hour in the gym. Start by walking for 10 or 15 minutes. Build from there. Add resistance training twice a week. Work on balance and mobility. Gradually increase the duration and intensity of your activity. The World Health Organization recommends 150 to 300 minutes of moderate-intensity aerobic activity each week, along with muscle-strengthening activity at least twice weekly. But I always remind people that something is better than nothing. Even short bursts of vigorous activity during the day can be beneficial. The most important thing is to get started. I often say that the best exercise program is the one you enjoy enough to keep doing. We don’t need everyone to become an athlete. We need everyone to become a little more active.

“One of the things I emphasize with my patients is that aging doesn’t mean you have to accept a steady decline in physical function. We lose muscle, strength, and aerobic capacity as we get older, but much of that decline is modifiable. The goal isn’t necessarily to compete with LeBron James. It’s to be the strongest, healthiest, most capable version of yourself at every age. Longevity is not about having the most expensive recovery equipment. It’s about doing the right things consistently over decades. I am still running marathons and doing triathlons, and I have changed the way that I train and compete over time. But I’m still out there and plan to be for years to come!”

Dr Metzl’s latest book, PUSH: Unlock the Science of Fitness Motivation to Embrace Health and Longevity is out now.

The scariest thing on a physician’s desk this October is the fourth-quarter estimated tax worksheet, propped against a 403(b) statement that hasn’t moved since spring.

Most retirement articles are written for someone worried about running out of money. You should worry about that too. On top of it, you carry a problem the average saver never meets: a tax code that takes 37 cents of every married dollar above $768,700, trims your itemized deductions once you get there, shrinks your SALT break somewhere past $505,000, and reaches two years backward to set your Medicare premiums.

Every mistake on this list costs a little more in that bracket.

This list is built for physicians with six figures before the comma, including those who collect some or all of it on a 1099.

Physicians are one of the few groups positioned to collect the maximum Social Security benefit, because most of you clear the taxable wage base ($184,500 in 2026) months before December. That makes claiming age a bigger lever for you than for almost anyone.

According to AARP, a worker at the 2026 maximum who files at 62 collects about $2,969 a month; the same worker gets $4,152 at full retirement age and roughly $5,181 by holding out until 70. Claiming early trims the benefit permanently (5/9 of 1% per month for the first 36 months, 5/12 of 1% per month beyond that), and every year you wait past full retirement age adds 8%.

Dr. Addams claimed at 62 because he “wanted the money while the government still had it.” Six months later he picked up locums shifts at $200 an hour. Before full retirement age, Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480, so his own paycheck ate his benefit. (Social Security credits some of that back at full retirement age, but the cash-flow plan he built was toast.) Semi-retired physicians are exactly the people who keep earning after they file.

Two other quirks hit doctors harder. The formula averages your 35 highest-earning years, and residency plus a late start can leave early retirees with zeros in that average; the bend points in the formula soften the blow for high earners, but pull your record at ssa.gov before assuming anything.

If you’re married, the higher earner’s claiming age also sets the survivor benefit, so delaying to 70 works like inflation-adjusted life insurance for your spouse at a price no insurer will match.
