After taking Neat Apparel to the Shark Tank stage, entrepreneur Jim Huffman is betting on performance-driven apparel, smarter marketing, and the power of consistency. But his biggest motivation goes far beyond building a nine-figure brand.

Sweat is practically a badge of honor in fitness. It represents the final rep, the last sprint, the extra mile, and the work that happens long before anyone sees the results. For athletes and gym-goers, it’s part of the process.

As legendary soccer star Mia Hamm once put it, “The vision of a champion is bent over, drenched in sweat, at the point of exhaustion, when nobody else is looking.”

But while sweat might be a welcome sign of hard work in the gym, it’s not always something people want showing through their clothes.

For entrepreneur Jim Huffman, that everyday frustration presented an opportunity to rethink an overlooked wardrobe staple.

That opportunity became Neat Apparel, a performance-driven clothing company built around technology designed to prevent sweat from showing through clothing. Now, following an appearance on ABC’s Shark Tank, Huffman is looking to take the brand to an entirely new level.

The idea wasn’t necessarily born from a lifelong ambition to build an apparel company. Instead, it came down to recognizing a familiar consumer problem, understanding the potential of a differentiated product, and seeing an opportunity to apply his experience in business growth to something of his own.

Huffman is also the founder of GrowthHit, a growth marketing agency specializing in helping businesses scale. After spending years developing strategies and building growth systems for other companies, he began looking for an opportunity to put those same principles to work on a business of his own.

Neat presented an interesting proposition: a product with a clear point of differentiation, a problem consumers could immediately recognize, and technology that could demonstrate its value without requiring a lengthy explanation.

And while the business opportunity is compelling, his perspective on sweat extends beyond the product itself. In a world where fitness culture celebrates visible effort, Neat is built around a different side of the experience: helping people feel comfortable and confident whether they’re training, working, traveling, or navigating everyday life.

For Huffman, the challenge now is turning a product built around a relatable problem into a brand that can reach a much bigger audience.

And perhaps that’s where the connection between entrepreneurship and fitness becomes most apparent: Both demand consistency, a willingness to embrace challenges, and the ability to keep showing up when the results aren’t immediate.

After all, if sweat is proof that you’ve put in the work, why should it determine how confident you feel walking out of the gym?

Neat’s story began with technology originally developed through performance apparel research, with applications being explored for sports and military uniforms.

Huffman’s business partner, Tyler, had connections to the performance apparel industry, where the team was working with emerging fabric technologies. Through that process, they encountered intellectual property that eventually became the foundation for Neat.

The challenge was finding the right consumer application.

As Huffman explained, the technology had initially been considered for soccer, but the team recognized that athletes weren’t necessarily concerned about visible sweat during competition. The opportunity was to bring that technology to consumers who wanted to stay comfortable and presentable throughout the day.

Huffman became familiar with the product through his work with the apparel team. Having grown up in Oklahoma and spent time in Texas, he understood the frustration of trying to look presentable in hot weather.

“I used to have go in the bathroom and pat my shirt off to look somewhat presentable,” he recalled.

After receiving a sample, his reaction was immediate.

Rather than immediately jumping into the business, Huffman took a more calculated approach. He spoke with approximately 20 existing customers to understand whether the product had genuine demand.

The response was encouraging. Customers weren’t simply complimenting the shirts. They were asking the company not to go out of business, requesting additional colors, and wanting more products.

For an entrepreneur focused on growth, that feedback was important.

It suggested that Neat wasn’t just a clever product looking for an audience. It had an audience that was already looking for more.

One of Neat’s biggest advantages is that its technology can be demonstrated visually.

In an increasingly crowded apparel market, simply telling consumers that a shirt is different isn’t necessarily enough. Huffman understood that the company needed to show people why it was different.

The brand’s creative approach includes demonstrations that make the product’s purpose immediately recognizable, including videos featuring water balloons and fabric tests.

“We wanted to hit on not just the benefit but the use case,” Huffman explained.

That thinking also inspired one of the company’s more memorable marketing concepts: a wall of sweat-soaked shirts, displayed almost like a sports memorabilia exhibit.

Rather than relying on traditional product photography, the campaign allowed consumers to see the problem Neat was attempting to solve.

Neat isn’t necessarily asking consumers to abandon their favorite athletic brands. It’s asking them to consider another factor when choosing what to wear: how their clothing performs when temperatures rise.

Appearing on Shark Tank brought Neat to a much larger audience, but Huffman understands that television exposure is only one part of building a sustainable business.

The company’s next challenge is turning that attention into long-term growth.

Huffman has already seen how marketing decisions can dramatically affect a company’s ability to scale. Through GrowthHit, he’s worked with businesses across different stages of development, and those experiences have shaped how he approaches Neat.

One of the biggest lessons he’s learned is that businesses need to understand their market before investing heavily in growth.

“Honestly, it’s market selection,” he said. “I think people are like, ‘Oh, this thing’s cool. Let me see if I can sell it.’ And they’re not intentional of, is this a market that in five to 10 years is going up and to the right?”

He believes that even an excellent product can struggle when it’s introduced to a market that isn’t willing to pay for it.

His second consideration is the business’s financial model.

When Huffman and his team became involved with Neat, the shirts were selling for approximately $38. But the existing pricing structure made it difficult to support the advertising costs required to grow the company.

The team shifted its approach toward bundles and discounts designed to increase average order value, while also adjusting pricing.

The goal wasn’t simply to sell more individual shirts. It was to establish Neat as a wardrobe staple that consumers would purchase repeatedly.

“We’re trying to villainize the cotton T-shirt,” Huffman joked.

He clarified that the company isn’t against cotton. Rather, it’s trying to educate consumers about the difference between an everyday cotton shirt and a performance-driven option designed to stay with them throughout the day.

Huffman’s experience also reflects a broader shift in how fitness and lifestyle brands connect with consumers.

Traditional advertising still has its place, but polished production doesn’t automatically translate into stronger performance.

Neat discovered this firsthand after investing approximately $30,000 in a high-production video that failed to perform as well as expected.

Meanwhile, simpler creator-produced videos featuring the product generated stronger results.

“Our best performing ads are not the fancy overproduced ads,” Huffman said. “We spent $30,000 on a high production video, did not perform as well as I liked, and then we’ll throw a T-shirt at some 20-something, and they make an ad that really scales for us.”

That experience pushed the company toward user-generated content, influencers, and creators who could demonstrate the product in a more natural environment.

The approach makes sense for Neat because the product is inherently visual. Consumers want to see how it works, how it fits, and how it performs in everyday situations.

Huffman also recognizes that different social platforms require different strategies. TikTok audiences may respond to quick demonstrations and impulse-driven purchases, while Meta platforms can support a different consumer journey.

The lesson is that successful marketing isn’t necessarily about producing the most expensive content. It’s about understanding the audience and communicating the product’s value in a way that resonates.

While Neat’s growth and its Shark Tank appearance have brought Huffman plenty of professional excitement, his definition of success has changed considerably over the past year.

During the interview, Huffman shared the deeply personal experience that led him and his team to establish the Wrenegade Fund, an initiative supporting pediatric cancer research.

In May, his youngest daughter, Wren, began complaining of what initially appeared to be growing pains. Knowing that she was a tough child who rarely complained, the family decided to take her to the hospital.

The following day, they received devastating news: Wren had a rare form of bone cancer.

The diagnosis came at an especially demanding time for the family. Huffman had recently become involved with Neat, the business had taken on significant financial commitments, and the company was preparing for a major order.

Suddenly, the priorities that had once dominated his attention looked very different.

“You’re just like, how am I going to do all of this, right?” he recalled. “And so that’s where you really figure out real quick what you need to focus on and not what really matters.”

Wren underwent 23 rounds of chemotherapy and a life-changing amputation surgery known as rotationplasty.

Today, Huffman describes her as stronger than ever.

Her experience also inspired the family to turn an incredibly difficult chapter into an opportunity to help other children facing similar diagnoses. Through GrowthHit, the team began donating 1% of its profits to pediatric cancer research. They also launched the Wrenegade Fund to make supporting research a larger part of their mission.

In September, the family organized a fundraiser called “Pie Hard,” raising $60,000. For every $1,000 raised, Wren earned the opportunity to throw a pie in someone’s face.

The event brought a little humor into a mission rooted in something much bigger.

Huffman also shared how the family’s openness about Wren’s experience connected them with other families navigating similar circumstances.

One particularly meaningful connection involved a young girl in Montana who had been following Wren’s story. She was facing a difficult decision about surgery and learned about rotationplasty through Wren’s experience.

The families eventually met, and the girl was able to pursue the same procedure.

For Huffman, those moments have become a reminder of how much impact one family’s willingness to share its story can have on another.

“If there’s  an exit with this, it’s like pouring that money into pediatric cancer research,” he said of his long-term business ambitions. It’s a mission that gives the company’s growth a different kind of purpose.

For an entrepreneur balancing a marketing agency, an apparel company, and family life, consistency is essential. But Huffman’s approach to fitness is less about chasing an impressive physique and more about maintaining the mental clarity required to lead.

He currently completes three to four 30-minute HIIT workouts each week, usually at 6:15 in the morning.

“If I do it any time afternoon, I’m too tired and lazy and I won’t do it,” he admitted.

Getting his workout in early helps establish momentum before the demands of the day take over.

More importantly, he notices a difference in his mood and leadership when he maintains the routine.

“I am in such a better mood and a better leader when I get that going,” he said. “If I skip my workout, I’m probably a grump.”

It’s a familiar challenge for anyone trying to balance work, training, and personal responsibilities. Huffman’s solution isn’t necessarily complicated. He plans his workouts around his calendar and accepts that some weeks won’t go perfectly.

He also credits his wife, who works at Amazon and maintains her own fitness routine, with helping establish healthy habits at home.

“Partner selection is so crucial to this,” he explained.

For Huffman, having a partner who prioritizes fitness makes consistency easier. He also recognizes that maintaining a healthy relationship is essential to keeping his focus on the things that matter.

A demanding professional life can quickly become overwhelming when personal relationships suffer. Having someone who understands the ups and downs of entrepreneurship, supports the risks, and provides perspective has been invaluable.

His approach to fitness mirrors his approach to business: small, consistent actions can compound into something much bigger.

“We all know it’s like you need to be the 10-year overnight success where these small things compound,” he said. “That’s what works with fitness. That’s what works with diet. That’s what works with business.”

Huffman’s ambitions for Neat are substantial.

He wants to build the company into a recognizable household brand, beginning with men’s apparel before expanding into additional markets and product categories.

That could eventually include women’s apparel, wholesale opportunities, and international expansion. The company is also exploring additional styles, including polos, henleys, long sleeves, and potentially underwear.

For now, however, Huffman is resisting the temptation to expand too quickly.

“Shiny object syndrome is something I suffer from, and that can hurt a lot of businesses,” he said.

His immediate priority is to meet demand for the existing men’s collection, continue improving the product, and build a strong foundation before moving into new categories.

When asked what advice he would give someone entering the apparel industry, he emphasized two things: understand your customer and establish a genuine point of differentiation.

“Don’t be afraid to go smaller rather than bigger. Niche down because I think that’s where the future is going,” he said.

He also believes businesses need something more defensible than a recognizable brand name alone. For Neat, its underlying patent and product technology provide a point of differentiation that helps separate it from competitors.

Ultimately, Huffman isn’t measuring his success solely by revenue milestones, television appearances, or the possibility of building a nine-figure company.

When asked about his greatest accomplishment, his answer had little to do with business.

“It’s just like having a family that is along for the ride and loves being together with all of this,” he said.

He explained that he’s seen how professional success can sometimes come at the expense of family relationships, something he has no interest in sacrificing.

“It’s not a sexy answer, but it’s just like the biggest success is the little family we built.”

For an entrepreneur who has spent much of his career helping businesses grow, that may be the most important lesson of all: Success isn’t just about how far you can take a company. It’s about what you’re building along the way, who you’re building it with, and what you ultimately want that success to accomplish.

Taxes may be the last thing on your mind right now. The kids are studying for mid-terms and the holidays are almost upon us. But with less than 3 months left in 2026, you have a small window to implement strategies to minimize your tax bill for 2027.

According to Medscape’s 2026 compensation report, physicians earn, on average, $386,000 a year. Primary care physicians earn $298,000 and specialists make, on average, $417,000.

In 2026, a single filer’s taxable income of $256,225 puts them in the 35% bracket. Same for an income of $512,450 MFJ (married filing jointly). The 37% bracket starts above $640,600 for singles and $768,700 for couples.

The One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) made permanent many provisions that had been scheduled to expire after 2025. It also added limits and phaseouts that affect higher earners specifically. In this guide, I’ll cover the changes that matter to physicians and what you can do before the year is up.

You can’t always choose when you receive income but some form of income like bonuses, self-employment income, Treasury bill income, and voluntary retirement distributions can be timed to reduce your tax bill for 2026.

Deferring income means you receive it in 2027 instead of 2026, and thus pay the tax a year later. Accelerating work in the opposite way. You can also defer or accelerate deductions to either lower this year’s bill or leave it on the table for next year.

If your employer pays a $20,000 bonus on Dec. 20, it counts as 2026 income. If your employer pays it on Jan. 5, it counts as 2027 income. At a 35% rate, that single date change delays $7,000 of federal tax by a full year.

If you expect to be in the same bracket with lower rates next year, you can defer the bonus. If you think you’ll be in a higher bracket next year, go ahead and take it in 2026.

According to this comprehensive guide by Plante Moran, pushing income into 2027 and pulling deductible expenses into 2026 delays tax, which usually helps. A higher bracket next year means you should take the opposite approach because you pay tax on 2026 income at your lower current rate.

If you’re starting as an attending in 2027, you fit the second group. Taking taxable gains or converting pre-tax IRA money to Roth this year will cost you less than doing it after your pay jumps.

Learn more: The Best Time for Roth Conversions May Be Now

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Employed physicians don’t have much control but ask your group whether it can pay a year-end bonus in January. Locums and 1099 physicians can, however, control invoicing and equipment purchases.

Check your Alternative Minimum Tax (AMT) exposure before you defer anything. AMT works like a second tax calculation.

First, you calculate your regular tax, then, you recalculate with certain deductions added back, including your SALT deduction. Then you subtract an AMT exemption, which in 2026, is $90,100 for single filers and $140,200 for joint filers. You then must pay whichever tax is higher.

The OBBBA shrank that exemption for high earners in 2026. It starts the reduction at $500,000 of AMTI for singles and $1,000,000 for couples. It then cuts the exemption by 50 cents for every dollar above those thresholds.

The exemption disappears at $680,200 for singles and $1,280,400 for couples.

All that is to say that each extra $1,000 of income inside the phaseout range costs you $500 of exemption, so $1,500 becomes taxable at 28%. That equals a 42% marginal rate, which beats the 37% top regular rate.

Once the exemption disappears, your marginal AMT rate drops to 28%. Estimate your marginal rate for 2026 and 2027, then move income toward the lower-rate year.

Your employer withholds the additional 0.9% Medicare tax only on wages above $200,000, regardless of your filing status or your spouse’s pay. The tax itself applies above $250,000 for joint filers.

Two married physicians who each earn $300,000 have an employer who starts withholding the extra 0.9% Medicare tax once that physician’s pay passes $200,000. Each physician has $100,000 above that line, so each employer withholds $900. Together, the couple has $1,800 withheld.

With a combined wages of $600,000 the joint cutoff is $250,000, so the couple owes 0.9% of the rest of the $350,000. That’s $3,150. After subtracting the $1,800 withheld by the employers, the  couple owes $1,350 more when they file.

You can raise your W-4 withholding before Dec. 31 to cover it. This will require you to submit a new W-4 to your employer and enter the extra amount per paycheck in Step 4(c).

Withholding counts as paid evenly across the year so it beats a late estimated payment. Penalty protection requires payments of at least 90% of your 2026 tax or 110% of your 2025 tax. The 100% safe harbor covers only taxpayers with 2025 AGI of $150,000 or less, which rules out most attendings.

The annualized income installment method helps when income skews toward year-end, as locums and bonus income often do.

The 3.8% net investment income tax (NIIT) starts at $200,000 of MAGI for single filers and $250,000 for joint filers.

Those thresholds have stayed the same since 2013, so every raise adds more of your investment income into the tax. Anything that lowers MAGI, including retirement contributions and HSA deposits, lowers your NIIT too.

The IRS raised the 2026 employee limit for 401(k), 403(b) and governmental 457 plans to $24,500. Catch-up contributions add $8,000 at age 50 or older, for a total of $32,500.

There’s also a bonus catch-up of $11,250 for ages 60 to 63, which brings the total to $35,750. If your hospital also offers a governmental 457(b), that plan carries its own limit of $24,500.

SECURE 2.0 now requires employees who earned more than $150,000 in 2025 wages to direct catch-up contributions to Roth accounts. That’s all attendings. If your plan offers no Roth option, you can’t make 2026 catch-up contributions at all.

Direct Roth IRA contributions phase out between $153,000 and $168,000 for single filers and between $242,000 and $252,000 for joint filers.

Employed physicians can contribute $7,500 to a nondeductible traditional IRA and convert it. This works best when neither spouse has funds in a traditional IRA, and you owe tax only on growth between the contribution and the conversion.

A pre-tax IRA balance makes part of the conversion taxable, so roll it into your 401(k) before Dec. 31 if your plan accepts rollovers.

Practice owners have bigger options. A profit-sharing plan allows total contributions of $72,000, or $80,000 with catch-up, or $83,250 at ages 60 to 63.

A SEP allows $72,000 and requires at least $360,000 of self-employment income before the deduction.

A defined benefit plan can allow larger deductible contributions than either, depending on your age and target benefit. The 2026 maximum is $290,000 or 100% of your highest 3-year average earned income, whichever is lower.

Self-employed physicians can set up a plan and make 2026 contributions as late as the tax return due date, including extensions. If you have employees, you likely must let them participate.

Also read: Backdoor Roth IRA 2026: A Step by Step Guide with Vanguard

For 2026, the HSA limits are $4,400 for self-only coverage and $8,750 for family coverage, plus $1,000 at age 55 or older. Contributions reduce AGI and qualified withdrawals come out tax-free. A family contribution of $8,750 can save you about $3,063 in federal tax at a 35% rate.

A health FSA is limited to $3,400 and you can carry over up to $680 of unused funds to 2027. The dependent care FSA limit rose to $7,500 from $5,000, which saves you $2,625 at a 35% rate. Those contributions reduce the expenses you can claim for the child and dependent care credit.

Today’s relatively low rates raise the odds that your retirement rate will be higher.

Permanent rates have no expiration date but Congress can still raise them. Converting in chunks over several years keeps each year’s income from jumping into a higher bracket. But a Roth conversion adds to your taxable income in the year you convert so confirm you can pay the tax from outside the IRA.

Early-retired and part-time physicians must now deal with expiration of the enhanced premium tax credit. This means that the ACA cliff now applies to them.

If you earn $1 above 400% of the poverty line, you lose all marketplace subsidies. The threshold is $62,600 for a single person and $129,000 for a family of 4 in 2026.

Tommy Lucas, a CFP at Moisand Fitzgerald Tamayo recommends pairing a high-deductible plan with HSA contributions, which lower your AGI.

Two new rules have reduced the value of itemized gifts.

A 0.5% of AGI floor is now in effect which means a physician with $500,000 of AGI can’t deduct the first $2,500 of donations.

The OBBBA also caps the tax benefit at 35 cents per dollar for filers in the 37% bracket.

Bunching charitable giving can fix most of the floor issue. The floor applies once per year, so 5 years of $10,000 gifts at $500,000 of AGI forfeit $2,500 each year and leave $37,500 deductible.

One $50,000 gift forfeits $2,500 once and leaves $47,500 deductible. The extra $10,000 saves $3,500 at a 35% rate.

Charissa Anderson, a CFP at Ferguson Wellman Capital Management, says that bunching works best when you pair a donor-advised fund with appreciated stock. A donor-advised fund lets you make 1 large gift now and send grants to charities over time.

Plante Moran warns that you should get written acknowledgment that the sponsoring organization holds exclusive legal control of the assets.

If you itemize, shares held for more than 1 year before donating let you deduct full market value and skip the capital gains tax you’d pay otherwise. Most physicians pay 15% on long-term gains plus the 3.8% NIIT, which totals 18.8%.

Physicians with taxable income above $545,500 (single) or $613,700 (joint) pay 20% plus the NIIT, which totals 23.8%. If you donate $50,000 of shares with a $20,000 basis, you can avoid up to $5,640 at 18.8% or $7,140 at 23.8% of the $30,000 gain.

The deduction is capped at 30% of AGI for public charities and you can carry the excess forward 5 years.

Donors can use tax lot selection, as in choosing which specific shares to give. Lots with the largest gains usually make the best candidates. Never donate shares that trade below your basis. Sell them, claim the loss and donate the cash.

Physicians who take the standard deduction ($16,100 single, $32,200 joint) can now deduct up to $1,000 of cash gifts or $2,000 for couples. A couple in the 35% bracket can save $700.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Physicians aged 70 1⁄2 or older can send up to $111,000 from an IRA directly to charity in 2026. That transfer counts toward required minimum distributions and steers clear of taxable income.

For 2026, the SALT cap is $40,400. As your MAGI exceeds $505,000, the cap drops by 30 cents for every extra dollar.

A couple with $550,000 of MAGI have an excess of $45,000. The cap drops by 30% of $45,000, which is $13,500. Their cap falls from $40,400 to $26,900. As your MAGI approaches $606,333, the cap reaches its $10,000 minimum. Above that, it stays at $10,000.

If your 2026 state and local taxes will fall short of the cap, prepay your 2027 property tax bill by Dec. 31. Your county needs to have assessed the bill already.

Plante Moran estimates a single filer in the 35% bracket saves $14,140 by deducting the full $40,400. Check your AMT first, though. A large SALT deduction can trigger it. You also need enough total itemized deductions to beat your standard deduction.

The Section 199A deduction is permanent and equals up to 20% of qualified business income.

Medicine counts as a specified service business, so as your income increases, the deduction gets smaller before eventually disappearing.

The 2026 phase ranges from $201,750 to $276,750 for single filers, with double those amounts for joint filers. Part-time physicians, lower-earning specialties and couples with taxable income below $553,500 can still claim some deduction. Retirement contributions that lower your taxable income can pull you back into the range.

S corporation owners can take part of their income as distributions instead of salary, which avoids payroll taxes and the 0.9% Medicare tax. The IRS scrutinizes this closely, so make sure your salary is reasonable.

The OBBBA also lowered the cap on business losses that offset other income to $256,000 for single filers and $512,000 for joint filers in 2026. Rental income and losses count as passive unless you qualify as a real estate professional.

That status requires more than half of your personal services and more than 750 hours in property businesses. Special rules can help spouses meet material participation.

Equipment buyers can deduct 100% of the cost of qualifying property in the first year through bonus depreciation. This applies to property you acquire after Jan. 19, 2025. Section 179 expensing reached $2.56 million in 2026 and phases out above $4.09 million of purchases.

The equipment must be placed in service by Dec. 31.

Dec. 31 for most moves, including charitable gifts, payroll retirement deferrals and property tax prepayments. Self-employed physicians can set up and fund a retirement plan until the 2026 return due date, including extensions.

Add up your deductions and pick the larger amount. The standard deduction is $16,100 for single filers and $32,200 for joint filers. Itemize when your SALT, mortgage interest and charitable gifts exceed it.

Defer if you expect the same or a lower tax rate next year. Accelerate if you expect a higher one. A fellow who starts as an attending in 2027 fits the second group.

It is 0.9% of wages above $200,000 for single filers and above $250,000 for joint filers. Employers start withholding at $200,000 regardless of your filing status, so couples often owe extra when they file.

Pay at least 90% of your 2026 tax or 110% of your 2025 tax. Raise your W-4 withholding before Dec. 31 to cover any shortfall.

You can contribute $24,500 to a 401(k), 403(b) or governmental 457 plan. Add $8,000 at age 50 or older. Ages 60 to 63 can add $11,250 instead.

Employees who earned more than $150,000 in 2025 wages must make catch-up contributions to Roth accounts. If your plan has no Roth option, you can’t make 2026 catch-up contributions.

Direct contributions phase out between $153,000 and $168,000 for single filers and between $242,000 and $252,000 for joint filers. Most physicians use a backdoor Roth, which converts a nondeductible traditional IRA contribution of up to $7,500.

It affects early-retired and part-time physicians who buy marketplace coverage. Earn $1 above 400% of the poverty line and you lose all subsidies. CNBC reports the 2026 threshold at about $63,000 for a single person.

The cap is $40,400. It drops by 30 cents for every dollar of MAGI above $505,000 and bottoms out at $10,000 at about $606,333.

Often only in part. Medicine counts as a specified service business, so the deduction phases out between $201,750 and $276,750 of taxable income for single filers and disappears above that. Joint filers get double those amounts.

The 0.5% of AGI floor applies once per year, so one large gift loses less than several small ones. At $500,000 of AGI, a $50,000 gift saves $3,500 more than 5 yearly gifts of $10,000 at a 35% rate.

Yes. If you itemize and held the shares for more than 1 year, you deduct full market value and avoid the capital gains tax you’d owe on a sale. Donate publicly traded shares directly to the charity or donor-advised fund.

Yes. A CPA who knows your state and practice structure can model your return for you before you act.

The bonus-timing example is concrete: a $20,000 bonus paid Dec. 20 lands in 2026 wages, while a Jan. 5 pay date pushes the same dollars into 2027 and, at a 35% marginal rate, delays about $7,000 of federal tax for a year. Pairing that with the 2026 HSA ceilings ($4,400 self-only / $8,750 family, plus $1,000 catch-up at 55+) and the checklist on accelerating or deferring deductions gives employed physicians a short year-end punch list even when W-2 wages themselves are inflexible.

#8570. The Strongest Pre-Workout Powders to Fuel Your Training in 2025

We tested more than 80 pre-workouts and chose the strongest ones to enhance your physical and mental performance.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Mar 4, 2025

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Whether you’re starting your fitness journey or you’re a weightlifting junkie, there are several supplements that should be staples in your stack. As a certified personal trainer and nutrition coach, I’d put a high-quality whey protein powder and one of the best creatines at the top.

Not far behind would be another supplement that can help you achieve your muscle-building and weight-loss goals: pre-workout.

However, just like not all barbells are created equal, neither are supps. The strongest pre-workouts stand out from the pack because they are formulated with research-backed doses of four key ingredients — caffeine (at least 200 milligrams), L-citrulline (at least 4,000 milligrams), beta-alanine (at least 3,200 milligrams), and betaine (at least 2,500 milligrams) — for physical and mental performance enhancement.

To save you the trouble of sipping on something that won’t give you an effective muscle pump, our team of expert product testers tried more than 80 pre-workouts and reported which supplements delivered the most focus, power, and tingles. Then, with some guidance from a few other experts, our squad of CPTs, CNCs, CrossFit enthusiasts, and dedicated weightlifters narrowed down the list to the eight strongest pre-workouts so you can select the perfect match for your goals and preferences.

Medical disclaimer: This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If your goal is to improve your athletic performance and power output in the gym, then we recommend Transparent Labs BULK BLACK. This supplement contains a potent combination of 4,000 milligrams of beta-alanine, 2,500 milligrams of betaine anhydrous, and 10 other active ingredients. Beta-alanine, a nonessential amino acid, may improve potential power output by reducing muscle fatigue, allowing you to push out a few more reps while you exercise. And studies show betaine anhydrous may improve muscular endurance. These ingredients work together to enhance your training, paving the way for strength gains over time.

Each serving of BULK BLACK also contains 350 milligrams of caffeine, which is close to the recommended daily limit of 400 milligrams. Overall, the impressive formulation earns 4 out of 5 stars from our team, as we docked a point for the high caffeine content since it may be too intense for some people.

However, this high-stim pre-workout is certainly effective.

Cory Kessler, C.P.T., C.F.N.C., has tried more than 25 pre-workouts. He tested the Blue Raspberry flavor of BULK BLACK before a cardio workout, noting that he felt more energized and focused throughout his workout. “I started sweating almost immediately, and within five to 10 minutes, I had a boost of energy, a massive pump, and felt like I could lift harder and stronger,” he says. Cory also experienced the tingling sensation common with high doses of beta-alanine.

Cory also enjoys using BULK BLACK before bodybuilding workouts since it contains 8,000 milligrams of citrulline malate. While more research is needed, some studies suggest citrulline malate may boost exercise and muscular performance.

Two other areas where BULK BLACK stands out: solubility and taste. Our team gave Transparent Labs perfect scores in both categories.

“BULK BLACK completely dissolved in my shaker bottle in only a few seconds with no clumps, grittiness, or residue,” Cory says.

Available in eight flavors ranging from Black Cherry to Watermelon Peach to Strawberry Mango, one of our other product testers chose the Blue Raspberry option, giving it 5 out of 5 stars for taste. However, there are some mixed reviews on Amazon about the taste, depending on which flavor you choose.

“It’s hard to describe the taste of Blue Raspberry, but that’s exactly what it tastes like. Not too sweet, which is a good thing,” he says.

Related: Transparent Labs BCAA Glutamine Review

Legion Pulse is our pick for the strongest natural pre-workout because it’s free from artificial sweeteners, flavors, and colors and contains six active ingredients that support enhanced energy.

As a CPT and CNC, I look for four main ingredients in a high-quality pre-workout supplement: caffeine, beta-alanine, betaine anhydrous, and L-citrulline. Each plays a key role in enhancing athletic performance. Research shows:

Legion Pulse contains all four, including 350 milligrams of caffeine per serving, which is very close to the recommended daily limit of 400 milligrams. Keep in mind that if you decide to try Pulse, it’s a good idea to monitor your caffeine intake from other sources like coffee or tea.

“To get the most out of pre-workout supplements without stomach issues, start with a lower dose to see how your body reacts,” says Dr. Christopher Mohr, Ph.D., RD. “Choose supplements with fewer stimulants if caffeine bothers you, or go for stimulant-free options.”

Luckily, if you’re new to pre-workout or are caffeine-sensitive, you can also choose the non-stim version of Pulse. So, even though we’d like to see creatine in the formulation, we still give this a strong score of 4 out of 5 stars, especially since there’s a caffeine-free version.

One of our product testers has tried five different brands of pre-workout and puts Pulse atop her list because of its effectiveness.

“I’ve been using Pulse three times a week for six months, and it always makes me feel energized and focused,” our tester says. “My goal is to improve my personal records and lift harder, so Pulse is my go-to when I train.”

She reports that it typically takes 15 minutes for this high-stim pre-workout to kick in, and while it does give her tingles, it’s not overwhelming. “I never feel a drop-off, but rather a slow energy release,” she says.

Pulse comes in 22 flavors, including Pink Lemonade, Cherry Limeade, and Strawberry Kiwi, so there’s something to satisfy everyone’s taste buds. That said, one of our testers gave Pulse 4 out of 5 stars for taste, noting that while it tastes sweet, there’s a “weird aftertaste.”

While the formulation and flavor options make this a top-rated pre-workout, Pulse is by no means a budget-friendly option. At around $45 for a 20-serving tub, it earns the lowest score of 1 out of 5 stars for price per serving.

While many strong pre-workouts cost around $2 per serving, Nutricost Pre-X is our pick for the strongest budget pre-workout because it costs less than half of that. At about $0.93 per serving, one tester called it “the best value on the market,” and I agree, giving this a perfect score of 5 out of 5 for price per serving.

Although some budget pre-workouts lack key ingredients, Pre-X contains the four main ones we like to see in a pre-workout: caffeine, beta-alanine, betaine anhydrous, and L-citrulline. “The price is better than most other pre-workouts I’ve tried, especially for a supplement this good,” says one tester.

Each serving of Pre-X has 300 milligrams of caffeine and 4,000 milligrams of L-citrulline, so you should feel energized and get a good pump with this pre-workout. “I got a decent pump and had a calm focus without feeling overstimulated,” one tester says.

Some testers say Pre-X has a slightly lower dosage of beta-alanine than some other pre-workouts on our list, but others say they experienced noticeable tingles during their workout.

While testers did not experience any negative side effects when trying Pre-X, this pre-workout is made with the artificial sweetener sucralose. Some health experts have raised concerns about taking sucralose in high doses. As a CPT and someone who pays close attention to everything I put in my body, I tend to steer clear of artificial sweeteners. Because of this, we docked a point off the formulation score, giving Pre-X 4 out of 5 stars.

Nutricost Pre-X comes in five flavors, including Blue Raspberry, Peach Mango, and Watermelon. Collectively, our team gave this strong pre-workout 4.5 out of 5 stars for taste.

“This tastes great ice cold or at room temperature. I look forward to drinking it before my workouts,” says one tester who tried Blue Raspberry.

Another tester who tried Peach Mango also gave Pre-X his stamp of approval.

“No artificial sweetener taste at all. It has a nice flavor that’s not overly sweet.”

Whether you like a strong pre-workout that’s sweet, sour, fruity, or tart, Jacked Factory NitroSurge has a fit for you. With 11 options, you can stick to your favorite or keep a few flavors in rotation to keep your taste buds on their proverbial toes. Between the deep lineup and satisfying flavors, NitroSurge earned a perfect score for taste.

One of our testers tried Strawberry Margarita, and let’s just say she was more than satisfied with her sipping experience.

“It’s wildly delicious. I’d drink this by the side of the pool over ice all day.”

Another tester prefers Jacked Factory NitroSurge to some other strong pre-workouts he’s tried. “I did not like the Pink Lemonade flavor of Legion Pulse, but I would definitely use the Grape NitroSurge again,” he says.

As for its effectiveness? For one of our product testers, it took about 20 minutes to feel NitroSurge kick in. At that point, he felt like he could lift harder.

“I usually work out in the morning because I feel most rested then, but even after taking this in the afternoon, I felt ‘jacked up’ and ready to go,” he says, adding that he experienced tingles and a slight drop off, but neither was overwhelming.

Another tester who regularly takes strong pre-workouts doubled the dosage. He said he got “a bit of a boost from it” but nothing like what you’ll get from other strong pre-workouts. Ultimately, this makes NitroSurge a solid choice for beginners, as you can see how you respond to a single serving before upping it to two scoops.

Besides the taste, I like that it’s budget-friendly while still including evidence-backed ingredients, like L-citrulline, beta-alanine, betaine anhydrous, caffeine anhydrous, L-theanine, theobromine, and AstraGin. AstraGin, also found in Transparent Labs BULK BLACK, is a plant-based compound formulated to enhance nutrient absorption. While AstraGin is safe at 0.5 milligrams per kilogram of body weight per day, more research is needed on the potential performance-enhancing benefits.

Like some of the other pre-workouts on our list, NitroSurge is made with the artificial sweetener sucralose, which some health experts have raised concerns about taking in high doses. Also, Jacked Factory supplements do not undergo third-party testing, which ensures products include the ingredients listed on the label and nothing else. This is especially important for athletes who undergo drug testing for banned substances. We only gave Nitrosurge 3 out of 5 stars in this category since it is made in a Current Good Manufacturing Practice (cGMP)-certified and FDA-registered facility.

For bodybuilders, a “pump” is a sign of a successful training session. Increased blood flow to the muscles makes them feel fuller and appear larger and more vascular during and after a workout. A pump also promotes muscle growth by delivering essential nutrients and oxygen to the muscles as blood flow increases. While you can achieve a pump through high-rep sets, drop sets, and supersets, high-stim pre-workouts like Gorilla Mode are specially designed to improve your pump.

Gorilla Mode contains several pump-enhancing ingredients in each scoop, including 5,000 milligrams of pure L-citrulline (more per scoop than any other pre-workout on our list) and 2,000 milligrams of Hydro Prime glycerol powder. L-citrulline works to widen blood vessels, increasing blood flow to the muscles. Glycerol powder is rapidly absorbed by the muscles and draws in water, which can cause muscle cell swelling.

If you’re caffeine-sensitive or budget-conscious, this intense pre-workout may not be the best for you. Although one serving only contains 200 milligrams of caffeine, you will need to take two servings to get research-backed doses of some key ingredients, including creatine monohydrate (only 2.5 gram per serving). At that point, you’d be at 400 milligrams of caffeine, which is the total amount the FDA says is safe for adults to consume per day. For this reason, we docked a point off the formulation, giving Gorilla Mode 4 out of 5 stars in this category.

Don’t forget that this also impacts how much bang you get for your buck. A 40-serving tub costs $60, and you’ll end up going through it that much quicker if you take two scoops before your training sessions. That would bring the cost to $3 per serving. So, from a value standpoint, we can only give Gorilla Mode 2.5 out of 5 stars.

On the other hand, this pricey supplement earned a strong score of 4.5 out of 5 stars for its effectiveness. One of our testers uses strong pre-workouts several times a week and tried Gorilla Mode before an upper-body workout. “Not only did I have a good pump, I also felt more focused. I knocked out a few more reps than usual during my workout,” he says. “I like the Fruit Punch flavor, although it was sweeter than I thought it would be.”

While our tester enjoyed Gorilla Mode’s taste, he says the powder was gritty and difficult to mix properly. This is likely due to the glycerol powder, which absorbs moisture, leading to clumping.

If you like feeling skin tingles after taking your pre-workout, check out Crazy Nutrition Intensive Pre-Train. I love the prickly skin sensation because it lets me know my pre-workout is kicking in and it’s time to train. This temporary side effect, called paresthesia, is caused by beta-alanine, which works to increase muscular endurance.

Intensive Pre-Train has 3,500 milligrams of beta-alanine per serving, which is more per serving than almost all of the other pre-workouts on our list. “Beta-alanine is found in most pre-workout supplements, likely because it helps reduce fatigue and improve endurance in the short term,” says registered dietitian Alex Oskian. “This is because it reduces acidity in the body, which comes from lactic acid build-up.”

Our product tester used Crazy Nutrition Intensive Pre-Train before a high-intensity interval training (HIIT) workout and felt the tingles within 15 minutes. “These were strong compared to some other pre-workouts I’ve tried,” he says. “I felt good tingles in my hands and face, which lasted for about an hour.”

Earning a 5 out of 5 for effectiveness, Intense Pre-Train is also available in a caffeine-free version for those who don’t want stimulants in their pre-workout. The non-stim version comes in Green Apple, which our tester says tasted more like a greens powder than a sour apple.

“I’m rather caffeine-dependent, so I didn’t feel a burst of energy. I prefer caffeinated pre-workouts, but this is a great option for a late-night lifting session,” she says. Other testers who tried the Fruit Punch flavor say they enjoyed the tangy taste. To enhance the flavor, Crazy Nutrition is sweetened with the artificial sweetener sucralose. With some mixed reviews on the different flavors, we give this pre-workout a 3.5 out of 5 for taste.

Onnit Alpha Brain is designed to increase mental acuity and focus. Testers say that’s exactly how they felt after trying Onnit Alpha Brain, which is why it’s our pick for the strongest pre-workout for focus.“What makes this pre-workout stand out is the cognitive effects. I felt significantly more focused after taking Alpha Brain than any other pre-workout I’ve tried,” says one of our testers.

Other testers agreed, saying Alpha Brain helped them feel present and ready to work out without being overstimulated, leading to an effectiveness score of 4 out of 5 stars.

Onnit Alpha Brain’s formula differs from most other strong pre-workout supplements on our list — it contains nootropics, substances that enhance learning and memory. One of the key ingredients, NooGandha, is an ashwagandha extract that can reduce stress and enhance well-being by reducing cortisol levels in the body.

Another key ingredient, AlphaSize, may promote the production of acetylcholine, a powerful neurotransmitter that enhances cognitive function. However, studies demonstrating the effect of alpha-GPC on cognitive performance used 200 to 400 milligram doses per day, and a serving of Onnit Alpha brain has 125 milligrams.

The other unique ingredient in Onnit Alpha Brain is Dynamine. It works similarly to caffeine, by blocking the body’s adenosine receptors that cause you to feel tired. However, this ingredient is banned in all sports supplements in Australia. While Dynamine is still allowed for sports competitions in the U.S., it is possible it will be banned in the future. Competitive athletes may want to steer clear of this product.

One of our testers says Alpha Brain is only middle-of-the-road compared to other strong pre-workouts when it comes to physical energy. “After taking other strong pre-workouts, I usually experience a boost in energy. After taking this pre-workout, the mental effects were much more noticeable than the physical ones,” she says. That may be in part because Alpha Brain lacks ingredients like betaine anhydrous, taurine, and creatine, which can support muscle growth and recovery.

We give the formulation 4 out of 5 stars thanks to the inclusion of nootropics, which are quickly becoming more prevalent in the supplement market. But be aware that this probably isn’t your best bet for boosting your physical energy levels.

Long before the days of gummy and ready-to-drink (RTD) pre-workout options, the most popular choice was the original C4. The latest version, C4 Ultimate, is more concentrated than the classic formula, combining both exercise performance and cognitive-enhancing ingredients.

One of our testers tried C4 Ultimate before a 30-minute HIIT workout, reporting that the caffeine blend got her zoned in before her training.

“I felt great throughout the entire workout,” she reported, giving C4 Ultimate a perfect score for effectiveness.

This high-stim pre-workout is sweetened with sucralose, which some health experts have raised concerns about. While our tester doesn’t mind a very sweet pre-workout, the Icy Blue Razz flavor was a little too sugary for her liking. Mixing it in more water than recommended balances out the sweetness.

However, another tester was blown away by the Sour Batch Bros flavor, saying it tasted “just like Sour Patch Kids.” Taking both of their experiences into consideration, we’ll meet in the middle and give C4 Ultimate a 4 out of 5 for taste, especially since it comes in multiple flavors.

Another plus for this product: It contains creatine — a popular supplement among athletes and bodybuilders for its ability to boost strength, enhance recovery, and prevent injury. Because of its performance-enhancing capabilities, some people like to take creatine in addition to their pre-workout. If you want the best of both worlds, we recommend C4 Ultimate.

Keep in mind that one serving contains 1.5 grams of creatine per serving, which is less than the recommended value of 3 to 5 grams daily. If you want to get the most performance-enhancing benefits from creatine, you should invest in a standalone supplement to help support your fitness goals.One final note: If you compete in a sport that requires drug testing, C4 Ultimate may not be the best strong pre-workout for you because it’s made with Dynamine, which is currently banned for use in Australia.

Our team of expert testers includes certified personal trainers, nutrition coaches, and CrossFit enthusiasts. As dedicated lifters and lovers of all things health and fitness, we’ve collectively tried more than 80 pre-workouts, giving us a broad perspective of what’s available on the market.

We tested each supplement before a workout, and in some cases, for several weeks or months, to evaluate its performance-enhancing benefits, taste, and whether the supplement had any negative side effects.

Using a 1-5 scoring system, we rated each pre-workout on a variety of factors, including:

At the end of the testing period, we compared feedback to whittle our list down to only the best of the best. We also received valuable input from nutrition experts on what makes a strong pre-workout.

A strong pre-workout contains a combination of performance-enhancing ingredients in research-backed dosages. “Usually, the strength of a pre-workout is based upon the amount of stimulants it contains. High doses of caffeine (300+ milligrams) are usually a quick identifier of the pre-workout’s strength,” registered dietitian Alex Oskian says.

However, the potency of a pre-workout goes beyond the caffeine content. Other active ingredients like L-citrulline, beta-alanine, and betaine anhydrous can impact energy, focus muscular endurance, and power output.

“Stronger via the amount of caffeine isn’t always better. If the goal is a bigger pump in the gym, other ingredients like L-citrulline may be better,” says Alex. “Another common ingredient that can help a pre-workout feel stronger is beta-alanine, which may cause a tingling or ‘pins and needles’ sensation on the skin.”

It’s also important to remember that “strong” is a subjective term. For example, I can handle a full scoop of RedCon1 Total War without a problem, but I have friends who get too many tingles from a single serving.

“Everyone’s body reacts differently to various compounds, so what works for one person might not be best for another,” says Dr. Christopher Mohr, Ph.D., RD.

A strong, well-dosed pre-workout supplement may help you train harder by boosting your energy, focus, and endurance during intense workouts.

“There are a few things that are really helpful when you are looking for a great gym session: energy to do the work, mental clarity to help focus on what you are doing (not just to work the muscle, but to prevent injury), and a great workout,” registered dietitian Alex Oskian says. “Using a pre-workout may just help you achieve all of these.”

Let’s explore the potential benefits of taking a strong pre-workout before you start your training session.

Caffeine is one of the most popular stimulants used in pre-workout supplements to enhance energy levels and improve focus. Almost all of the pre-workouts on our list use caffeine and L-theanine. Studies have shown when paired with caffeine, L-theanine may improve cognitive performance.

“Most pre-workouts contain the stimulant caffeine in higher dosages. L-theanine helps counteract the unwanted effects of caffeine supplementation: jittery feelings and a post-caffeine crash,” Alex says. “You might see less mental fatigue, improved reaction time, and fewer headaches while regularly supplementing with L-theanine.”

I like taking a pre-workout to improve my focus because it helps intensify my workout and keep me #lockedin. Several pre-workouts on our list contain Alpha-GPC and tyrosine to give you that zoned-in feeling. Research suggests Alpha-GPC may improve cognitive function, and tyrosine may increase dopamine levels and cognition. One study found L-tyrosine helped improve people’s memory while they worked on a demanding task.

A pre-workout may help you squeeze out a few more reps as you work to build strength and muscle. Two ingredients commonly used in pre-workout, beta-alanine and betaine anhydrous, may help reduce fatigue and support muscular endurance.

“Research suggests betaine anhydrous can improve muscle strength and power via increased total work capacity and improved protein synthesis within the body. Simply put, you can do more work, which leads to increased strength and muscle growth,” says Alex.

Another common ingredient, taurine, may improve your performance and power.

Registered dietitian Alex Oskian says not every pre-workout is created equal, so it’s important to pay attention to what’s on the label. “Supplements are not regulated by the Food and Drug Administration (FDA). This means the supplement might not contain all the ingredients you’re looking for and may even contain unwanted ingredients,” she says. Alex recommends looking for supplements that undergo third-party testing.

If you choose a high-stim pre-workout, be mindful of your caffeine intake from other sources like coffee, tea, or soda so that you don’t go over the daily recommended value of 400 milligrams. This will help prevent potential negative side effects like jitters, anxiety, or trouble falling asleep.

“Consuming caffeine at the end of your day may cause sleep disturbances, which only hurts performance in the long run,” says Oskian.

No matter which pre-workout you choose, it’s important to follow the recommended intake guidelines. Remember, pre-workouts should not be taken more than once per day.

“Pre-workout supplements are generally safe for healthy adults, but they can have some potential side effects,” says Dr. Raj Dasgupta, MD, FACP, FCCP, FAASM. “It is important to start with a low dose and talk to your doctor before taking them, especially if you have any underlying health conditions.”

There are a number of important factors to consider when deciding which strong pre-workout is right for you, including:

Many strong pre-workouts incorporate a variety of active ingredients. When choosing a pre-workout supplement, consider your goals. For example, a bodybuilder may prefer a pre-workout powder that’s highly caffeinated and contains ingredients such as L-citrulline, betaine anhydrous, and creatine to help improve performance. On the other hand, an endurance athlete may want a pre-workout that has less caffeine but includes beta-alanine, BCAAs, and mineral electrolytes.

Whenever possible, I choose supplements that are tested by a third party for purity and have transparent labeling. Athletes who undergo drug testing should look for certifications from Informed Choice and NSF, which ensure the product does not include any banned substances.

Although we test all of the products we recommend, it’s important to check out customer reviews, especially from people with similar fitness goals and preferences. They can provide valuable insights into the product’s overall effectiveness, potential side effects, and the most popular flavors.

“Recommended brands and products are ones that are highly rated by users and contain ingredients that have been backed by scientific research,” says Dr. Raj Dasgupta.

“Taste plays a big role in pre-workout selection. If you don’t like a particular flavor, then you likely won’t drink the pre-workout no matter its benefits,” Oskian says. It’s also important to consider the use of artificial flavors, colors, and sweeteners.

The price of a pre-workout doesn’t necessarily reflect its effectiveness. Understanding the ingredients list and dosage levels is important to ensure you’re paying for a high-quality supplement and not just expensive marketing.

There are a few potential red flags you want to avoid when picking out a pre-workout.

I like to avoid supplements made using proprietary blends. These blends are combinations of ingredients, but the individual doses are not fully disclosed. This lack of transparency makes it impossible to assess the effectiveness and safety of the supplement.

Many fitness enthusiasts and athletes prefer all-natural ingredients and products free from unnecessary fillers or additives. “If sugar alcohols and artificial sweeteners wreak havoc on your stomach, make sure those aren’t on the ingredient list,” registered dietitian Alex Oskian says.

Athletes who compete in sanctioned organizations should make sure the supplements they use are third-party tested and certified banned substance-free.

If you have big fitness goals, choosing a strong pre-workout formulated with safe and effective doses of science-backed ingredients is worth it to deliver performance-enhancing effects. Keep in mind that even the strongest pre-workouts on the market won’t make you run faster, lift heavier, or exercise longer on their own. These supplements are designed to help you put in the work at the gym to make gains and enhance your performance over time.

Ultimately, though, a strong pre-workout is only part of the equation to becoming the strongest version of yourself. At the end of the day, you have to put in the work, follow a sound nutrition plan, and prioritize rest and recovery to crush your fat-burning and muscle-building goals.

Yes, technically, you can take a pre-workout made with 400 milligrams of caffeine. However, that is the maximum daily dose recommended by the FDA. This means if you’re using a high-stim pre-workout, you may want to avoid caffeine from other sources like coffee, tea, soda, or energy drinks. Since 400 milligrams is the maximum recommended daily dose, I do not advise using a pre-workout containing 600 milligrams of caffeine.

A pre-workout can directly and indirectly make you stronger. A well-dosed pre-workout may help you add a few pounds to your lifts or allow you to push out a few more reps during your workout. However, real strength gains will come from consistent training, proper nutrition, and recovery. If a pre-workout supplement helps you stay consistent in the gym, it may also help you gain strength and muscle mass.

Yes. Depending on your sensitivity to stimulants like caffeine, you may experience side effects, including jitters, anxiety, or difficulty falling asleep. If this is the case, use a half serving or a more moderately dosed pre-workout to assess your tolerance.

Warren Buffett has spent decades telling anyone who’ll listen that he lives simply. Same house in Omaha he bought in 1958 for $31,500. No mansion, no car collection, nothing flashy.

He eats at McDonald’s, drinks Coke by the case and has said more than once that a person could live like him on a fraction of his fortune and lose nothing that actually matters.

A physician two decades into a cardiology career already has a six-bedroom house on two acres with a three-car garage. Something that would put Buffett’s Omaha home to shame.

But Buffett flies private. On his personal jet. Which he owns. (He also owns the company that made his plane just FYI).

That cardiologist couldn’t touch a private jet with a ten-foot pole. Not on a $600,000 salary carrying a jumbo mortgage, two kids in private school and a home equity line he opened for the kitchen renovation.

Buffett could write a check for that physician’s entire house and still have money left for the furniture.

My point is, quantifying wealth is not a black and white endeavor. McMansions don’t lead to private jets. And “modest” lifestyles don’t rule them out.

It’s a strange world we live in. One where most people are blindly chasing perception rather than what actually matters.

Also read: Why Most Doctors Retire With Too Much Money (And What to Do About It)

The Federal Reserve’s Survey of Consumer Finances states that the median American household net worth is $192,084. The average is more than 5x that at $1.06 million due to a relatively small number of extremely wealthy households that pull the average up.

Physicians, as a group, are ahead of that median and the gap keeps widening.

Medscape’s 2026 Physician Wealth & Debt Report found that 24% of physicians now report a family net worth of $5 million or more — largely thanks to stock market gains and rising home values.

However, the same report makes it clear this wealth isn’t evenly spread. The physicians in the $5 million group are mostly in procedure-based specialties which have the highest earning ceilings to begin with.

Plenty of physicians in lower-paying specialties spend most of a career well short of that mark despite carrying the same title, the same debt load at the start, and the same years of deferred income during training.

All physicians start with some sort of student debt — small or big — regardless of specialty. The median medical school debt for the class of 2025 is $215,000, not counting undergraduate loans.

Or any non-education debt, credit cards and car loans that tend to accumulate during residency for that matter.

A newly minted attending earning six figures can still have a negative net worth. It takes years to pay down debt and bring it up to zero.

Years more to enter the black. Those early years are the reason for the gap between a $5-million-net-worth radiologist and a physician twenty years into practice who still hasn’t crossed seven figures.

Let’s talk about two doctors who have the same degree and the same starting debt but two very different philosophies on spending money.

For this example we’ll play into the most common stereotypes doctors have faced — and fought hard to shed — for years.

Dr. Flashy “invests” in a new Range Rover every three years. He’s got a lake house two hours outside the city, a boat he uses maybe four weekends a summer — if the weather cooperates.

And surprisingly to some, he’s not broke. He makes real money and a part of his lifestyle is funded from that same income.

Almost every single one of these major purchases generates its own follow-on bill which continues to recur exponentially.

The Range Rover’s routine maintenance costs more than a lot of people’s monthly car payment. The lake house needs a new roof eventually, landscaping every season, comes with a property tax bill that rises every time the county reassesses and someone to physically check on it every time a storm rolls through three states away.

The boat comes with marina fees, winterizing and a marine mechanic who bills by the hour. Buying something nice is the equivalent of signing up for a subscription with an indefinite term and a rising rate.

This is called the hedonic treadmill. Once someone upgrades something in their life, the old version stops being satisfying, permanently. And the new version only delivers that same satisfaction for as long as the novelty lasts.

Eventually the purchase itself becomes pointless. It was the feeling of upgrading that felt good but that feeling fades fast enough that the next upgrade becomes necessary just to get back to the baseline.

Luxury goods are sneakily good at triggering this because so much of what they deliver is the status attached to the price tag. Any functional improvement or value they bring is usually beside the point.

Dr. Flashy’s income may be large. He might even be a neurosurgeon earning $829,161. But at some point his lifestyle needs additional funding to keep up. That’s when he turns to financing.

Eventually, the bank becomes something he is increasingly dependent on.

To be clear, I’m not speculating on his character. Forbes reports that the highest-income American households, those above the 90th percentile, carry the largest average credit card balances of any income group (over $11,000 on average) despite being the group least likely to carry a balance at all.

So data shows us that the people who look the most financially comfortable are disproportionately dependent on revolving debt to stay there. Not all high earners are predisposed to open lines of credit, but when they do, they tend to rack up more of it because the lifestyle they’re financing costs more to maintain than anyone else’s.

The thing is, money is finite even with a large income. Spending more of it means you need more just to sustain the spending at its current level. And that treadmill doesn’t slow down as the years go by.

Dr. Net-Worth has the same income as Dr. Flashy. Same specialty, even, same call schedule, same patient panel.

But Dr. Net-Worth drives a Honda he’s had since fellowship. It’s got a cracked bumper he keeps meaning to fix. He lives in a house that’s nice but completely unremarkable from the street — not something you’ll see featured in Architectural Digest.

Still, his investment accounts feature a sum that would make your eyes water. No one except him and his accountant know what it is.

We have come to perceive net worth as some concrete evaluation of a person’s wealth. But it really isn’t. In fact, the more zeroes it has, the less real it is.

I mean, this year we saw Elon Musk become (briefly) the first ever trillionaire. But does that mean he’s got a Scrooge McDuck vault full of gold coins stacked to the ceiling?  Well, he might — but he won’t have an actual trillion in there to dive into and swim around in.

That number is mostly the market’s opinion of his equity stakes on a given day. An opinion that can — and does — swing by tens of billions of dollars before lunch and back again by dinner. All without a single dollar changing hands or a single decision on his part.

Dr. Net-Worth’s number works the same way just on a smaller scale. Most of it lives in a house he’s still making payments on every month, a retirement account he can’t touch before a certain age lest he trigger a penalty, and an ever-growing brokerage account he could never imagine drawing from.

All of it is his. Yet, he doesn’t use a dollar of it beyond the mortgage payment and the grocery bill. He’s rich! Technically. Psychologically, it might as well be someone else’s money.

You can’t fault him for being this way. Sometimes it’s just temperament. Plenty of high earners are simply frugal by nature, genuinely uninterested in the lake house and actually happier to keep the Honda running for another hundred thousand miles. Nothing wrong with that. At least Dr. Net-Worth doesn’t need rescuing from the life he has chosen.

But sometimes the hesitation to spend stems from fear. Constant worry that the money could vanish overnight, that one bad market year or one malpractice suit could erase everything you’ve built.

That spending on anything beyond the bare essentials is an invitation for disaster to strike. Dr. Net-Worth worked his butt off to build a financial fortress that classifies him as financially free. Yet the day may never come when he actually gets to taste that freedom.

Dr. Flashy is one bad year/one slow season at the practice/one unexpected repair bill on the boat away from a very uncomfortable conversation with a lender.

Dr. Net-Worth has already won the game by any objective measure but refuses to enjoy it.

Financial planner Derek Hagen says that money that isn’t pointed at anything in particular just accumulates, and accumulation without a purpose behind it isn’t freedom. Dr. Net-Worth has plenty of money with no real purpose for it.

Dr.  Flashy has an answer: status and visible proof that he has “made it”. But his answer costs more to maintain with every passing year, never quite delivering the sense of arrival he’s chasing.

There’s no handbook that outlines exactly where the divide between enjoying the money and hoarding it is. And anyone who claims there is one wants to sell you something.

You, the physician reading this, are probably nothing like Dr. Flashy or Dr. Net-Worth. And asking which one is better or worse isn’t the point either.

Your money, no matter how it is accumulated or spent on, deserves to be used to fund a life you chose on purpose. Not one assembled by accident out of habit, fear or…what the neighbors might notice.

Buffett kept the house and bought the plane because both of those choices added up to a life he actually wanted. That is rich (of course being worth $144.6 billion doesn’t hurt).

Everything else is just perception in a strange world that will never stop raising the bar.

Good, thoughtful article, Thanks! I have to agree about the ongoing obligations that the treadmill gets us into. I have to identify with Dr Net-Worth, but rather than having no purpose, I would say that one real, tangible benefit he has is security. Knowing he or his spouse can incur some life altering accident or illness and not affect the well being of the rest of the family. As an example my mother in law has dementia and has been in memory care for a decade. Her current bill is 200k per year. She and her husband planned very well and regardless of how long she lives she will be taken care of. The kids have not needed to contribute at all. My household has planned in a similar way. I know I will never need to be supported by my kids.

Thank you for separating a headline net worth figure from a life actually funded by it. The contrast between Dr Flashy and Dr Net-Worth is useful precisely because neither extreme answers the question of what the money is for. I found the follow-on costs point especially practical: a purchase is rarely a one-off price, and marina fees, maintenance and rising property taxes can quietly turn a status purchase into a continuing obligation. On the other side, treating a net worth statement as a market snapshot, rather than spendable security, helps explain why accumulating without a purpose can still feel anxious. A more useful middle path might be to define, in advance, what ‘enough’ looks like in cash-flow terms — housing, time, work flexibility and family priorities — and then judge each upgrade against that, rather than against another physician’s lifestyle or another year’s market valuation.

Of course, $5 million in a West or East Coast city means something entirely different than $5 million in a medium sized town in the Midwest or South. By way of information, if anyone is interested in how their assets compare relative to the U.S. net worth figures (by age, education or region).

Also, in another 6-8 weeks, the Federal Reserve Bank will issue the results of the 2025 Survey of Consumer Finance (SCF), which presents its own set of (updated) net worth and income figures.

The lingering question is – how do you determine the net present value of future social security payments or a pension, if eligible for one? Do you include that in a net worth statement or not?

The takeaway I have this article is to be neither a hoarder nor a ‘flashy’. Be comfortable in your spending style. And, in spite of the stress of the medical profession, it is good to practice gratitude for the opportunities to serve and have a roof over our heads.

Btw, I think the US government is going to face financial headwinds over the next 10 years. Social security and Medicare are going to run out of money (2032, 2033). In 2027, a large number of long-term bonds are going to mature and need re-financing. The real details can be found on the web, but you have to go digging for them. Carpe Diem.

Thanks for reading, and for adding so much to the discussion.

You’re right about geography. Five million in Manhattan or the Bay Area buys a smaller house and a longer commute than the same number buys in Omaha, which might explain why Buffett never bothered leaving. (Your link to the net worth comparison looks like it got eaten by the comment system, by the way. Feel free to repost it.)

On Social Security and pensions: I leave them off the net worth statement. You can’t sell them or borrow against them, and most of their value dies with you, so folding them in puffs up a number that’s already mostly opinion. Where they earn their keep is the retirement income plan. A pension paying $40,000 a year does roughly the work of a $1 million portfolio at a 4% withdrawal rate, which means the nest egg you need to build shrinks accordingly. I’d count them in that spreadsheet and keep them out of the other one.

On the trust funds, one detail tends to get lost in the headlines. When the reserves run dry in the early 2030s, benefits don’t drop to zero. Under current projections, incoming payroll taxes would still cover something like three quarters to four fifths of scheduled payments. Painful, sure, but a haircut is a very different problem than a guillotine. For younger docs, penciling in about 75% of your statement estimate seems like reasonable caution without veering into doom.

And I’m with you on gratitude. Most of this job’s stress comes with a roof, meaningful work and the chance to retire on our own terms, which is more than a lot of people ever get to complain about.

Carpe diem right back at you. -Jorge Sanchez, MD
