#8566. 5 Strategies From ‘Bear Brawl’ to Help You Train for the Impossible

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

Revenge may be a dish best served cold, but when your target is a giant black bear, you’d better bring a perfect plan—or you may end up as the appetizer.

That’s the premise of Jon Finkel’s latest novel, Bear Brawl, an outrageously well-thought-out mix of modern training methodology soaked with an over-the-top ’80s action movie scenario that every Stallone and Schwarzenegger film fan has wanted answered: Is it possible to plan a fight against a rogue, 450-pound bear—the same unrepentant ursid that killed Brick Bridger’s mother and left his brother in a wheelchair—and win in a hand-to-hand duel?

As an ’80s expert who speaks fluent Roadhouse, I was able to read Bear Brawl in one sitting—something I’d never done with a book before—and that’s exactly the experience Finkel was aiming for. It’s also why the book would absolutely make a solid stocking stuffer this Christmas. Picture Bear Brawl as Rambo, John Matrix, and Dalton, all trained by Mr. Miyagi.

That brings us to Brick Bridger, a beast in his own right. He’s an Arkansas-bred 6’6”, 265-pound former UFC heavyweight and two-time collegiate wrestling champion who wasn’t around the night “Macho,” the quarter-ton Colossus, killed his mother and crippled his brother. He’s been living with that guilt ever since, convinced none of it would have happened had he been there.

“He’s the perfect human specimen,” Finkel said. “Brick’s a two-time NCAA wrestling champion, with eight fights in the UFC heavyweight division before retiring because of injury. And a rogue black bear—the one night he’s late to a barbecue—kills his mom and puts his brother in a wheelchair. So now we have the man, we have the means, we have the motivation.”

Instead of spiraling, he uses his depression as fuel to take on Macho. Only with the help of several experts and a commitment to a plan does the idea of fighting the bear seem, well… still ridiculous. But somewhat more attainable than going into the woods carrying nothing but rage.

For Finkel, an M&F contributing writer and editor who witnessed fight camps with UFC legends such as Brock Lesnar, Randy Couture, and Frank Mir, the novel is more than a tribute to the ’80s action adventure genre. There’s also a bit of strategy readers can incorporate into their own goal-setting, without actually having to grapple a grizzly.

“Turn your grief or stress into a healthy challenge,” he said. “A lot of people, they’ll start triathlons. They’ll do Ironmans to get over something, to occupy their mind. In this case, it’s not an Ironman or a marathon. It’s to fight a bear.”

Whether it’s losing weight, running a marathon or staying true to a 12-week training program for a BJJ tournament, each of these will have its own set of obstacles that may appear overwhelming at certain points. Like Bridger, with the right help and strategy, even the most ridiculous of challenges can become attainable—on paper at least.

1. Choose a Goal that Gives Your Training Direction

A clear target can turn scattered and inconsistent workouts into preparation with purpose. Whatever your type of activity you’re into, select an event or milestone that excites you, then break it into manageable steps. Study its requirements, plan your training, then execute and track your progress.

“You take a task and whether it’s impossible or not—or you think it’s impossible—and you train all your energies toward it,” Finkel says. “Yours may be completing an Ironman or marathon. Brick’s was fighting a bear.”

2. Find the Obstacle—and Make a Plan for It

No matter what your skill level is, there will come a point in which your progress stalls. When it happens, don’t assume that the solution is simply to work harder. Take inventory of what may be the cause of your plateau. Is it a physical weakness? Technique? Consistency? Recovery? Brick understood the challenge and searched for an opening. For your fitness goals, it could mean hiring a coach, making program adjustments, or even giving yourself more time to build your skillset.

“You got to know your enemy, and you have to be humble,” Finkel says. “He looks until he eventually finds the Achilles’ heel. Maybe there is always a way.”

3. Work on Weak Points While Still Enhancing Your Strengths

A smart plan is a combination of making improvements while also capitalizing on your primary abilities. Brick used his own size and MMA skills as the foundation while also putting in the work in the “classroom” to search for new ways to victory. For you, build on your strengths, too, from choosing a training style that fits your abilities, then working and progressing on the secondary skills that will help get the job done.

“Lean into your strength,” Finkel says. “Brick’s not an in-his-prime Mike Tyson knocking out guys in the first round. Every fight is now a grind for him. I even did this myself—I was trying to do triathlons, and I realized the only thing I actually like is swimming. So I just became a really fast swimmer and forgot the two parts I hated. As soon as I leaned into the thing I was best at, I enjoyed it so much more. So pick one and be really good at it.”

A go-it-alone strategy heavily reliant on brute strength and past personal achievements ends in disaster for nearly all of us. For Brick, filling the gaps for this task meant incorporating experts who knew the right tendencies and could spot openings and weak spots the untrained eye would overlook. So when it comes to goal achievement, it helps to find a coach, training partner, or knowledgeable source who can add to your preparations, spot problems, and offer candid feedback.

“Brick had a zoologist and a wrestling coach explaining the ways it can’t work,” Finkel says. “Being creative is one thing, but being resourceful within that creativity can really make a project like this work.”

An outrageous goal will take longer than you expect, and there will be stretches where it looks like you’re losing. Brick’s MMA motor keeps him moving forward when every fight becomes a struggle. He keeps working his way toward that small but decisive opening he knows is there but isn’t quite visible yet.

“He doesn’t quit,” Finkel says. “Brick might not be the most technically sound guy. He might not even be the strongest. He’s the guy with the motor, the size, and the will to keep figuring things out until he can exploit the weakness. Most people’s goals die right at the point where it stops feeling good—keep grinding until it does.”

It’s almost Halloween, and much like everyone else, I have been sucked into the tradition of watching horror movies with my wife before we take our daughter trick-or-treating. One of the movies I’m still thinking about from last week is Backrooms. It is the highest-grossing film A24 has ever released, and most of it takes place in rooms that look like a hospital at 3 a.m.

Yellowed walls. Fluorescent tubes that buzz loud enough to notice. Carpet that has absorbed something you would rather not identify. Corridors that turn left, then left again, until you’re somehow back where you started. If you trained at a big academic center, you have walked these halls, and probably still dream about them.

The film grew out of Kane Parsons’s YouTube series about a dimension of endless, empty rooms. Instead of the creature feature I expected, I got a picture of the doctor who is close to financial independence and can’t bring themselves to leave.

Full disclaimer: only read ahead if you’ve watched the film because there will be spoilers!

Clark is a failed architect running a struggling furniture store in San Jose. He drinks too much, his marriage is over, and he has started sleeping at the store. One night he goes down to check the breaker box, notices a glowing slit in the wall, and falls through it.

On the other side is a copy of the world that is slightly wrong. Rooms that almost look like rooms. Furniture that seems to have melted at the edges. Hallways longer than the building could possibly hold. Later in the film it gets described as a faulty, misremembered version of reality.

That description fits medical training better than anything I’ve heard in a wellness lecture. Residency is a copy of adult life with the proportions off. You have a title and real responsibility for people’s lives, but you’re 31 with a negative net worth, and you haven’t made it to a friend’s wedding without checking your phone in years.

Real life is always one room ahead: after boards, after fellowship, after the loans, after partnership. So you keep walking.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

After a few trips in and out, Clark leaves his therapist a message. He’s staying in the Backrooms, and he won’t be coming back. He has found a way out of the failing store, the drinking, the empty house. The place he picked is worse than the one he’s leaving, but it’s familiar, and it doesn’t ask him to deal with anything.

The FIRE crowd has a name for this: one more year. You hit your number, or get close enough to see it, and you sign another contract anyway. The reasons all sound sensible. The market is choppy. The kids start college in four years. The group is short two partners.

Besides, what else would you do on a Wednesday morning?

Plenty of physicians keep working after financial independence because they love the work, and that’s a good outcome. The question worth asking is whether you’re staying because you chose to, or because the hallway is the only place you know how to stand.

Early in the film, Clark shoots a cheap TV commercial for the store dressed as its pirate mascot. It’s a little embarrassing and a little sweet. It is the version of himself he has to perform to keep the business alive.

By the end of the film, the costume becomes a towering, distorted Clark in the pirate outfit, peg leg and all, is waiting for him in the Backrooms. Clark tries to calm it down the way you’d talk to a dog you raised from a puppy. It kills him.

The Backrooms in this film make monsters from what people carry in, their memories and their feelings, and build with it.

Doctors have a costume too. The white coat, the title, the steady voice you use to tell a family the scan came back bad. You need it, and your patients need you to have it. The trouble starts when it stops coming off after the shift. You introduce yourself as Dr. at your kid’s soccer game. The hobbies lapse one at a time. Every close friend works in your department. Your income, your marriage, and your sense of being a decent person all run through one job.

Then the job goes sideways. A lawsuit, a patient death you can’t stop replaying, an RVU target that climbs every year, a private equity buyout that changes everything except your title.

What turns on you in those moments is the professional self you spent fifteen years building, now bigger than the person wearing it.

The second half belongs to Clark’s therapist, Dr. Mary Kline (Renate Reinsve). Worried about her patient, she goes to the store and walks into the Backrooms after him.

She doesn’t walk in clean. Mary is still working through the demolition of her childhood home and her mother’s institutionalization. A professional helper carrying a stack of her own unprocessed losses into someone else’s crisis is a fair description of a lot of people in medicine.

Inside, Clark ties her to a chair in a fake dining room. Three human-shaped figures sit around the table with them. They don’t move or react to anything. Clark shows her they’re made of an edible white substance, and it becomes clear the Backrooms feed on them.

It might sound odd, but I couldn’t watch that scene without thinking about the Maslach Burnout Inventory. It measures three things: emotional exhaustion, a fading sense of accomplishment, and depersonalization.

Doctors are familiar with depersonalization. Patients start to feel like tasks, and after a while you feel like one too. You’re at the table every day, and you look fine from across the room, while the place slowly takes what it needs from you.

The pirate gets rid of Clark comes for Mary next. Her survival is noteworthy.

Cornered in a lopsided replica of the furniture store, she snaps the monster’s peg leg with a hat rack, then hits it in the face with a chunk of concrete from her childhood home. The thing she has been grieving the whole movie turns out to be the thing she fights with.

For a physician, that chunk of concrete is whoever you were before medicine. The kid who played bass in a garage band. The person who built bookshelves, or ran trails, or cooked for twelve friends on a Saturday. Those parts didn’t vanish when you matched. They got buried under a decade of training.

The doctors I’ve seen leave clinical work well, or drop to part-time without falling apart, usually started digging some of that back up long before they needed it. They had a corner of life the job wasn’t allowed into, and they’d been living in it for years by the time they gave notice.

This is where the analogy gets uncomfortable.

Mary’s fight with the pirate sets off a gas trap. Researchers in hazmat suits haul her out to a facility run by Async, a company that used to make MRI machines before it found the Backrooms and made them its main business.

Whether or not the filmmakers meant anything by it, a medical imaging company ending up in charge of the maze is a hard detail to ignore if you work in a hospital.

In the last scene, Mary sits in an interrogation room across from Phil, one of Async’s scientists. She asks whether they’re going to let her go. He tells her the decision isn’t his.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

A lot of doctors make it through the burnout, the bad years, the cases that almost broke them, and end up in that room. They’re ready to leave, and they find out the exit belongs to someone else:

None of these are sinister on their own. Each one just moves the decision a little further from you and a little closer to a contract, a lender, or an employer.

For a physician, that’s what financial independence is really for. It’s less about retiring at 45 and more about who gets to answer the question Mary asks.

The film’s final shot is a copy of Mary, deformed and silent, sitting in a rough replica of that interrogation room somewhere deep in the Backrooms. The place has learned her. Whatever happens to the real Mary, a version of her stays behind.

Medicine leaves a copy of you behind too, and that isn’t all bad. The judgment, the pattern recognition, the calm you have in a code are yours for life. The goal isn’t to get out with nothing of the doctor left. It’s to make sure the doctor isn’t the only thing left.

A few things that help, roughly in order of effort:

Clark stayed because the maze was easier than his life. Most doctors who stay too long do it for a version of the same reason. Staying in medicine can be a great choice, as long as you’re the one making it.

The Pro Forma Never Paid Anyone’s Mortgage

If you bought into a multifamily syndication around 2021, you remember the deck. Glossy photos, a tidy IRR, a confident exit year. Then rates climbed, valuations slid, and plenty of investors watched distributions pause while their capital sat locked inside a deal that no longer penciled out.

Private real estate lending puts you in a different seat. The lender gets paid ahead of equity, holds a lien on the property, and collects interest from monthly loan payments rather than waiting on a sale that may never hit its number. You give up the home-run upside. In exchange, nobody calls you about a broken water heater at 2 a.m., a perk I’ve come to value after enough overnight shifts.

In a recent webinar, I joined Dr. Christy Burakovsky and Chris Lopez of Property Llama to discuss how private real estate loans are underwritten, where the actual risks lie, and what investors should ask any fund before wiring a dollar.

We also covered the importance of looking beyond projected returns and understanding the fundamentals behind a lending strategy.

The takeaway? Before investing, know how the loan is structured, what protects your capital, and what happens when a deal doesn’t go according to plan.

#8561. Dwayne Johnson Breaks Out the ‘Rock Bottom’ on Pat McAfee

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

It may be thirty years since Dwayne Johnson made his debut with the WWE, but the “Most Electrifying Man in Sports Entertainment” can still break out his signature “Rock Bottom” slam at a mere second’s notice—just ask Pat McAfee.

Sparks flew when Johnson attended ESPN’s College Gameday as guest picker on Nov. 21. During the live broadcast from the Lakeside Patio at the University of Miami, the Hurricanes took on the Virginia Tech Hokies, but the action off the field got just as intense when McAfee brought up a questionable call that had gone in Miami’s favor. Johnson, who played for the Hurricanes as a defensive tackle in the early 90s, took exception to those remarks and things got physical, fast.

Tension was in the air as Johnson made his way to the commentary position, complete with his WWE theme music on blast, and decked out in his number 94 shirt, because McAfee tried to pour cold water on the Hurricane’s 28-20 win. “Already talking trash about Miami,” responded The Rock.

“Didn’t it feel a little soft,” teased McAfee of the Hurricane’s performance. “I mean like, maybe, the softest I’ve ever seen Miami,” he went on.

At first, it looked like McAfee might have gotten a free pass as Johnson pulled him in for a close handshake, but in a moment that reminded us why The Rock is one of the most iconic pro wrestlers of all time, the former WWE champ grabbed McAfee and proceeded to execute the Rock Bottom, slamming the former football player straight through a nearby table.

With McAfee out for the count, “The Great One” then basked in the adulation of his home team. Of course, McAfee has dabbled in the world of grappling, and has even made wrestling appearances for WWE, but he certainly met his match in Miami.

Making his debut as “Rocky Maivia” on November 17, 1996, at the Survivor Series pay-per-view, Johnson went on to become one of the most popular wrestlers of all time. While the big man now concentrates on a full-time career in Hollywood, “The People’s Champion” did step through the ropes at WrestleMania XL in 2024. And, to celebrate 30 years of The Rock, Johnson recently confirmed that he will make an appearance at the 2026 Survivor Series on Nov. 28.

Whether or not he gets mixed up in the action there remains to be seen, but with a big money WrestleMania planned in Saudi Arabia next year, there’s plenty of hope that Johnson could have at least one more match. Either way, Pat McAfee can attest that The Rock’s still got what it takes.

#8559. The Best Smith Machine for Your Home Gym in 2025

The Smith machine sometimes gets a bad rap, but it can be a solid addition to any home gym.

Written by Stephen Sheehan, CPT × The Expert Panel is a network of specialized health and fitness professionals who help ensure we present the most accurate information to our readers. This includes physicians, certified trainers, elite-level coaches, and more. Learn more about our experts. expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC Last updated on Nov 2, 2026

expert-verified Amanda Dvorak, ISSA-CPT, ISSA-CNC

Other than the almighty treadmill, there may not be a piece of equipment more synonymous with commercial gyms than the Smith machine. Boasting tremendous versatility and functionality, this muscle-building tool is popular among lifters of all experience levels.

However, you don’t need a gym membership to enjoy its benefits. While it may have not been a home gym staple years ago, the Smith machine has become a must-have for many fitness enthusiasts. Offering added protection without a spotter for your bench presses, back squats, deadlifts, and other strength exercises, the Smith machine is a wise investment for those trying to build the ultimate garage gym.

With options spanning from traditional Smith machines to all-in-one home gym solutions, you might feel a bit overwhelmed about which direction to go. Luckily for you, our team of expert product testers did all the due diligence necessary to separate the cream from the crop. From analyzing the build materials to testing the smoothness of the bar path to assessing the value, we took the time to dissect each element in order to narrow down our list to just five.

In addition, we got some valuable insight from Mauro S. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness, on the benefits and what factors to consider when you’re shopping for a Smith machine.

This content is meant to be informative, but should not be taken as medical advice. It is not intended for use as diagnosis, prevention, or treatment of health problems. Always speak with your doctor before starting any new supplement or exercise regimen.

If you’re searching for a multifunctional Smith machine that’s compatible with a ton of attachments, the Force USA G15 is the machine that can truly do it all — albeit at an expensive price point of around $5,500. However, there’s a reason it earned 4.5 out of 5 stars for versatility from our top product tester: you can perform a wide variety of exercises by taking advantage of all of its functionality.

Tipping the scales at nearly 1,000 pounds, the G15 combines a functional trainer, half rack, and Smith machine into a single, sturdy unit. Measuring over 6 feet wide, over 4 feet deep, and about 7 feet tall, the G15 earns a 4-star footprint rating. While there are more compact options, it’s still a good option for folks with limited space, especially considering the versatility you get.

Offering dual 289-pound weight stacks that keep it well-anchored, the G15 also scores 4 out of 5 stars for durability and construction.

“This thing is like a tank,” our tester says. “Once it’s assembled, it’ll basically be stuck in place.”

Unfortunately, our tester wasn’t as impressed with the cable pulley material. Asthey’re made from nylon instead of aluminum, they don’t move as smoothly and won’t be as durable as their metal counterparts.

Something that separates the G15 from many competitors is its ability to go from a 2:1 or 4:1 pulley ratio. This gives you the ability to make the weight feel like half or a quarter of the actual weight. While our tester would prefer a 1:1 ratio for more effective resistance, he says the 2:1 or 4:1 ratios “will be adequate for most people working out from home.”

The G15 comes with a lengthy list of attachments, including J-hooks, safety spotter arms, multi-grip dip handles, a multi-grip pull-up bar, band pegs, and a low row footplate. If you want to unlock even more training possibilities, the $700 G15 Upgrade Kit includes three additional strength training stations, three functional attachments, a TV mount, and four storage shelves.

Two knocks against this ultra-versatile machine: assembly and value.

Although some of the parts arrive pre-assembled, our assembly expert recommends budgeting “at least 20 man hours” to get the G15 fully put together. And if you want to leave it to the professionals, you’ll need to pay an additional $800.

At nearly $6,000 on its own, the G15 certainly isn’t made for budget-conscious shoppers. Our top product tester gave it 3.5 out of 5 stars for value, noting that Force USA could use better quality components, cables, and accessories, including one of the key parts of this premium-priced unit: the built-in barbell.“The knurling is super passive and not going to allow for an adequate grip for the user if you were to go heavy on any Smith machine movements,” he explains.

Want to crush a full-body workout with a single piece of equipment? The Titan Fitness Smith Machine can be the all-in-one solution that allows you to train your upper body, lower body, and core in a safe, effective manner.

Is it as versatile as the G15? No. Is it far more affordable? Yes.

For less than a third of the price, you can still get an excellent workout experience from the $1,7000 Titan Smith Machine. One of our more seasoned product testers used it for a variety of strength training sessions, highlighting how impressed she was by the smooth glide of the barbell and the angled design. In addition, this Smith machine is counterbalanced so you don’t have to support the entire 45-pound barbell like you do on other machines. Beginners will appreciate this, as the bar only feels like 15 pounds.

Unfortunately, like Force USA, Titan left our team wanting more out of the knurling.

“It’s fine for a Smith machine, but it’s definitely not the most grippy bar,” our tester says.

On the other hand, this machine earns high marks for its ergonomics. Our tester rated it 4 out of 5 stars in this category. She found the single-axis, angled design helped improve her muscle activation during lower-body weight training exercises like Smith machine squats and lunges.

Most importantly, she felt completely secure using this Titan machine. Not only was there no wobbling or shaking, but the bar moved smoothly, leading her to give a 5-out-of-5 rating for stability.

“This is a super stable machine; there was no give to it even when we were using heavy weights,” our tester says. “This was ultra-smooth.” While Titan priced this machine fairly, we’d like to see a better warranty. A one-year policy falls well short of what we expect from most brands. Plus, if you want to return a piece of equipment, you must pay the return shipping costs and a 20% restocking fee. That results in a disappointing customer experience score of just 2 out of 5 stars.

Don’t want a standalone Smith machine? Bolt Fitness has a space-saving solution in the form of the Storm Series Stinger Smith Machine Attachment. Compatible with any 3” x 3” frame using 1” hardware, this universal attachment can seamlessly integrate with your existing squat or power rack, opening the door to even more training possibilities.

We rate this Smith machine attachment a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers 12 different positions totaling 60” of vertical adjustments. That means you can quickly go from a steep incline bench press to a Romanian deadlift, making your workouts more efficient, too. Plus, we also like that this attachment has a 43” built-in multi-grip pull-up bar, giving you the ability to develop your vertical pulling strength and endurance.

Bolt also earns solid marks for construction, earning 4 out of 5 stars in this key category. However, our chief product tester warns not to expect quite the same level of craftsmanship as some better-known brands.

“You won’t see the same quality welds or powder coats from Bolt as you will from Rogue or REP,” he says.

Like several other nominees on this list, our tester was also disappointed with the Smith bar’s knurling. The passive knurl pattern won’t give you a particularly stable grip, especially when using heavier weights.

“You definitely won’t mistake this for an Olympic barbell,” our tester says.

As for the price? At around $1,100 this is on the expensive side for a Smith machine attachment. For example, the Bells of Steel Smith Machine Rack Attachment is much more affordable at $800. We rate it a 3 out of 5 for value, especially since you already need a rack to use it. Otherwise, expect to invest a significant chunk of change to get a fully functioning setup.

Just because you can’t afford to splurge on something like the G15 doesn’t mean you can’t find a Smith machine that fits within your budget. If you don’t have a ton of financial wiggle room, the RitFit Smith Machine is the most affordable option that earned our stamp of approval.

As our top product tester puts it, “If you’re looking for a Smith machine and you’re on an ultra-budget, this is it.”

At about $500 on Amazon, this machine is less than a third of the price of the Titan Fitness Smith Machine and less than a tenth of the cost of the G15. Of course, it’s not the most durable option on the market, but it offers sufficient versatility at a very attractive price point to earn a near-perfect value rating of 4.5 out of 5 stars.

Dubbed the “sleeper pick” by our tester, he notes that “the low price covers so many sins.”

Before we dive into some of RitFit’s shortcomings, let’s highlight some of the strengths of this machine. First, we rated it 4 out of 5 for versatility, as it offers built-in low row and lat pulldown capabilities using a plate-loaded cable pulley system that holds 165 pounds. The RitFit Smith Machine also comes with several attachments, including a pin-on landmine row and two multi-purpose pull-up handles.

Secondly, it has a compact design that makes it suitable for home gym setups with limited  space. It also weighs just 140 pounds, making it easier to move than other options on this list.

However, our tester had several callouts about the RitFit Smith Machine that deserve mentioning. With cheaper build materials and a lightweight design, it didn’t prove to be as stable as he would have liked, earning just 3.5 out of 5 stars for both construction and stability. Needless to say, this isn’t the best option if you want to lift heavy weights. Still, considering you could pay around the same price for a high-quality Olympic barbell, the RitFit Smith Machine is a solid option if you’re on a limited budget.

Imagine if you could turn your squat rack into a Smith machine in a matter of minutes. That dream can be a reality if you’re willing to invest around $700 on the VTS Lite Rack Attachment from Bulletproof Fitness, a lesser-known fitness equipment manufacturer that’s caught our attention.

While we haven’t gotten our hands on this attachment just yet, it’s hard not to get excited about the concept and execution by Bulletproof. The Versa Trolley System (VTS) Lite allows you to convert your squat rack into a Smith machine using your own barbell. The rollers are made from UHMW plastic, an ultra-durable material we’ve seen used on other racks. This attachment only weighs 15 pounds, making the VHS Lite a more user-friendly alternative than the full-sized VTS, which weighs in at 24 pounds. From a construction standpoint, we feel comfortable giving the VTS Lite 4 out of 5 stars.

In addition, we like that Bulletproof offers a wide range of options to accommodate different racks. You can choose between a 3” x 3” pair, a 2” x 3” pair, or a 2” x 2” pair. You also can choose different hook sizes based on the diameter of your barbell. This optionality, along with the added exercise variety you get from using the attachments, earns a 4.5 out of 5 for versatility.

Set to be released in May 2025, we’re excited to see this product in action. If you want a more streamlined solution than getting a standalone Smith machine, this is an attractive space- and money-saving solution. Based on the price and versatility, we give it a value rating of 4 out of 5 — though it could go higher once we get our hands on it.

As Smith machines have become more popular among the home gym community, we’ve ramped up our efforts to test ones from a variety of brands. This has allowed us to develop a thorough evaluation process that examines a number of key factors that impact your workout experience.

With options ranging from standard Smith machines to all-in-one trainers with cable machines, here’s what we assess during testing using a 1-5 scoring system:

What makes a Smith machine such a valuable training tool? If you’ve ever used one, you already know there’s added peace of mind knowing you have built-in support. Here’s an overview of the different benefits of utilizing this popular piece of equipment.

Unlike when you use a barbell and squat rack, the Smith machine provides a fixed bar path. This can help reduce the risk of injury and ensure a stable lifting environment.

“The Smith machine helps the athlete feel supported and gives them greater control and stability when performing an exercise,” says Mauro M. Maietta, district fitness and education manager for Crunch Fitness.

In particular, new lifters can benefit from starting out on a Smith machine so they can focus on their form while being supported by the machine.

“Maintaining correct form is important for avoiding injuries and maximizing the effectiveness of your workouts,” says Dr. Christopher Mohr, PhD, RD. “Beginners might benefit from working with a personal trainer initially or taking a beginner class to learn proper techniques.”

The guided motion and added stability of a Smith machine makes it an ideal training tool for those returning from injury or anyone with mobility issues. It encourages proper form and can be a safer way to increase your strength and joint stability before moving on to free weights.

Maietta recommends starting with lighter weights to get a feel for the range of motion before progressing. “The fixed range of motion is not for everyone, so be sure to speak with your local fitness professional and listen to your body and joints if you feel any discomfort or pain during the planned movements,” he says.

If you prefer to work out alone or don’t have a training partner available, the Smith machine can act as a “spotter” for you. These machines offer an extra layer of safety, as you can easily rack the bar or set the safety spotters to a specific point that will keep you out of harm’s way.

In addition, this advantage allows you to safely follow progressive overload, a proven method for increasing muscle size and strength.

“This continual challenge helps your muscles grow stronger,” says Mohr. “It’s important to start with manageable increments to prevent injury.”

You won’t find many machines that offer as much versatility as the Smith machine. Want to train legs? You can knock out squat and lunge variations. Want to grow your chest and shoulders? Grab an adjustable weight bench and work on your bench press and overhead press without having to worry about keeping the bar stable. A high-end option like the Force USA G15 gives you the ability to perform cable exercises like cable crossovers, chest flys, and overhead triceps extensions.

“The Smith machine can be seen as the Swiss army knife of the weight room since it allows for several strength training exercises in its fixed vertical path, ranging from squats to overhead pressing movements,” says Maietta.

What should you consider when choosing a Smith machine? Based on our experience as equipment experts and dedicated lifters, here’s what we recommend:

Consider the machine’s footprint when determining if it is a good fit for your needs. One benefit of Smith machines is all-in-one trainers are available to consolidate the space needed for multiple workout stations.

Many of the home gym Smith machine options on this list are designed as all-in-one trainers designed to provide multiple workout functions with one convenient machine. The machine can include stations for a power rack, functional trainer, low-row attachment, chin-ups/pull-ups, dips, suspension trainers, and more.

Smith machines offer pulley systems with varying weight ratios, including 1:1 and 2:1. A 1:1 ratio means the weight you load is the exact weight you lift. A 2:1 ratio means you lift half of the weight you load. For instance, with a 2:1 ratio, if you load 100 pounds, you lift 50 pounds.

Some Force USA Smith machines, including the G15, allow users to easily switch between 2:1 and 4:1 ratios, which is helpful when people of various skills use the same machine.

Weight capacities vary depending on the functions offered by the machine. The weight capacities on this list start at 300 pounds. Be sure to confirm the machine’s weight capacity can accommodate your needs..

If you are looking for versatile strength-building home gym equipment to achieve a full-body workout, a Smith machine can help you achieve your goals. Since the 1950s, this game-changing machine has allowed gym-goers to work out safely without a spotter. Today, there is a wide range of consumer options, allowing you to experience the benefits of the Smith machine in the comfort of your own home gym.

Smith machines all perform similar functions, but there are different types of Smith machines available. For instance, some Smith machines provide a vertical path for motion, while other Smith machines provide a slightly angled path. Some Smith machines may be limited to the Smith machine function, while others are designed to be all-in-one machines with multiple stations for different exercises. Smith machines vary based on the manufacturer.

Yes, you can deadlift on a Smith machine, but whether you should depends on your skills and ability.Maietta suggests thinking through the following questions before performing moves on a Smith machine:-How is your range of motion?-Do you have the proper form or mobility to perform these compound moves?If you do not know, Maietta suggests working with a local fitness professional who will be able to help coach you and correct your form if necessary.

Yes, you can build muscle with the consistent use of a Smith machine. Smith machines are considered a good strength and muscle training option for beginners or those without a spotter. However, the drawback is motion is limited to a specific vertical (or slightly angled) path. For sports-specific muscle building, some experts prefer free weight exercises.

Yes, you can squat with a Smith machine. Safety features such as hooks and stoppers can help provide extra protection. Again, be mindful of your abilities and consult with a fitness pro if you are unsure of how to do this safely and with proper form.

#8554. Denny Giamazzo Sees Resilience and Fitness as Gifts to Navigate Adversity

A mantra (from the Sanskrit man, meaning “mind,” and tra, meaning “tool” or “instrument”) is an instrument of thought: a sacred word, sound, or phrase repeated aloud or silently to anchor and focus the mind.

While its origins are rooted in ancient Vedic, Hindu, and Buddhist traditions, mantras are used today across both spiritual practices and secular psychology for anchoring focus in meditation, calming the nervous system, or cognitive reframing.

Denny Giamazzo has relied on a mantra throughout his life to get through many difficult times and challenges, and he still lives by it today.

“Someone else out there has had it worse. They have come back stronger, and they are doing more with less. I am not allowed to feel sorry for myself.”

When Giamazzo talks about facing adversity throughout his life, he means literally. Born two months premature and never finding out who his biological father is, young Denny’s life began in Worcester, Massachusetts with his mother. At least he was supposed to be with her. Giamazzo recalled numerous times when she would leave him for hours or even days at a time without him knowing where she went. An upstairs neighbor would watch him if he knew young Denny was alone.

By the time he was five, his mother passed away from AIDS and Giamazzo entered the foster care system. He would eventually live with his aunt. As tragic as that story appears, Giamazzo managed to find a silver lining that serves him to this day.

He said, “I think what I took from that was just an insane amount of resiliency.”

That resiliency would be an anchor throughout his younger years. Giamazzo would stay with his grandfather while his aunt worked, but an uncle also lived there and was physically abusive. This continued into Giamazzo’s teenage years.

“We got into it a lot,” he recalled. Fortunately, he found another anchor in sports and fitness. He played organized baseball before high school but went on to play basketball and football at the high school level. The physical challenges and improvement that came from playing served as driving forces for him.

“At a young age, I just loved putting my body through things and seeing what I was capable of.”

Giamazzo joined the Army in 2006 and served for nearly seven years. During that time, he was deployed to Afghanistan from 2010 to 2011. Giamazzo was simply looking for direction when he entered the military, but the infantry team leader found more than that as his career progressed.

He shared, “I really didn’t join with this burning desire to go serve my country or anything like that. That’s what it turned into after really getting embedded in that lifestyle and working with the guys I got to work with every day.”

Giamazzo did not leave Afghanistan unscathed. He needed two right shoulder surgeries, and like many soldiers, he had to navigate Post-Traumatic Stress Disorder (PTSD) in the aftermath of that deployment. Once again, Giamazzo leaned on the resilience he forged in childhood to move forward.

“That inner strength and those lessons of resiliency that I learned early on as a kid have kind of been a barometer for me my entire life,” he explained. “It led me through just about any pain, adversity, or objective that I’ve hit and then had to overcome throughout my entire life.”

Giamazzo also credits the gym and training. He trains five days a week and will mix it up between weights and High Intensity Interval Training (HIIT). He particularly likes the CrossFit workout “Cindy.”

A 2023 review by researchers at Duke University and Mount Sinai found that regular exercise can be just as effective as medication for easing depression. Having a positive and aggressive outlet that negatively affected no one else is something Giamazzo leaned on then and continues to now.

“It really has been probably the most integral part of addressing my PTSD.”

Giamazzo has found several ways to turn negativity into positivity and is now committed to sharing what he learned with others. His experiences hold more lessons than a single interview can capture, which is why he put them into his book, Wired for Action, which serves as both an autobiography and a guide for others who may be facing their own challenges.

Giamazzo said, “It’s easy sometimes to feel like we’re on an island by ourselves. That’s just not the case.”

He also hosts the Be the Standard Podcast, where he and co-host Mike Barnes cover a variety of topics such as men’s mental health, combat trauma, PTSD, identity, personal responsibility, discipline, faith, leadership, and more. The public speaker and leadership consultant also directly helps others break self-destructive habits and explore new ways to meet their potential despite the traumas they face.

“I would say that for each individual, it’s on them,” he shared. “It comes down to ‘What type of person do I want to be? What action do I need to take to reach those objectives?’ If you know what you want out of life, you know exactly the type of person you want to be, and you’re willing to put the work in, I think that’s going to give you a substantial amount of purpose.”

That is advice that comes from experience, but Giamazzo offers a shorter version that could be another mantra for those needing a source of hope to take with them into the future.

“Cindy” is one of the more popular CrossFit benchmark workouts and can be used for either a quick challenging full-body session or for a way to monitor your fitness periodically. All you need is a pull-up bar and your bodyweight.

Perform as many rounds as possible in 20 minutes of these exercises.

Track the number of rounds you can complete and set a goal to beat it in the future. Beginners can shoot for 8 rounds and work their way up from there. The competitive CrossFit (Rx) standard is 20 rounds, with 25 and more being considered “Elite.”

You can order Wired for Action on Amazon. Follow Giamazzo on Instagram @dennygiamazzo.

“I’m sick of the scaring, the terror, the fright. I’m tired of being something that goes bump in the night. I’m bored with leering my horrible glances, And my feet hurt from dancing those skeleton dances. I don’t like graveyards, and I need something new. There must be more to life than just yelling, ‘Boo!'”

—Tim Burton, The Nightmare Before Christmas

Dr. Wednesday Addams sat alone in her office at 11 PM, glaring at her retirement calculator the way you’d glare at a pathology report you already suspect is bad.

Twenty years of serious income, the kind that makes the neighbors assume you’re rich, and the screen looked like a crime scene.

Projected retirement age: 79. Probability of success: 23%. Her portfolio had roughly the life expectancy of a jack-o’-lantern left on the porch until Thanksgiving.

She was 58. She wanted out at 61, and blocking the exit stood a tangle of whole life policies her cousin had sold her, a 401(k) ignored for a decade, a pre-tax balance quietly wiring itself into a tax bomb, and a household burning $35,000 a month like a furnace nobody remembered to turn down.

Her story isn’t rare. It isn’t even interesting.

Physicians stumble into the same open graves with the reliability of a zombie shuffling toward the nearest brain, and the tax code waiting at the bottom helps itself to 37 cents of every married dollar above $768,700. Some of these graves are fresh. A few were dug by Congress.

The AMA’s latest national data has 41.9% of physicians reporting at least one symptom of burnout in 2025, down from 48.2% in 2023. Progress, technically. Emergency medicine and hematology-oncology still sit near 50%, coin-flip odds that the physician running tonight’s code is cooked.

Burnout steals your joy first and your retirement date second. You plan to work until 68, the call schedule wins at 61, and the seven years of full income your plan quietly assumed shrink to a few years of part-time pay, or nothing at all.

The itch is arriving earlier, too. In Doximity’s polling, the share of physicians aged 45 to 49 considering early retirement nearly doubled between 2023 and 2026, from 23% to 44%.

Dr. Smart and Dr. Addams both started at 35 earning $300,000. Smart saved 25%, or $75,000 a year. Addams saved 10%.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Run that $45,000 annual gap through 25 years at a 5% real return and it grows to about $2.15 million by age 60, a fortune separating two doctors with the same income at the same hospital, parked in the same doctors’ lot, one of them driving home to a plan and the other to a calculator that reads like a death certificate.

Addams spent every productivity bonus. You’ve already met her at 11 PM.

You go from a resident making $65,000 to an attending earning $350,000, and the word “deserve” moves into your vocabulary. A bigger house. Then tens of thousands sunk into renovating it, followed by the new car, the au pair, private school, and first class to Maui.

Nobody warns you how hard it is to downshift once you’ve gotten used to the view. Your brain resets “normal” to match your paycheck and refuses to reset it back, so the spending tags along into retirement like a party guest who showed up uninvited and also brought luggage.

I watched an Arizona cardiologist discover at 66 that he needed $400,000 a year to keep living the way he lived. His portfolio could safely throw off maybe $180,000. He’s 71 now. Still full-time.

Simple, boring solution: live like a resident for two to five years after training, bank the gap, kill the student loans, and upgrade slowly enough that your brain never registers the drift.

Nearly every physician gets pitched whole life insurance, usually by a friend or relative whose licensing exam ink is still wet. The illustration promises cash value, tax-free growth, and a death benefit, all in one tidy package.

For most physicians who need life insurance, it’s mostly garbage. Premiums run many times higher than term. Commissions feed on the early years, and the cash value grows like it’s been bled.

Run an illustrative comparison: one physician pays $3,000 a month into whole life, while her colleague buys 20-year term for around $150 a month and invests the other $2,850, and at a 7% return that side account sits near $1.5 million after 20 years, with the policy’s cash value usually trailing by hundreds of thousands, still waiting for the illustration to come true.

Sold by family, illustrated in optimistic colors, and funded for 15 years by a doctor too busy to read past page two, Dr. Addams’s three policies carried combined premiums of $8,400 a month and a total cash value of $780,000.

Term plus investing would likely have left her near $1.9 million. She surrendered all three at 58. Ate the surrender charges. Started catching up.

In plenty of physician households, one person earns the money and the same person manages it.

Then the doctor dies, divorces, or has a stroke at 63, and the spouse inherits decades of decisions made behind a closed door, written in a language nobody bothered to teach them.

I’ve sat with widows who found out their physician husband had:

A spouse at the table pulls decisions toward the conservative side, a handy counterweight when the 2 AM version of you thinks genius has struck.

Build the plan simple enough that they could run it alone. Keep the account list and passwords somewhere they can actually find, which rules out your head.

Business school professors have a phrase for the bad investments that circulate in medical circles: deals that can only be sold to doctors.

Time poverty and overconfidence do the damage. Researching an investment takes hours you don’t have, so you trust people, and you assume that mastering the coagulation cascade somehow qualifies you to underwrite private equity. It doesn’t.

Physicians I know have poured money into restaurant groups that folded within 18 months, real estate “opportunities” that smelled faintly of Ponzi, and crypto tokens launched by a nephew’s roommate’s brother.

Index funds are boring. They work. Put $50,000 a year into low-cost index funds for 30 years at a 5% real return and you end up with about $3.32 million.

Lose 2% a year to fees and the same contributions grow to about $2.38 million, close to a million dollars handed to people in nicer suits than yours. If your portfolio needs a 40-page binder to explain, you’re the mark.

Most physicians blow past the taxable wage base ($184,500 in 2026) months before December, which puts you among the few groups who routinely qualify for the maximum benefit. Claiming age is a bigger lever for you than for almost anyone.

According to AARP, a worker at the 2026 maximum who files at 62 collects about $2,969 a month. Wait until full retirement age and that rises to $4,152. Hold out to 70 and it’s roughly $5,181.

Dr. Lucky filed at 62 because he “wanted the money while the government still had it.” Six months later he picked up locums at $200 an hour, and because Social Security withholds $1 for every $2 you earn above $24,480 before full retirement age, his own paycheck ate his benefit, which the SSA hands back after full retirement age in small monthly crumbs.

If you’re married, the higher earner’s claiming age also sets the survivor benefit, so delaying to 70 works like inflation-adjusted life insurance for your spouse at a premium no insurer will match. A serious diagnosis can justify claiming early.

For a healthy 62-year-old with a seven-figure portfolio, it’s usually the wrong call. You’ve delivered enough prognoses to know which patient you are.

Most physicians stuff nearly everything into pre-tax accounts during peak years, which makes sense at 37%. Trouble arrives when that’s the only move for 25 years, because a $4 million pre-tax portfolio is a smaller number dressed up for the party.

If you need $180,000 a year to live and pull it entirely from pre-tax accounts, you might withdraw $240,000 to get there. Your 4.5% withdrawal plan just became a 6% plan.

Required minimum distributions start at 73 (75 if you were born in 1960 or later) and stack on top of Social Security. Then Medicare notices.

IRMAA surcharges for 2026 begin at modified AGI of $218,000 for married couples, and at the top tier Part B jumps from $202.90 a month to $689.90, plus a $91 Part D surcharge, roughly $6,900 a year per person, a fine levied for the crime of saving diligently in the wrong bucket.

Medicare looks back two years, so the income you report at 63 sets your premiums at 65.

But if you retire at 58, delay Social Security, and you may get a decade of taxable income lower than anything since residency, a window for converting chunks of pre-tax money to Roth on purpose, in measured doses, the way you’d titrate a drip rather than push a bolus.

While you’re still working, fund a backdoor Roth IRA ($7,500 limit in 2026) and send part of your savings to the Roth side of your employer plan. If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages last year, the IRS already decided for you: your 2026 catch-up contributions go in as Roth.

Asset location matters too, and municipal bonds can help outside retirement accounts.

At 37% plus the 3.8% Net Investment Income Tax, close to 41 cents of every taxable bond interest dollar goes to Washington. Keep bonds inside the 401(k) or 403(b). Hold broad stock index funds in taxable.

Two physicians can retire with identical portfolios and identical withdrawal rates and still get completely different endings. Timing decides which. Finance calls it sequence of returns risk, and you’ll call it something less printable.

Retire in February 2020 and you watched the Dow fall from about 29,550 to under 19,000 in roughly six weeks. Retire into 2022 and the S&P 500 dropped about 19% as inflation spiked.

Even 2025 had teeth: the S&P 500 fell almost 19% between its February high and early April as tariff headlines rattled markets.

Dr. Smart retires into three good years and coasts. Dr. Lucky (whose name keeps aging badly) retires into a bear market, sells near the bottom to fund two years of travel, and never gets those shares back.

William Bengen’s 4% rule, published in 1994, tries to account for that, and Bengen has since nudged his own number up to about 4.7%. The real mistake is treating any figure as carved on a tombstone.

Retirees who trim spending after bad years, or who keep two to five years of withdrawals in cash and short-term bonds, give their stocks room to recover instead of selling them on the way down.

Dr. Addams checked her allocation at 59 and found 95% stocks, 5% cash, and no plan for a crash. She moved to 60/30/10 stocks, bonds, and cash and started building a three-year buffer. Her mix won’t fit everyone, but “I’ll figure it out when it happens” fits nobody.

Don’t overcorrect into a bond basement either. Retire at 57 and your money may need to last 35 years, so stocks still have work to do.

CPI peaked at 9.1% in June 2022. Inflation cooled. Prices didn’t.

A $200,000 retirement budget becomes about $361,000 in 20 years at 3% inflation, and any income stream that doesn’t adjust, whether a fixed annuity, a pension without a cost-of-living rider, or a practice buyout paid in level installments, shrinks every year you hold it, rotting quietly from the inside the way pumpkins do.

You already know this feeling from the reimbursement side. The AMA estimates Medicare physician pay has fallen by roughly a third since 2001 after adjusting for practice-cost inflation.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Give your retirement plan the same respect for erosion you’ve watched eat your fee schedule.

Your brother needs $50,000 for a business. Your sister needs $30,000 to stop a foreclosure.

A few years later your kid asks for $80,000 toward a house, because you’re the rich doctor, and the rich doctor is who people call, and nobody in the history of families has ever called the rich doctor to pay him back.

Treat money to family as a gift with no strings, sized to what you can afford to never see again. Dr. Addams lent her brother $120,000 for a restaurant. It failed. He filed for bankruptcy, and they haven’t spoken in six years.

Long-term rental losses usually land in the passive bucket, where they can’t touch clinical income. Short-term rentals play by different rules.

If the average guest stay runs seven days or less and you materially participate, most commonly by logging more than 100 hours a year and more than any other individual, the losses turn non-passive and can offset W-2 or 1099 income (a separate route from Real Estate Professional Status), the closest thing the tax code offers to a garlic necklace for your paycheck.

Pair that with a cost segregation study and 100% bonus depreciation, which the One Big Beautiful Bill Act permanently restored for property acquired after January 19, 2025.

A $500,000 short-term rental might produce $150,000 to $200,000 of year-one depreciation, worth roughly $55,000 to $74,000 in federal tax at 37%.

Locums, telehealth, medical director stipends, expert witness work: if any of it lands on a 1099, a Solo 401(k) usually beats the SEP-IRA most contractors open by default. For 2026 you can defer up to $24,500 as the “employee” (shared with any W-2 plan you also use), plus an employer contribution of roughly 20% of net self-employment earnings, up to $72,000 combined, with $8,000 in catch-up at 50 or $11,250 between 60 and 63. The SEP also poisons your backdoor Roth through the pro-rata rule.

Older 1099 physicians with steady income should price out a cash balance plan on top, where contributions often reach six figures for doctors in their 50s. Those deductions pull double duty because of the QBI cliff.

For 2026, married couples get the full 20% qualified business income deduction at or below $403,500 of taxable income, and it disappears at $553,500. A married 1099 doc with $500,000 of taxable income who funds both plans can slide below $403,500 and watch the deduction rise from the dead.

Medicine breeds a specific condition. You hit your number, decide you need a bigger one, and a market dip talks you into another year, then another, until you’re 68 with $9 million and a partner gently asking whether you’ve considered slowing down.

Every year worked past enough gets paid for with a year you’ll never get back at that age, a year of knees that still handle a trail and a back that still lifts a grandkid, traded for a margin of safety your spreadsheet stopped needing long ago, which makes one more year the only prescription in medicine with no ceiling dose.

Physicians who bolt without a plan for Monday get haunted by the opposite problem. You were Dr. Johnson, the cardiologist. Now you’re Bob, with 50 empty hours a week and no idea what to put in them.

Some Bobs end up unretiring just to have somewhere to be.

Easing out tends to go better than slamming the door. Dropping to 0.6 FTE, picking up locums, or teaching keeps income flowing and lets the portfolio grow untouched a few more years.

Watch for a malpractice tail bill on a claims-made policy, and remember that governmental 457(b) plans carry no 10% penalty once you separate from service, at any age.

In my experience, physicians who retire toward something stick the landing far more often than those simply running from the pager.

Dr. Addams caught her mistakes at 58 instead of 68, and that gave her room to work. She hired a fee-only fiduciary advisor, wrote a plan, surrendered the bad policies, sold the vacation home, and maxed every account she had.

She retired at 64 on about $18,000 a month instead of $35,000. Plenty, it turned out.

Several year-end moves for 2026 can’t wait for the week between Christmas and New Year’s:

For the rest of the year, check every beneficiary form, add up 12 months of actual spending, swap whole life for adequate term and disability coverage where it makes sense, and bring your spouse into the conversation. Then raise your savings rate 1 to 2 points every year until you hit 25% to 30% of gross.

You’ll make mistakes. Everyone does. What matters is catching them at 58, the way Dr. Addams did, while the options are still standing in the room, instead of at 70, when most of them have left the building and switched off the porch light behind them.

Pick one item from this list before the first trick-or-treater rings your doorbell. Make your CPA earn their fee in November instead of on a panicked phone call in March.

This article is for educational purposes and isn’t individualized tax, legal, or investment advice. Run any strategy past a CPA or fee-only advisor who knows your full situation.

Thanks for this informative and entertaining article. should be required reading for all docs. Made me realize that I am fortunate to have avoided the worst of bad decisions. I’m 78 now and comfortably retired with close family. Life is good.

I’ve made some of these mistakes in my 30s by falling into the luxury trap when decent salaries first hit the accounts. Living in Los Angeles it would be VERY easy to burn 35k per month without luxury cars or private schools. In fact we’re not too far off and we drive older EV cars that are paid off and the kids go to great public schools. The costs of living have increased to the point of needing to pay very close attention to all expenses and max out investment and retirement accounts even when it hurts. We’ve started catching rounding 40, traveling a bit less, no new cars, only making required fixes to the house. After reading this I’m more confident that we’ve made the right decisions to get smart and aggressive about this now.

Interesting article focused on finances with a smattering of other issues. Importantly, what are your support systems upon retirement, like spouse, friends, etc.? Sometimes friends are not there because they choose to move closer to their children or they are deceased. What are your interests in medicine and outside medicine? What are your hobbies? Do you want to volunteer? You have been going 90 miles mph and then slow down to 10 mph. Without some kind of plan to fill your time, with and without your spouse/significant other, this is a recipe for depression and disaster. Do you want to stay connected to medicine in some way? Maybe you can observe trainees doing an H&P and counseling. Maybe you can offer advice as to how to set up an office practice for senior residents. In another ote, how is your health and do you take care of yourself? Going into retirement with significant health issues can influence how your retirement goes and when you retire, perhaps restricting travel and other activities. Academic clinician educators: Confronting the challenges to successful retirement. Educ Health (Abingdon). 2023 Jan-Apr;36(1):24-32. doi: 10.4103/efh.efh_192_22. PMID: 38047344.). Planning ahead is the key, applying principles mentioned in this blog and our paper. We all have worked so hard…..we deserve a great retirement.

great article…great advice. As the offspring of depression era parents, I was taught (by example) early to be thrifty and save. When burnout came at age 62, I was ready and haven’t looked back. My only regret is being too conservative with my investments, but then again being more aggressive would have forced me to hang on some extra years after the 2008 market crash.

Most of us have limited our spending as our reimbursement has declined. Many of us have actually struggled even keeping a low profile and living with economic restraints. I stopped reading at that figure because it is just absurd.

I appreciate you taking the time to comment, even if you stopped reading at the $35K figure. Let me address your skepticism directly, because you’re right to be shocked—and that’s exactly the point. When I wrote this article, I had a word count limit on how much I could disclose on the background of Doctor Addams (who is really a he). What I did not go into detail about is how he arrived at where he is today. It’s not one absurd decision. It’s twenty years of reasonable-sounding decisions that compound like interest you can’t afford.

Dr. Addams didn’t wake up one day and decide to burn through $420K annually. He made decisions that seemed perfectly justified at each step. I would not have discovered what my friend was going through had I not asked him to invest in my startup back then. He then confided how illiquid he was and how much in a hole he was in.

The reality is that our monthly expenses are not the usual discussion physicians talk about in the physicians’ lounge. It’s really very personal, so I get it that this sounds absurd, but the reality is that there is a lot of shame ascribed to our salaries when we really aren’t visibly successful. So why would we share it? Which may explain why it sounds so absurd to you. Sadly, he is not the first person in such a financial hole since its more common than you think. So what happened?

His surgical group was thriving pre-COVID. She was making $400K+ and felt secure in budgeting for this lifestyle. Then the floor dropped:

Insurance reimbursements got slashed Hospital-based specialty groups ate their market share

His income dropped to $280K, then $240K (he was already burned out from trying to get bigger dividends he had to do more call, which was not sustainable. Yeah, many private groups make these kind of dead-end deals)

What happened next? He did not scale back his lifestyle because he was optimistic about his future. I don’t have the space here to list his expenses but what I remember after a very emotional and stressful session was that his parents were aging and he had to help financially. His sister-in-law had a business that he helped with some capital, which became a recurring theme. All these decisions are made with good intentions, but they add up. He leased a really nice car and could not figure out how to back out of that deal.

The real lesson: This story isn’t about judgment. It’s about prevention. Every physician should see this and think: “Could this happen to me with just 3-4 different decisions?”

Because here’s the truth: The distance between financial security and financial disaster for a high-earning physician is about five bad decisions over twenty years. That’s it.

Your restraint is admirable. But I wrote this article for the physicians who haven’t shown that restraint yet—and who still have time to fix it before they’re staring at a retirement calculator at age 58.

The $35K isn’t absurd. It’s terrifyingly more common (than you think) among physicians who started making big money without a financial plan. If this article makes even one physician audit their spending before it’s too late, it was worth writing—and worth your discomfort reading it.

As someone who spends at 30k per month, let me help with this: $2500 per month goes to an aging parent on one side, $2000 to an aging parent on the other. 3.5k per month goes to a vacation home mortgage and expenses, although it has appreciated enough over time that that will be eventually recovered. Travel is a big one as our 6 children and 6 grandchildren live all over the place, and flights, airport parking etc are $5000 per month. Life insurance is a big one, at 2k per month, health for myself is only $600 per month but it’s $1500 for my wife. I’ll stop there, but we are not driving fancy cars and our primary residence is only worth 330k, hardly a mansion. I retired with over 6 million NW and 60k in pension/ss, which will probably cover it: once the elderly parents have passed it should work out, but we might have to sell the vacation house when we are older.

This should be required reading for every resident – and required re-reading every year of residency and beyond! I appreciate the comments about spouses being involved in all finances – that goes for us, too! Many of us are married to high-earners who manage their own (and sometimes our) finances and find out too late that they were terrible at it.

Thank you! You’re absolutely right—this should be mandatory reading starting in residency, before the income jump happens and the mistakes become expensive.

Your point about spouses needing to be involved cuts both ways, and it’s critical. I’ve sat with too many people who discovered their high-earning spouse was: – Flying blind with no actual plan – Paying 2% in fees to an advisor who was just collecting checks – Invested in their buddy’s restaurant/startup/crypto scheme – Carrying three whole life insurance policies they didn’t understand – Making $400K but somehow living paycheck to paycheck

Financial competence doesn’t correlate with income or intelligence. A physician making $500K can be just as clueless as anyone else—sometimes more so, because the high income masks the problems until it’s too late.

Being involved doesn’t mean you need to manage everything. It means you know where the accounts are, understand the plan, can access everything if needed, and serve as that crucial second set of eyes. Your spouse’s overconfidence plus your informed questions might prevent a catastrophic mistake.

Money is a team sport. Whether you’re the earner or the spouse, staying informed and involved isn’t optional—it’s survival.

#8549. Want Stronger Bones? Weight Training May Only Be Part of the Solution

Sign up below to receive our newest workout routines, recipes, news stories, and offers from our partners

With the right plan and the right discipline, you can get seriously shredded in just 28 days.

At age 62, "Big Bill" shares his wisdom to dominate one of the ultimate strength marks.

Follow these fit women we're crushing on for inspiration, workout ideas, and motivation.

For decades science has been demonstrating, quite effectively, that weight training is good for your bones. It’s one of those physical truths that has become so thoroughly accepted nobody bothers arguing about it anymore. Lift weights, build muscle, strengthen your skeleton, and keep pushing. Excellent. Another axiom etched in stone.

Except for the fact that science has this annoying habit of reopening cases we thought were long closed.

A new meta-analysis published in Sports Medicine—Open looked at 24 clinical studies involving 1,238 healthy adults and found something you wouldn’t expect. When researchers examined biological markers associated with bone formation, the biggest responses weren’t coming from walking, jogging, step aerobics, or even conventional resistance training. They came from high-intensity activities involving acceleration, impact, sudden changes of direction, and explosive movement. Recreational soccer and handball produced some of the strongest responses, with certain bone-formation markers increasing by as much as 45 to 46 percent.

Impressive data for sure, but I wouldn’t go abandoning weight training just yet.

Bones are living tissue. They respond to mechanical stress, just like all the other structures involved, but apparently they pay particular attention when that stress arrives suddenly and from different directions. Running, jumping, cutting, stopping, accelerating, and changing direction produce forces that conventional lifting doesn’t produce, despite being extremely demanding muscularly. A brutally slow leg press can make your quads beg to be amputated, while your skeleton experiences something much less severe than it would if you were dribbling a soccer ball downfield dodging opponents.

That does not mean lifting weights is useless for bones. There’s plenty of existing evidence supporting resistance exercise for skeletal health, and strength training also improves muscle, balance, and physical function—all things you’d rather possess when gravity eventually reminds you who’s boss.

It means this particular analysis suggests resistance training may not be the entire answer.

There’s also a practical problem with telling older people worried about osteoporosis to immediately start jumping, cutting, and playing handball. The people most concerned about fragile bones are precisely the people we shouldn’t suddenly send sprinting through an obstacle course. For younger lifters, however, I think there’s a useful message here. Somewhere along the way, bodybuilding taught us to eliminate unnecessary movement. Machines got better. Exercises became more controlled. We learned how to isolate a muscle so effectively that the rest of the body barely has to participate. That’s great if the sole objective is hypertrophy.

Maybe occasionally sprint. Jump. Carry something. Change direction. Play a sport. Do something that requires your skeleton to deal with forces that don’t arrive on a perfectly greased track at exactly the same angle every repetition.

I’m still going to lift weights. You should too. But apparently your bones may appreciate being reminded that the human body was designed to do more than sit on a machine and push.

It’s really quite simple, if you want to look and respond like an athlete then you have to train like an athlete, which means you have to do athletic stuff. One trick ponies don’t age well.

My first patient was already dead. She arrived zipped in a vinyl bag, smelling of formaldehyde and phenol, and she taught me more anatomy in one semester than any lecturer managed in four years.

Somewhere between the first incision and the nervous jokes about her coral nail polish, I figured out that the human body runs stranger than the textbook admits. The mind bolted to it runs stranger still.

The years since have only confirmed the suspicion. Some of what I’ve seen belongs in a haunted house. The rest belongs in a haunted house with a billing department.

For Halloween this year, I’m recalling some of the odd things about being human you learn as a physician over the years.

Retirement is optional for the dead. Donated bodies pick up second careers the day their first one ends. At Wayne State University in Detroit, cadavers have ridden impact sleds for decades so engineers could learn what a steering column does to a sternum when a sedan meets a bridge abutment.

Seatbelts, airbags, and padded dashboards all carry the fingerprints of people who signed a donor form and then absorbed the kind of blow no living volunteer would accept. Count the people who walk away from highway crashes today, and a fair share owe a thank-you note to somebody in a body bag.

My cadaver spent her retirement teaching a roomful of first-years how a hand works. Meanwhile I spend Tuesday afternoons on hold with a prior authorization line. She was more productive, and she never billed.
