Stranger Things Day slipped past earlier this month. Fans mark it every November 6, the anniversary of the night in 1983 when Will Byers rode his bike home from Mike’s basement and never made it.

One minute he was pedaling through Hawkins, Indiana, and the next he was gone, swallowed by a dimension running parallel to his own. Same streets, same house, just darker, colder, and coated in a black rot that fed on everything it touched.

If you missed the rewatch and the Eggo waffles, you have 354 days until the next one. You have 44 until December 31.

Your retirement savings took the same trip Will did. Nobody stole the money. It got relocated. The IRS built a gate decades ago, and your 401(k), your IRA, and your SEP all got pulled through it. The balance shows up in your statement. Touching it before 59½ costs a ransom.

By the time Stranger Things Day rolls around again on November 6, 2027, the 2026 tax year will be closed and filed. Every move in this article that opens an exit, the conversions, the contributions, the rollovers you make or wisely skip, has to happen before the ball drops on New Year’s Eve. The IRS doesn’t hand out extensions on the calendar.

Stranger Things needed five seasons to explain the Upside Down: what it was, how it touched the real world, where the gates opened and closed. Viewers watched the characters stumble through it for years with Christmas lights and homemade gear because no one who understood the place ever sat them down and drew it out.

That is the average physician’s relationship with the tax code.

Thousands of pages, scattered across decades of amendments and rulings and bills with names like SECURE Act 2.0 and the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.

Medical school skips it. Residency skips it too. And the advisor managing your portfolio, assuming you have one, probably maxed your employer 401(k), mentioned a backdoor Roth in passing, and called it a day.

The exits are sitting right there in the code, seven of them, penalty-free and legal, like the hidden passages in the Creel house. Physicians retire years later than they want to, or burn out before they get there, because nobody drew them the map.

This is the map, updated for 2026, a year when the rules changed in your favor for once.

Season one gave us the Demogorgon, a faceless predator that dragged people into the Upside Down and fed on them. The whole town lived in fear of a thing it didn’t understand.

The 10% early withdrawal penalty is the Demogorgon.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

Pull money from an IRA or 401(k) before 59½ and the IRS adds 10% on top of ordinary income tax. For a physician in a high bracket, the combined hit can eat close to half of whatever comes out.

The Demogorgon doesn’t negotiate. Burned out at 57, practice imploded, three kids in college and a cash crunch right now? It takes its cut regardless.

What the residents of Hawkins never learned was that the monster had weaknesses. Enough heat and it retreated. Eleven could stop it cold. The penalty has weaknesses too, seven of them, and the rest of this piece walks through each one.

Eleven could move objects, close gates, and stop the worst things the Upside Down produced. She’d spent years locked in a government lab, and most people had no idea she existed.

The assumption bleeding W-2 physicians dry is that a Solo 401(k) belongs only to private practice owners and full-time contractors. Any physician with self-employment income and no full-time employees qualifies.

The hospitalist picking up two weekend locum shifts a month qualifies, as does the employed cardiologist who took a single paid speaking gig and the academic who cashed a CME honorarium check.

The size of that income sets how much you can contribute. It never decides whether you’re eligible.

For 2026, total contributions to a Solo 401(k) cap out at $72,000 per person. Inside that structure lives the Mega Backdoor Roth: after-tax contributions to the Solo 401(k), converted to Roth either in-plan or by rolling them out to a Roth IRA.

A tax-free bucket that grows without the government touching the back end, with contribution basis you can reach when you need it.

You and your spouse both work in a practice with no other full-time employees? Each of you can put in up to $72,000, which means $144,000 a year flowing into Roth. Let that run five years and you’re sitting on a pool of penalty-free basis the IRS has no further claim on.

The 2026 wrinkle that tilts the math further: under SECURE Act 2.0, anyone who earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages from an employer last year and makes catch-up contributions to that employer’s plan must now make them as Roth.

The pre-tax catch-up option is gone for high earners. The government forced your hand on $8,000 of after-tax money. The Solo 401(k) lets you do the same thing deliberately, at scale, with $72,000.

Most physicians never open one because most content written for physicians stops at the employer 401(k). Setting one up takes an afternoon. Leaving it unopened while the income to fund it is already landing in your checking account is an information problem, and information problems are cheap to fix.

Season two introduced the Mind Flayer, a massive psychic entity that didn’t kill its victims outright. It possessed them. Its hosts acted against their own interests, convinced the whole time they were doing the right thing.

Physicians who botch the backdoor Roth rarely make obvious errors. The pro-rata rule has possessed them, and they don’t know it.

The backdoor Roth, done right: make a non-deductible contribution to a Traditional IRA ($7,500 in 2026, $8,600 if you’re 50 or older).

Confirm you hold zero pre-tax IRA dollars anywhere under your name, meaning no SEP-IRA, no rollover IRA, no forgotten traditional IRA from residency parked at a custodian you haven’t logged into since 2015. Convert. No income limit, no penalty.

The pro-rata rule wrecks the whole thing the moment pre-tax IRA dollars enter the picture. The IRS won’t let you convert only the after-tax portion. It blends every IRA you own into one pot and taxes the conversion proportionally. One forgotten pre-tax account turns a clean transaction into a partial tax event.

Career transitions are where physicians get exposed. Leaving academics and rolling the 403(b) into a rollover IRA.

Switching from group practice to 1099 work and parking the old 401(k) “temporarily.” Starting a new employed role months before the new plan opens its doors. Each one plants a pre-tax IRA landmine that quietly breaks the backdoor Roth for years.

The fix is to roll every pre-tax IRA dollar into the Solo 401(k) before running any backdoor conversion. The Solo 401(k) accepts incoming rollovers and clears the pro-rata calculation entirely. Close the gate before the Mind Flayer gets through, and the rest of the plan stays intact.

Season three ended on what felt like a win. The gate closed, Billy sacrificed himself, Hopper appeared to die, and Hawkins seemed to heal. Then season four arrived and Vecna had been working the whole time, building and feeding while everyone celebrated.

Physician burnout runs on the same script. Roughly half of physicians report burnout in Medscape’s annual surveys, which makes it less a risk factor than a coin flip. We acknowledge it at conferences, tape mental health flyers to the break room wall, and go back to the 60-hour weeks we call resilience.

A financial plan that only works if you never burn out is a prayer dressed up as a spreadsheet.

Enter the Rule of 55, one of the most useful provisions most physicians have never heard of. Separate from your employer (quit, retire, get laid off) during or after the calendar year you turn 55, and you can tap that employer’s 401(k) with no 10% penalty. Income tax still applies. The Demogorgon, though, is gone.

Dr. Addams burns out at 56. Dr. Smart at 57. Both qualify, provided they left the employer 401(k) alone.

That proviso is where the plan dies. Roll the 401(k) into an IRA before you separate and the Rule of 55 no longer applies, because the provision covers employer-sponsored plans only. Once the rollover clears, the window shuts for good.

A second move widens the window. Old 401(k) balances from prior employers that now sit in rollover IRAs can be consolidated into your current employer’s plan before you separate. Leave at 55 or later and the Rule of 55 covers the entire consolidated balance.

Some plans refuse incoming rollovers, so check with the administrator. For a physician who has collected balances across three hospitals and two practices, this can multiply the penalty-free pool available the day they decide they’re done.

If you’re in your early 50s and have so much as daydreamed about an early exit, stop rolling employer 401(k)s into IRAs. Leave them where they sit. You’re protecting an option.

Season four revealed that the Upside Down had a full tunnel network connecting distant points across Hawkins. It had existed all along. The kids who survived did so partly because they found the tunnels early enough to use them.

The Roth conversion ladder is the tunnel system.

In any low-income year, meaning any year your taxable income sits well below normal physician earnings, convert a chunk of pre-tax retirement money (Traditional IRA, SEP-IRA, Solo 401(k)) to a Roth IRA. Pay income tax on the converted amount at that year’s rate.

Five years from January 1 of the conversion year, those dollars become accessible penalty-free, regardless of your age.

2026 is an unusually good year to run conversions. The One Big Beautiful Bill Act made the lower TCJA brackets permanent and locked in the 20% pass-through deduction for physicians with 1099 income. Conversions done at today’s rates cost less than they would have under the old sunset schedule, and Congress rarely improves things twice in a row.

Each conversion year runs its own five-year clock. Convert in 2026 and those dollars open January 1, 2031. Convert again in 2027 and that tranche opens January 1, 2032. Run conversions every year and you build a rolling pipeline, a new tranche unlocking every January.

The years physicians routinely waste: the sabbatical between positions (a six-month gap is one of the most valuable tax-planning windows of an entire career), parental leave with no 1099 income, the ramp-up after joining a new practice, the W-2 to 1099 switch, the wind-down to part-time locums before full retirement.

Size each conversion to fill the 22% or 24% bracket without tripping IRMAA surcharges on Medicare premiums. The tragedy is the physician who takes six months off, earns half a year’s income, files a clean return, and converts nothing. Five figures of lifetime tax savings, gone.

Ted Weschler’s story makes the point. One of Warren Buffett’s deputies at Berkshire Hathaway built a Traditional IRA worth north of $100 million, then converted the entire thing to Roth and paid a reported $28 million in tax to do it.

Every dollar in that account now grows and distributes tax-free. The mechanics are identical whether you’re converting $50,000 or $50 million.

In season three, the Russians ran a secret facility beneath Starcourt Mall, funded and staffed outside every rule the people upstairs lived by.

The Solo 401(k) participant loan is your private underground operation.

Borrow up to $50,000 or 50% of the account balance, whichever is less, at any time and for any reason. There’s no credit check or underwriter, and no waiting period. You approve your own loan. The rate runs around prime, and every dollar of interest flows back into your own account, so you’re paying yourself.

The physician use cases are specific: a down payment on a rental property during a cash-lean year, bridge funding during a practice startup before revenue normalizes, or covering a surprise expense without selling appreciated holdings in a taxable account and triggering capital gains.

Employer 401(k) loans carry a risk the Solo 401(k) deletes. Leave your job with an outstanding employer loan and the full balance comes due by your tax filing deadline; fail to repay and the IRS reclassifies it as a distribution, taxable plus the 10% penalty. You cannot fire yourself from your own plan. That risk doesn’t exist here.

The series finale didn’t end through brute force. It ended because the characters finally understood the rules of the dimension well enough to find exits nobody had used.

SECURE Act 2.0 added penalty exceptions that read, with only slight exaggeration, like admission criteria. Physicians should recognize them on sight. Few have seen them applied to their own accounts.

The terminal illness provision stops physicians cold the first time they hear it. If a physician certifies that a patient’s condition is expected to result in death within 84 months, that patient can tap any retirement account penalty-free, with optional repayment within three years if the patient recovers. You write this certification regularly. It applies to your own accounts in exactly the same way, and almost no one knows it.

The claim that retirement accounts lock money away is far less true than it was five years ago. These accounts now double as a safety net. A physician who dismisses them as untouchable before 59½ is running on stale data.

In the finale, Hopper and Murray prepared to detonate a bomb to destroy the machine opening the gate. Bluntest instrument available, and at that moment, exactly the right tool.

IRS Rule 72(t) is a bomb. Understand what you’re detonating before you light the fuse.

Under 72(t), you commit to Substantially Equal Periodic Payments (SEPP) from your IRA or 401(k), penalty-free at any age, for the longer of five years or until you turn 59½. Start at 40 and you’re locked in for nearly two decades. Start at 57 and you serve five years.

Three calculation methods exist: Required Minimum Distribution (smallest payments, recalculated annually), Fixed Amortization (highest payments, fixed), and Fixed Annuitization (similar to amortization, also fixed). Most people pick fixed amortization.

The 2026 tax rules changed how charitable gifts are deducted. Join Earned and Physician on FIRE to learn what changed, how to give more tax-efficiently, and what to do before year-end.

Featuring Carole Foos, CPA, Managing Director at Earned, and Jorge Sanchez, MD, of Physician on FIRE.

Takeaway: A practical year-end giving checklist to help you act before December 31.

Tue, Nov 17  ·  2:30 pm ET  ·  11:30 am PT

The catch is severe. Break the schedule in any way, a missed payment, a modification, a single deviation, and the IRS retroactively applies the 10% penalty to every distribution already taken, plus interest. Seven years into a schedule, that bill can be devastating.

One structural move contains the damage. Before starting, split the IRA into two accounts. Apply 72(t) only to the smaller one, sized to produce exactly the income you need, and leave the larger account untouched. An error then costs you the small account’s history, while the bulk of your savings keeps compounding.

72(t) fits the physician who retires well before 55 with a large IRA and needs predictable income before the Roth ladder finishes building. Right tool for a narrow situation, and a poor first resort.

Good diagnosticians don’t commit to one diagnosis before ruling out the alternatives. They build a differential and sequence the workup around probability, available data, and the patient in front of them.

These seven strategies work the same way. No single provision fits every physician, and the right sequence depends on age, income type, career stage, and how close the exit door really is.

Any age, any 1099 income at all: open a Solo 401(k) and max the Mega Backdoor Roth at $72,000. Over 50 and high-earning? Your catch-up contributions have to be Roth anyway, so lean in at scale.

Any low-income year, whether sabbatical, parental leave, practice transition, or a W-2 to 1099 switch: run a Roth conversion. The OBBBA rate environment favors you. Fill the lower brackets and start the five-year clock.

Early 50s and still employed somewhere: stop rolling old 401(k)s into IRAs. Consolidate into the current employer plan and protect the Rule of 55 window.

55 or older and separating from an employer: tap the 401(k) under the Rule of 55 before considering any rollover. That window, once lost, does not reopen.

Pre-55 retirement with a large IRA: the Roth conversion ladder is the primary engine, with 72(t) as backup if the ladder can’t bridge the early years.

Any career stage: learn the SECURE Act 2.0 exceptions. Terminal illness certification, disability, unreimbursed medical expenses. The provisions exist, they’re legal, and they apply to you. Read them before you need them.

The most unsettling reveal in Stranger Things wasn’t the Mind Flayer or the Demogorgon or the Russians under the mall. It was Vecna, one entity pulling strings from the beginning, before anyone knew there were strings.

By the time the kids understood what they were up against, years had passed, and some of them never fully recovered.

Dr. Addams didn’t fail because he earned too little. He failed because no one showed him the exits, and by the time he needed one it was too late to build it. His plan was designed for Dr. Lucky, the physician who never burns out, earns steadily into his mid-60s, and retires on schedule into a fully funded life. Dr. Lucky is a statistical outlier. Dr. Addams and Dr. Smart are the population.

The tax code wasn’t written with physicians in mind, and it doesn’t discriminate against them either. The rules work the same whether you trained at a top academic center or a community program, whether you’re W-2 or 1099, whether you’re planning an exit in three years or still convinced you’ll never burn out.

Right now, in November 2026, you have time. The 2026 tax year is still open. Conversions completed before December 31 start a clock that opens January 1, 2031. Solo 401(k) contributions for 2026 can be made up to your business tax filing deadline. The IRS is expected to announce 2027 limits any day now, with Milliman and Mercer both projecting $25,500 for 401(k) deferrals and $75,000 for total Solo 401(k) contributions. More room to build.

April 15, 2027 arrives the same way every year. The gate doesn’t wait for you to feel ready.

The physicians who retire on their own timeline read the map before they needed it. They found Eleven, ran conversions during the low-income years everyone else treated as inconveniences, stopped rolling accounts into IRAs at 52, and walked out of their last job with options.

The Upside Down has exits. All seven have been there the whole time.

Friends don’t let friends pay the early withdrawal penalty.

Which move fits depends on whether you’ll itemize this year.

#8512. How Much Does A Million Dollar Life Insurance Policy Cost?

Home » Insurance » Life » How Much Does A Million Dollar Life Insurance Policy Cost?

Understanding the cost of a million-dollar life insurance policy can be pivotal in securing your family's financial future. But have you ever wondered just how accessible or costly such a policy might be?

Do you think a million-dollar term life insurance policy sounds like too much insurance?

As a Certified Financial Planner, I see underinsured people every day.

A million-dollar term life insurance policy might actually be the minimum coverage needed for the typical middle-class household, but it’s affordable.

That might sound like an exaggeration, but if you crunch the numbers – just as we’ll be doing a little bit – you’ll realize that a million-dollar policy might be just what you need.

The good news is term life insurance isn’t nearly as costly as most people think.

What makes term life insurance even better is that larger policies cost less on a per thousand basis than smaller policies do. You may find the premium on a $1 million policy is only a little bit higher than it is for $500,000.

Probably, but let’s find out. A general rule of thumb is that you should get 10x your income as baseline coverage for life insurance.

If you’re young, that may be low because you may want to provide your family with enough to replace your income for 15 years or more.

Today, $1 million has become the new baseline for life insurance by a primary breadwinner. Anything less could leave your family financially impaired.

Here’s a list of all the different obligations you may want to have life insurance cover in the unfortunate event you pass away early.

Now that you have an idea of these obligations, let’s punch them into this life insurance calculator to find out if you need a million-dollar policy.

According to Policy Genius, the average cost for a 20-year $1 million term life insurance policy for a 35-year-old male is $53 per month. However, your rate will vary according to the following factors.

The best, and easiest place to start is online. I recommend having two or three insurers compete for your business to make sure you get the best rate and coverage. To see how cheap term life can be, choose your state from the map above to be matched with top life insurance providers instantly.

Let’s look at the individual components that can quickly add up to over a million-dollar policy.

This is where things can get a bit intimidating. Even if you earn a modest income, you may need close to $1 million to replace that income after your death in order to provide for your family’s basic living expenses.

The conventional wisdom in the insurance industry is that you should maintain a life insurance policy equal to between 10 times and 20 times your annual income. So if you earn around $50K per year, that would mean policy coverage between $500K and $1 million.

The complication today is that with interest rates being as low as they are that might not be enough either.

For example, if you have a $1 million policy that could be invested at 5% per year, your family could live on the interest earned – which conveniently comes to $50,000 per year – for the next 20 years.

That would still leave the original $1 million intact to cover other expenses. But with today’s microscopic interest rates, there’s no way to get a guaranteed return of 5% on your money, certainly not for 15 or 20 years.

Also, keep in mind that most insurance companies have a maximum multiplier you can apply to your income for life insurance coverage. For example, it wouldn’t make much sense for a 22-year-old making $27,000 per year to get a $2 million life insurance. Or a 65-year-old that is retired to secure a $3 million dollar policy.

The table below is approximately how much you’re allowed to multiply your income based on your age and income:

Using the table above as a guide, a 35-year-old making $150,000 per year would be capped at taking out a $4.5 million term policy ($150,000 x 30 = $4,500,000).

Here we start with the basics – wrapping up your final affairs.

This will include funeral costs and any lingering medical costs. A reasonable estimate for a typical funeral is around $20,000.

Crazy, right? You can get burial insurance to cover only the most basic of final expenses.

Debt burdens are high in the US, and debt can be especially crushing on remaining family members. Many life insurance customers make sure they can pay off most of their debt with the policy.

Medical costs are a serious variable. Even if you have excellent health insurance, there are likely to be unpaid medical bills lingering after your death. This has to do with copayments, deductibles, and coinsurance provisions.

Collectively, they can add up to many thousands of dollars. But where things get really complicated is if you die of a terminal illness.

For example, if you are stricken by an illness that lasts for several years, you could incur a number of expenses that are not covered by insurance. This may include the cost of personal care and even experimental treatments.

A home may be a large asset, but it’s also often a homeowner’s largest debt. The average mortgage balance in the US is roughly $236,443 according to Experian data. So you could easily use a life insurance policy to pay off that debt and relieve your loved ones of a monthly mortgage payment.

Credit card debt and other personal debt are some of the most expensive obligations carrying rates upward of 20% in some cases. Make sure you have enough to cover this very expensive debt.

Below is a sampling of major expenses your family is likely to incur, either on an annual basis or at some point after your death.

Tuition costs continue to skyrocket. The Department of Education suggests that four-year public college tuition has been rising an average of 5% per year, far exceeding the rate of inflation. If you have one child who attends an in-state public school, a second at an out-of-state public school, and a third in a private university, the total expenditure will reach $416,560.

Vehicles and other forms of transportation represent another large sum. Unfortunately, with increasing electronics and safety features, the average cost of a new car continues to grow.

If your family relies on your work for healthcare, take notice. According to eHealth.com, the average health insurance premium for a family is $22,221. That’s a shade under $2,000 per month in additional cost. This cost will only rise, and the need could last for years.

So far, we’ve been describing the financial obligations likely to affect a typical household.But there may be certain situations that will produce obligations that are less obvious.

For example, if you’re a business owner, there may be debts or other financial obligations that will need to be paid upon your death.

Even though no one in your family may be qualified or interested in taking over your business, the payoff of those obligations may be completely necessary to enable the sale of the business.

Another possibility is that you’re a real estate investor.

If your properties are heavily indebted, extra insurance proceeds may be necessary either to carry the properties until they’re sold, or even to pay off existing indebtedness to free up cash flow for income.

You may even need additional funds if you are taking care of an extended family member, like an aging parent.

These are just some of the many possibilities of expenses that will need to be covered by insurance proceeds.

Before we move on to specific life insurance quotes, let’s first consider the factors that affect term life insurance premiums.

This is typically the single most important premium factor. The older you are, the more likely you are to die within the term of the policy.

This is a close second and why it’s so important to apply for a policy as early in life as possible. Premiums on life insurances rates literally increase by each year.

If you have any health conditions that may affect mortality, such as diabetes or hypertension, your premiums will be higher. This is another compelling reason to apply while you are young and in good health.

It’s not that policies are not available to people with health conditions, it’s just that they’re less expensive if you don’t have any.

A 10-year term policy will have a lower premium than a 20-year term policy, which will be lower than a 30-year term. The shorter the term, the less likely it is the insurance company will have to pay a claim before it expires.

Size of the policy matters, but not the way you might think. Yes, a $1 million policy will cost more than a $500,000 policy. But it won’t cost twice as much.

The larger the policy, the lower the per-thousand cost will be.

When the size of the death benefit is considered, the larger policy will always be more cost-effective.

For example, certain occupations are more hazardous than others (think policeman versus librarian). Deep-sea diving is higher risk than golf. And smoking is the one activity guaranteed to raise your premiums substantially.

With this information in mind, let’s take a look at whether you should consider a $1 million whole life policy instead.

Any discussion on life insurance should include a comparison of whole life and term life insurance coverage. After all, both products can be immensely valuable in the right situation, yet one product (whole life) costs considerably more than the other.

Most of the time, the debate is settled in favor of term life insurance based on cost alone.

A whole life insurance policy can easily cost 10x the same amount of coverage you can get with a term policy.

With that being said, whole life insurance and other investment-type life insurance coverage can be valuable in terms of the cash value you can build up over time. Whole life insurance also offers a fixed benefit amount for your heirs that will last for your entire life, yet the cost of your premiums are guaranteed to stay the same.

The cash value of a whole life insurance policy also grows on a tax-deferred basis, and you can borrow against this amount if you need a loan. Further, many whole life policies from reputable providers also pay out dividends during good years, which can be substantial.

The problem with whole life and other similar policies like universal life is the fact that premiums can be exorbitant for the amount of coverage you might need.

A couple with young children provides a good example since they might need a $1 million dollar policy or more to provide income protection for their working years and have money left for college tuition and other expenses.

With young families, expenses are already high.

This includes costs for food for a family, childcare, heavy use of health care, and the seemingly endless demand for clothing, furniture, and even entertainment as the children grow.

As you can see from the cost comparison below from State Farm, there’s not enough room in the typical family budget to afford the type of life insurance that’s needed.

A 40-year-old mother and breadwinner in excellent health would pay $80.09 per month for a term life policy that lasts 20 years, whereas a whole life policy in the same amount would cost $1,266.69 per month (or $14,560 annually).

This is a classic situation where term insurance rides to the rescue. The family can afford to buy the amount of coverage they need at an affordable price, whereas paying for permanent life insurance coverage in the same amount would be difficult to justify.

And just as important for people of any age and in any circumstance, the extra funds not being spent on insurance premiums can be invested to gradually improve your financial situation.

So absolutely, term insurance will work best for most people.

As you’ll notice, each table has a wide array of information. Knowing that everybody is in a different situation, I wanted to make sure that I offered term life quotes for almost every conceivable situation.

I’ve included life insurance rates for a 30-year term, 20-year term, and a 10-year term million dollar life policies. If you’re a tobacco user, I’ve also included some quotes from life insurance for smokers.

For those that think that a million-dollar term policy is expensive, you’ll quickly notice that a 25-year-old male in good health only costs $645 per year while a 35-year-old costs $795.

On a monthly basis that’s almost next to nothing!

There is a big drop-off in life insurance rates between a 20 year and a 30 year since underwriters do not have to worry as much about life expectancy.

For many people, a 20-year policy gets them exactly where they want to be in life when the policy term runs out.

Once again, you get a $200 drop in the annual premium by losing another 10 years on the term.

If your life insurance agent isn’t giving you all these term options and is only focused on the death benefit, then you need a different agent.

For all you smokers out there – beware! The cost of your life insurance balloons as you’ll see here. If you’re considering kicking the habit, now is as good time as any.

Some life insurance companies will give you a lower rate if you complete a recognized smoking cessation program, and go on without smoking for at least two years.

It won’t help your immediate situation, but when you see the premium on smoker life insurance rates below, you might agree that it’s something to work toward!

If you’ve made the decision that $1 million of life insurance is the right amount of coverage you need and you’re ready to purchase a policy, here are the steps you’ll need to follow.

1. Determine How Much Coverage You Need: This is the first and most important step in securing a million life insurance policies. You need to have a clear understanding of how much coverage you actually need.

2. Choose the Right Type of Policy: There are whole life, term life, and Universal life policies available. Choose the one that best suits your needs.

3. Shop Around: Don’t just go with the first life insurance company you come across. It’s important to compare life insurance rates and coverage from a few different companies before making a decision.

4. Consider Your Health: If you’re in good health, you’ll likely qualify for lower rates. However, if you have health issues, you may still be able to get coverage, but it will probably be more expensive.

5. Consider Your Lifestyle: If you have a risky job or hobby, that could affect your rates.

6. Get Quotes From Multiple Companies: This is the best way to compare rates and find the cheapest policy.

7. Read the Fine Print: Make sure you understand all the terms and conditions of the policy before buying it.

8. Buy Online: You can usually get cheaper rates by buying life insurance online.

9. Pay Attention to Your Payment Schedule: Most life insurance policies require monthly or annual payments. Be sure you can afford the payments before buying a policy.

10. Review Your Policy Regularly: Life changes, and so do life insurance needs. Be sure to review your policy regularly to make sure it still meets your needs.

Following these steps will help you get the best possible rate on a million-dollar life insurance policy.

Make sure you understand all the terms and conditions before signing on the dotted line. Also, make sure to shop around and compare rates from multiple companies before buying a policy.

Yes, I know I’ve said that a few times in this article, but it’s worth repeating. Many people go with the first life insurance company they call, and that isn’t kind to their checkbook. It pays to shop around.

Here’s what you need to know about choosing the best life insurance company for your $1 million policy:

When choosing the best life insurance company, it’s important to consider the overall financial health of the insurance company. You want to make sure the company you choose is stable and will be around for years to come. You also want to consider things like the company’s customer service rating and claims-paying ability.

There are a lot of different life insurance companies out there, so it can be difficult to know which one is the best. Each company is rated by different organizations, so it’s important to look at multiple ratings before making a decision.

Rating agencies are the “Report Card” for life insurance companies. Choose a company with straight A’s!

The companies that rate insurance companies are A.M. Best, Moody’s, and Standard & Poor’s.

A.M. Best is a credit rating agency that specializes in the insurance industry. They rate insurance companies on their financial stability.

Moody’s is another credit rating agency. They also rate insurance companies on their financial stability.

Standard & Poor’s is a credit rating agency that rates companies on their financial stability.

The following life insurance companies are all rated A+ (Superior) by A.M. Best and are considered to be financially stable and have a good claim-paying ability.

Here are those same top life insurance companies with their respective ratings:

These are just a few of the many life insurance companies out there that could provide you with a $1 million life insurance policy.

When choosing a life insurance company, it’s important to consider their financial stability, customer service rating, and claims-paying ability. The companies listed above are all rated A+ (Superior) by A.M. Best and are considered to be financially stable with a good claims-paying ability.

Northwestern Mutual, New York Life, MassMutual, Guardian Life, State Farm, Nationwide, USAA, MetLife, The Hartford, and Allstate are all good choices for life insurance companies.

You can’t put a price on peace of mind, and with a $1 million life insurance policy you can have the peace of mind knowing that your loved ones will be taken care of financially if something happens to you.

Getting a one-million-dollar term life insurance policy is not as expensive as most people believe. You can start getting quotes today from a variety of top life insurers by selecting your state from the map above.

Even those who opt for the more expensive permanent life insurance policy will many times be surprised at the price.

Either way, you can get these larger amounts of coverage and still not break the bank. But get your policy now, while you’re still young and in good health.

The cost of a $1,000,000 life insurance policy will vary based on factors like your age, health, and lifestyle. However, you can expect to pay around $250 per year for a healthy 30-year-old. According to Ladder Life, a $1 million term life policy for healthy 30-year-old males costs around $2.08 per day.

A $1 million term life insurance policy is a type of life insurance that provides coverage for a specific period of time, usually 10-20 years. If you die during the term of the policy, your beneficiaries will receive a death benefit of $1 million. If you live past the term of the policy, the policy will expire and you will not receive any death benefit. A $1 million term life insurance policy is a good choice for people who want to make sure their loved ones are taken care of financially if something happens to them. It can also be a good choice for people with a lot of debt, like a mortgage or student loans, that they want to make sure is paid off if they die.

For the most part, yes; but there are examples of people who cannot buy life insurance. For instance, people with a terminal illness or those who have been diagnosed with a life expectancy of fewer than two years are not able to purchase life insurance policies. The other factors are your income, affordability, and suitability. If you cannot afford the premiums, then you will not be able to purchase the policy. And if your income is say less than $50,000 then the insurance company may not think it’s suitable to purchase a $1 million life insurance policy.

A million-dollar life insurance policy may not be right for everyone, but it can be a good idea if you have a lot of debt or if you want to make sure your family is taken care of financially if something happens to you. No one likes to think about their death, but it’s important to have a life insurance policy in place in case something happens to you. A million-dollar life insurance policy can give you and your loved one’s peace of mind knowing that they will be taken care of financially if something happens to you.

There is no one-size-fits-all answer to this question, as the best policy for you will depend on your specific needs and preferences. However, some of the top providers of million-dollar life insurance policies include AIG, Banner Life, and Prudential. So be sure to explore your options and compare quotes from different providers before making a decision.

Yes, insurance companies offer million-dollar insurance policies with no medical exam. However, the premiums for these policies are typically much higher than for policies with a medical exam.

Doc Wealth is a physician founded tax planning firm working exclusively with physicians. Our tax team of Tax Attorneys, CPAs, and Enrolled Agents provides proactive, year round tax planning, with prompt, dependable communication when physicians need answers. We help 1099 and independent physicians design, fund, and administer Defined Benefit and cash balance plans alongside the rest of their tax planning.

This material is intended for educational and informational purposes only and does not constitute tax, legal, accounting, or financial advice. The content is general in nature and may not apply to your specific circumstances. Tax laws and financial regulations are subject to change and interpretation, and the application of these laws can vary based on individual situations. Before making any decisions, you should consult with a qualified tax advisor, legal counsel, or financial professional.

Disclosure: This guest post was written by Doc Wealth , a Physician on FIRE partner and physician-founded tax planning firm.

Most of the tax decisions that matter for 2026 have to be made by December 31. After that, the year is closed, and the return you file in April mostly reports what already happened.

That’s especially true this year. Recent regulations have changed several rules that hit physicians directly, from how catch up contributions work to what a charitable gift is worth. Some habits that worked last year now cost more.

Below is a year end tax planning checklist built for physicians: the retirement and giving sections apply to almost everyone, and the practice section covers owners and anyone with 1099 income.

Work through what applies to you and bring the list to your tax team before the holidays take over December. Every year our tax team sees the same pattern: the plan was sound, but one deadline slipped past because you only hear from your CPA in April.

Start with these before you check any boxes:

The deferral limit for 401(k), 403(b), and governmental 457 plans is $24,500 for 2026. The catch up for those 50 and older is 8,000(11,250 if you turn 60 to 63 in 2026), and the IRA limit rose to $7,500 (IRS Notice 2025-67).

If you’re 50 or older and earned more than $150,000 in FICA wages from your employer in 2025, your 2026 catch up contributions must go in as Roth (IRC §414(v)(7); IRS Notice 2025-67).

The SALT cap is $40,400 for 2026, but it shrinks by 30 cents for every dollar of modified AGI above $505,000. It bottoms out at $10,000 around $606,333 of MAGI, which is where some physician households land (One Big Beautiful Bill Act, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §164(b)(7)).

Itemizers can only deduct charitable gifts above 0.5% of AGI (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §170(b)(1)(I)). If you’re in the 37% bracket, the tax benefit of your itemized deductions is limited to roughly 35 cents per dollar (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §68).

The dependent care FSA exclusion rose from $5,000 to $7,500, or $3,750 if married filing separately (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §129(a)(2)).

Employee deferrals to a 401(k) or 403(b) have to come out of a 2026 paycheck. Check your total so far this year, and raise your election for the last few pay periods if you’re short of $24,500.

If you also have a 457(b), it carries its own $24,500 limit on top of your 401(k) or 403(b).

457(b) plans at nonprofit hospitals and other tax exempt employers work differently. They are unfunded, so the money stays an asset of your employer and is exposed to its creditors if the employer runs into financial trouble.

Their distribution rules also differ, so read the plan terms before you defer more.

If you’re 50 or older, check that your plan moved your catch up to Roth if the new rule applies to you. If your plan has no Roth option, high earners can’t make catch up contributions at all in 2026.

Moonlighting, locums, expert witness work, and side practices can all fund a Solo 401(k). The catch is that the $24,500 employee deferral limit is per person, across every plan you participate in.

If you’ve already maxed your hospital 403(b), your Solo 401(k) is limited to the employer contribution, which is roughly 20% of net self employment earnings. If you don’t have a plan set up yet, ask your tax team now, because the deadlines for opening a plan and electing deferrals are different.

The pro rata rule looks at your pretax traditional, SEP, and SIMPLE IRA balances on December 31. A pretax balance sitting there at year end can make part of your backdoor Roth conversion taxable.

The usual fix is rolling those balances into an employer plan that accepts them, and finishing the rollover before December 31. This is one of the most common backdoor Roth problems we catch, usually an old rollover IRA from a prior job that nobody remembered.

A conversion counts in the year it’s completed, and it can’t be undone. Physician on FIRE has a thorough breakdown of when Roth conversions make the most sense, especially in the years between retirement and required distributions.

S-Corp owners have to run their reasonable W-2 salary through payroll by year end. Set it too low and it won’t hold up to the IRS.

Set it too high and you give back payroll tax savings, so true it up in the final payroll runs.

If your practice elected PTET, the payment has to leave the practice account by December 31 to be deducted on your 2026 return.

Wages paid to your children for work actually done in 2026 are deductible to the practice. Up to the 2026 standard deduction of $16,100 (Rev. Proc. 2025-32), your child owes no federal income tax on those wages, assuming they have no other income.

In a sole proprietorship, or a partnership owned only by the child’s parents, wages to children under 18 also skip Social Security and Medicare tax. Corporations don’t get that exemption. Keep timesheets and run the wages through payroll.

OBBBA permanently restored 100% bonus depreciation for property acquired after January 19, 2025, so qualifying equipment can be fully deducted in the year it’s placed in service (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §168(k)).

Equipment, software, and vehicles only count for 2026 if they’re placed in service by December 31. Buying in late December and installing in January moves the deduction into 2027. We see it every January: equipment ordered before the holidays that didn’t get installed until after New Year’s.

If you own your practice through an S-Corp or another entity, home office, cell phone, and mileage costs reimbursed under a written accountable plan are deductible to the practice and tax-free to you. Process 2026 reimbursements before the year closes.

Sole proprietors don’t need an accountable plan, since they deduct these costs directly on Schedule C.

The 0.5% floor means that with $500,000 of AGI, you get no deduction for the first $2,500 of gifts (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §170(b)(1)(I)). Add the roughly 35 cent limit for filers in the top bracket (IRC §68), and small annual gifts are worth less than they were.

Two year end tax planning moves work better under the new rules:

Bunch your giving. Concentrate several years of gifts into one year, often through a donor advised fund, so more of the total clears the floor.

Give appreciated shares instead of cash. Donating shares held more than a year generally avoids capital gains tax on the appreciation, and the gift still counts toward your deduction.

If you take the standard deduction, you can now deduct up to 1,000ofcashgifts(2,000 married filing jointly) without itemizing (OBBBA, Pub. L. 119-21; IRC §170(p)). It covers cash gifts to qualifying charities, but not gifts to donor advised funds or most private foundations.

The last 2026 estimated payment is due January 15, 2027. If your 2025 AGI was over $150,000, paying 110% of your 2025 tax through withholding and estimates protects you from an underpayment penalty (IRS Publication 505).

If you’re W-2 with outside income, you have an extra option. The IRS treats withholding as if it were paid evenly throughout the year, so raising your December withholding can cover a shortfall from earlier quarters.

Open enrollment is happening now at most employers. If you pay for child care, you can elect up to $7,500 for 2027, up from the old $5,000 limit.

Dr. Lee is a hypothetical hospitalist, age 52, married filing jointly, with $380,000 of W-2 salary and about $60,000 of 1099 income from moonlighting. Here’s how the checklist plays out for her:

Her 403(b) deferrals are on pace to reach $24,500 by her final paycheck. Her 2025 FICA wages were over $150,000, so her $8,000 catch up goes in as Roth.

Because her 403(b) used up her deferral limit, the Solo 401(k) on her moonlighting income takes only the employer contribution, roughly 20% of her net self employment earnings.

She has a $40,000 rollover IRA from a prior job. She moves it into her 403(b) before December 31 so the pro rata rule doesn’t make most of her backdoor Roth conversion taxable.

She usually gives $6,000 a year. With AGI around $400,000, the first $2,000 isn’t deductible. She bunches three years of gifts, $18,000, into a donor advised fund this December. She loses the $2,000 floor once instead of three times, so $4,000 more of her giving counts toward the deduction.

No tax was withheld from her 1099 income. She raises her December withholding to close the gap, which the IRS counts as paid evenly across all four quarters.

Nothing here is exotic. It’s the tax version of closing out your charts before a long weekend: routine work with a hard deadline.

Source: IRS Publication 505, IRS Publication 590-A, and IRC §404(a)(6). Chart: Doc Wealth.

☐ Solo 401(k) contributions planned for any 1099 income

☐ Pretax IRA balances rolled into an employer plan before a backdoor Roth

IRA contributions for 2026 can be made until April 15, 2027 (IRS Publication 590-A). Solo 401(k) employer contributions can wait until your return’s due date including extensions (IRC §404(a)(6)), and the final estimated payment is due January 15, 2027.

No. The 1,000deduction(2,000 married filing jointly) applies only to cash gifts made directly to qualifying charities, not to donor advised funds or most private foundations. Gifts to a donor advised fund still help itemizers, subject to the 0.5% floor.

Yes, but only on the employer side. The $24,500 employee deferral limit is shared across all your plans, so the Solo 401(k) takes an employer contribution of roughly 20% of your net self employment earnings.

It applies if you’re 50 or older and your 2025 FICA wages from the employer sponsoring the plan topped $150,000. Self employment income isn’t FICA wages, so catch ups to a Solo 401(k) funded only by 1099 earnings aren’t affected.

It depends on your MAGI. Below $505,000, itemizers can deduct up to $40,400 of state and local taxes. Between $505,000 and about $606,000 the cap shrinks, and above that it’s back to $10,000.

If your practice is in a state with a PTET, that election can still move state tax to the entity level.

The accountable plan reminder is the one people skip, because the reimbursement only works if there’s a record behind it. A phone bill is easy to pull up in December. Mileage from last March is not. We run a job board for traveling trades workers, and the ones on 1099 have the same headache as a doctor picking up locums: several assignments, a few states and a glove box full of gas receipts. #8508. Less Cars, More Money: My Visit to the City of the Future

In my role as Mr. Money Mustache, I do my best to be your one-stop-shop for Lifestyle Guru ideas. So over the years we’ve covered not just the Money side of life, but also the even more important stuff like health and fitness and the psychology of better, happier living.

But there’s one single area of life where all of these factors come together with an almost Nuclear Fusion level of synergy and effectiveness. And because of that, if I could have one single wish in the world, this is what I would wish for. It’s a change so massive that it would make every person on the planet better off and fix most of our problems in one grand sweep. And it’s probably not what you’d expect:

That we immediately switch to building our cities and countries around people, instead of cars.

(and then fix all of our existing ones too, so that our entire world is built around person-friendly living.)

The benefits of this are way bigger than almost anyone can imagine. We’re not just talking about eliminating a bit of pollution or a few traffic jams or car crashes. No. This is about far richer, healthier, and most importantly more fun living for everyone.

To put even conservative numbers to this, we’re talking about a life boost of over $20,000 per person per year, which compounds into well over two million dollars per adult lifetime.

On a nationwide scale, this would boost the wealth of the United States by about seven trillion dollars per year, which would compound into about 770 trillion over the next five decades.

Which happens to be more than the current total amount of human wealth on the entire planet.

You will have a house that is both cheaper and more beautiful and spacious. Your body and brain will be healthier and stronger and sexier and cost a lot less time and healthcare dollars to maintain.

And all of our wallets and investment accounts, both public and private will be absolutely overflowing with surplus income, reduced expenses, and fuel an investment and prosperity boom like the world has never seen.

“Isn’t city planning just a stuffy thing that your city council does in the background while we’re all off living our lives?”

Well, yes it is right now. And that’s the whole problem: cities are built by people whose primary job is to maintain the status quo and prevent disruptions. And those committes are elected and encouraged by crusty old companies and organizations, and plain old grumpy neighbors who just don’t have the vision to see what they are missing.

I’m convinced that if everyone could see through the smoggy haze of the status quo, we would all agree that this idea of a radical change is not only the best idea, but the only reasonable idea to even consider.

So our job is to learn and explain just how big and how easy this is. And what it boils down to is pretty damned simple.

So for the same amount of space you can have an entire pretty nice two bedroom apartment, or you can have just enough space for two (small) cars to park and pull out. But it gets even crazier than this. Check out this random intersection here in my own city:

WHAT?! So every time you have two big car roads intersect, which happens hundreds of times in every big city, you are wasting enough space to build a luxurious, resort-like living area with about one hundred two-bedroom apartments and still have room for a pool, a dog park, a grocery store, a couple of restaurants, and so on.

This is just the beginning of the insanity, because I have only shown you two parking spaces and one intersection. The reality is that our entire cities are made almost entirely of stupid, expensive wasted space like this.

And the problem is so extreme that the only reason we think we need cars to get around, is because we have wasted most of our space on accommodating cars, which spread everything out so far (and made everything so loud and dangerous) that nobody feels like walking or biking!

Whenever you propose any great new idea, you’ll always get a bunch of smartasses who like to complain and resist change, without even bothering to think it through.

“But how are we going to keep driving our cars just as much as we do now?”

Which is ridiculous – because the whole point is that as soon as you cut out all the huge wasted spaces we create to accommodate cars, you are suddenly FREE from needing cars so much!

Instead, you can just weave a brand new city, with a bunch of variations of this beautiful resort which also include offices, grocery stores, climbing gyms and every other amenity.

And yes, you’d still have some roads between them, but they would be mostly for deliveries, emergency vehicles and people who need mobility assistance.

I hope you’re not going to make me ride the bus?

I am all for public transit in theory, but to be honest I don’t usually have the patience for it. I don’t do lineups, and I don’t like to stand around waiting passively for my transportation to arrive – when it’s time to go somewhere, I just want to go, and go now, and get there fast. So my own personal choice is to take a bike for short distances (under 2 miles) or an e-bike for larger ones (up to about 15 miles).

Although this is often news to car drivers, bikes are much faster than cars for urban transport, plus they give me exercise and thrill, which is way better than being stuck at the red light with the cars.

If you take this already-superior method of urban transport and cut out the 90% of the land that we waste on accommodating the inferior cars, then you end up with a revolution: everybody gets where they are going ten times faster, at much lower cost, and has much more fun doing it.

And sure, there will also be light rail and faster buses. And sure, you can still hop in an Uber or even bring your own car into a city like this.But the point is that it will just happen much much less often.

Okay I’m convinced, but how can we actually accomplish this?

Mr. Money Mustache can talk a big game with all these fancy words and pictures, but the truth is that I’m way too impatient to put up with all the bureaucracy and complaints that arise when you try to actually change a city. I’ve been doing my best here in Longmont, and I have gotten just about nowhere. We’re still just stacking on more and more layers of ridiculous car shit where I live.

Thankfully, other people are much more patient and effective than I am at affecting change, and one group has made such incredible progress that you can now go LIVE in their first creation: a 1000-person car-free neighborhood called Culdesac Tempe. And as I write this, I am staying in a hotel right nearby, having spent the past two days touring and visiting and interviewing the founders*.

While we were at it, my Phoenix-area-house-fixing friend Tracy Royce and I also hosted a meetup for an enthusiastic group of our readers/viewers right there in Culdesac’s emerging central plaza.

Culdesac is Awesome and Could Change Everything

If you only look at the financial spreadsheet, you would think this first Culdesac project is just going to be a highly profitable 1000-person cluster of apartment buildings, spread out across 17 acres of land. And while financial sustainability is indeed a key reason why this model will succeed, the money is the least exciting part.

When you look at these pictures compared to a normal housing complex, the main thing you will notice is that all the space that would normally be wasted on parking lots, is instead used for beautiful walking and gathering areas.

The next big upgrade is that they mixed in the amenities for daily life right into the neighborhood, rather than forcing all the future residents to get into their cars to drive out to find them:

I was also impressed with just the feel of walking the Mediterranean-vibed spaces between the buildings, even at this early stage when everything is still under construction.

Due to the hot desert climate of the region, everything is built around providing shade, breeze, and reflecting heat during the summer, while also maximizing the joyful fact that there is no winter there (the coldest month of the year still has an average daily high of 65F/18C, which means palm trees, leafy gardens and fruits and flowers forever.)

With a setup like this, and 999 new neighbors to meet, I would rarely feel the need to leave the place. Which really cuts down on my desire to use a car. But on top of that, Culdesac has strategically placed itself in Tempe, a city right in the center of the Phoenix metro area, within walking distance of the main university and right on a light rail stop which allows you to reach almost everything (including the airport) for FREE, since an annual pass to the transit system is included with your rent.

But of course, you can also get around on foot, bike, e-bike, scooter, or hop into one of Culdesac’s fleet of rideshare electric cars for a trip to the mountains or whatever else you might want to do that’s outside of bike and transit range.

It’s insane. In fact it’s so good that I am going to attempt to move there myself at the end of 2023, enjoying my first escape from Colorado winter and celebrating the fact that my boy will be a legal adult at that time.

But even this is just a pilot project because Culdesac has much bigger plans.

From my conversations with the founders, I think they want to do this:

So How Can We Benefit From This, and Support it?

This whole change is exciting, and it is immense.

Understanding these ideas around city planning is the economic and social equivalent to being a doctor, and finding a 35-year-old patient in a hospital who is suffering from every chronic disease, but then discovering that they have been following a diet of Coke and Donuts for their whole lives and never been out on a walk, once.

In other words, the changes are so obvious, and the amount of win/win synergy so great, that every step we take towards making our cities better, and every car trip we eliminate, will absolutely explode our personal and national wealth upwards for generations to come.

Another collaborator in the overall effort for car free cities is a bank-founding multi entrepreneur local friend named Kevin Dahlstrom. His recent Twitter rant on building car-free cities from the scratch gathered a shocking amount of very positive feedback and interesting comments.

* Despite my positive raving about this neighborhood, I have no financial or business connection with the project or any of the team members. I am just really excited about their work and want them to succeed!

Damn that is exciting! Pedestrianism FTW!

Mr. Money Mustache April 8, 2023, 6:43 pm

Believe it or not, this is not a big problem in Phoenix and most other big desert cities. They have plenty of water for domestic use. It’s agriculture that uses the lion’s share of fresh water – about 80% of it in the Western US. Then our other industrial uses, then our houses are down near the bottom.

One major improvement in places like Phoenix and Las Vegas versus the rest of the country is that they have managed to mostly eliminate suburban lawns. A single patch of lawn watered in the desert will use more than an entire household, so as soon as you remove that you have made the whole city more sustainable.

Alas, here in the Denver area the lawn with the big sprinkler system still seems to be in style, despite the fact that our summer climate very closely resembles a real desert. The grass will die within a week or two if you leave it unwatered, which I think would be a great idea in most cases. There’s lots of cool stuff you can do with river rocks and native flowers and Yucca plants that takes almost no water to sustain!

Very accurate, MMM! I’ve got a good friend who works for whatever they call the “water” department of the city of Mesa (right next to Tempe), and whenever I bring up the metro Phoenix water supply issue, he basically says “we’ll be fine, but things will have to change with respect to agriculture in the southwest and lawns/golf courses”.

I worried about it for years, but a bit of research and several articles in the NYT helped calm me down. Here’s one: https://www.nytimes.com/interactive/2023/05/22/climate/colorado-river-water.html .

ALERT: Most retirees must start taking required minimum distributions, or RMDs, from pretax accounts at age 73. The first annual RMD is due by April 1 of the year after turning 73, and Dec. 31 is the deadline for subsequent withdrawals. If you miss your RMD due date, the IRS penalty is 25% of the amount you should have withdrawn.

Private real estate carries its own risks, illiquidity chief among them. They differ from the risks in your stock funds, and owning assets that don’t all sink on the same afternoon is the whole reason diversification exists.
