That little voice in your head that says “I don’t feel like it” is what the Stoics called “an impression.” You have clearly learned to apply “prosoche” (mindfulness would be a good translation of this Greek word) to interrogate that impression. Then you applied natural wisdom (one of the Stoic virtues) to reach the logical conclusion that surrendering to that impression would not be in your best interest.

There is another Stoic echo in your rediscovered commitment to exercise. The Stoics strongly believed that it was crucial to constantly test oneself, whether that meant fasting, walking barefoot in the now, or undertaking difficult or unpleasant tasks.

So well done! You are proving an apt “prokopton” (one who is making progress to becoming a Stoic sage).

As a retired person I can really relate to this. For me it’s not the lack of desire to do hard things, it’s the easy distracting nature of the phone. I get bored, pull out my phone, then wonder where the last eight hours went.

People with jobs and young kids have to put down the phone to go to work, or take the kids to school. I could spend 100% of my time on YouTube, and my brain will do that if I let it.

My retired quality of life improved immensely when I started keeping my phone and computer in my office out of reach.

Now I get bored, feel uncomfortable, then go and do something. That feeling of boredom and discomfort is critical to making me do the things that actually bring joy to my life.

Boredom is a signal that I have spare energy that should be used for something. Phones alleviate boredom and kill motivation

Hey RH, thanks for following along with that. Throughout my stay there, I kept this page updated, and it’s now in its final form with all my thoughts so far: https://mrmoneymustache.com/culdesac/

Summary: there is *some* community forming there, but not as much as I expected going in – they’re still working on building out the neighborhood so it’s a tough chicken-and-egg problem to crack. The Culdesac team are fantastic however, and of course the physical architecture of the place is beautiful. So I think they are doing the right things to build it out.

Glad to hear you’re picking up Extreme Ownership! As someone who is still in his working years, it’s made the way I think about getting work done much better. In software engineering, sometimes shit just goes wrong. Knowing that almost everything can be avoided by us engineers doing a better and robust job has improved the way I work and has made me _less_ stressed, because the work I do is better and more well thought out from the start. Even when something does go wrong, it’s just a learning experience that allows me to avoid those pitfalls in the future.

This book is even better for your social relationships though! Most of the time, you can be the ignition to a better relationship with someone. I’ve seen it many times where relationships you want drift away because neither side initiates social interaction enough with the other. “If they really care, they’d reach out.” Turns out, if you take ownership and reach out, you’ll see them a lot more and be happier as a result. The same thing applies for someone toxic in your life. Tired of this person bringing you down? Take ownership and remove yourself from the equation. Plus the narration of the audiobook is just great. Jocko has that Seal Team motivational way of speaking that makes you get your shit together!

I was in a similar situation. Thank you for writing this post. I thought everyone else had their act together, so hearing that you had similar challenges made me feel ‘normal’. I also discovered Goggins, and have been using it to do things I know I need to do, but procrastinated on

I have noticed a lot less posts over the past year.. Is this part of of “not doing” what you want to do.. or something else?

Thank you for posting this and articulating ideas many are feeling on this blog. I’ve been facing much of this same internal dialog from the perspective of working 20 years at a career I enjoy that pays well. With that job I enjoy I still think about quality of life and wonder about meaning as my children grow older and my spouse and I get closer to financial freedom.

It’s a weird place to be to doubt internally whether I actually want to retire as the feasibility becomes more real. Anyone else feeling the same and concerned not putting myself in the situation explained in the blog is actually easier than having to deal with the procrastination?

Secondly, a coworker in a similar situation volunteers for local search and rescue. It gives him a bigger picture reason to stay in great shape. It’s got me thinking about doing the same as I approach my late 40’s.

I have found a social approach works best for keeping me motivated to work out. My partner is training for a canoe trip in Canada, so we both ride our bikes to the gym twice a week. On both days I go to a weight training class for older adults. I like the work out, the instructors and my classmates. Oh yeah, and they play Beatles music.

I also get yearly DXA scans. Last year my scans were horrible and that motivated me to start regular strength training. This year I have improved and that motivates me to keep working out.

Not everything is mental unfortunately. I have all kinds of motivation and willingness to push myself, but no matter what I do, my body is just not in the condition that it was 10 – 15 years ago, and the aches and pains that result from pushing myself prevent me from doing anything more than walking at this point in my life. So, this advice is great if you don’t have any medical conditions preventing you from pushing yourself, however, I believe that there are many people out there like myself who are not built like Goggins.

I realise you have said you don’t swallow the whole Goggins creed, Mr. Moustache, but Goggins? In any measure? Really?

I am surprised you haven’t learnt by now that always pushing your limits, redlining your body, is not a formula for health, fitness and well-being; it is the road to injury and burnout.

There are countless examples of exercise fanatics who started off thinking, with Nietzsche, that ‘That which doesn’t kill me makes me stronger’. They end up realising that ‘That which doesn’t kill me can still cripple me’.

Just look at poor old Ronnie Coleman. https://youtu.be/kq0Sm4kAp4Y?si=_ma2zjT_WoWVi4wC

But after many injuries, all self-inflicted and therefore avoidable, I have developed a different philosophy: Progress over perfection; You won’t improve from something you can’t recover from; Little by little, step by step, work on your weaknesses and limitations; No brain, no gain.

Could your procrastination stem from thinking that exercise is a gruelling, penitential task? Why not just resolve to show up everyday and just do something — some mobility work, an easy jog, a few sets of easy pull-ups and hanging leg raises? Some days that will put you in the mood to push harder, go further— fine. Other days you can stop there — also fine. Just keep showing up and making deposits into the Bank (or ETF, or whatever) of Fitness. They will add up, and sometimes compound, just like money. Health and fitness is a long game, just like saving and investment.

There is definitely a time and place to test your mettle — generally in a competition or emergency. But suffering is not how you get fitter. ‘The ability to suffer during a workout is just one skill. Don’t over-focus on it. You also need to train a hundred other skills’.https://youtu.be/0h23IANIg6Q For most workouts, the goal should be to finish feeling better than when you started. Energised, not exhausted. If tired, sore, and injured are the side-effects, is it worth it?

Of course, who am I to say what will motivate you? But I know that when I changed my outlook from struggle-&-suffer to small, manageable steps, every day my hesitation vanished and I became keen to show up.

#8451. Historic Drought Looms Over Arkansas Duck Opener. What Few Ducks Show Up Face Heavy Pressure

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 20, 2026 4:45 PM EST

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

If you asked any serious waterfowl hunter to name their dream duck-hunting destinations, Arkansas would be at the top of nearly every list. Its classic flooded hardwoods and bayous along with the state’s rich rice and grain fields, lure massive flights of puddle ducks and geese to its hallowed waters every year. This has made Arkansas stand out above other southern states as the beating heart of the Mississippi Flyway.

Yet in 2026, Arkansas’ waterfowl season is suddenly looking bleak. A historic drought has many duck hunters worried ahead of the Nov. 21 opener, as the serious lack of water could bring duck hunting to a standstill. Duck hunters on both public and private land may have some serious decisions to make to safeguard ducks and future duck seasons.

For 14 months Arkansas has been without any serious rainfall, leaving rich croplands and, more importantly for ducks, wetlands, drier than they’ve been in decades. Every corner of the state is under a severe drought status, with some areas being more than 20 inches behind in cumulative rainfall totals.

To put the drought in perspective, this is slated to be the state’s third-driest October through January since record keeping began in 1895.

This leaves the Arkansas Game and Fish Commission with very little water to spare, to the point where the agency expects it will only be able to flood around 40 of its more than 70 moist-soil public-land hunting units.

“In my 50 years of duck hunting in Arkansas, I don’t remember it ever being as dry as this,” says Brent Birch, founder of Arkansas’ Greenhead magazine. “It’s been this way all summer and well into the fall. And even with the prospects of a Super El Niño, we have nothing the forecast that says it’s going to resolve anytime soon.”

Without an incredible amount of rainfall in a short amount of time, Birch and other waterfowlers around the state are worried not only about not having places to hunt, but that the ducks may not even show up.

“So far, we are seeing a few groups of gadwalls, pintails, and other early migrating ducks but not in anything close to their usual numbers,” Birch says. “And when it comes to incoming mallards, you can pretty much forget it. It’s just too dry for them. The fact is the closer it gets to 2027 under these conditions, the worse the entire duck season is going to be. And if we don’t start getting some wet weather soon to push ducks down here, we’re looking at a poor outlook for the entire season.”

The reason that Arkansas waterfowl hunting is so good is that it lies at the north end of the historic feeding grounds for ducks and geese in the Mississippi Flyway. Once the cold sets in around their spring and summer breeding grounds in Canada, the birds come south to binge on Arkansas’ rich wetlands throughout the winter. However, with the current drought, the fear is that the incoming ducks will be forced to fly elsewhere.

“Ducks coming south to Arkansas aren’t like ducks in northern states,” says Ducks Unlimited Arkansas regional biologist Jake Spears, who lives in Jonesboro. “Northern birds are more apt to feed in dry fields so long as they have a body of water to roost on nearby. However, in the Southern U.S., they stop feeding in fields and primarily feed in water. They look for things like water plants and waste grains in flooded fields, which Arkansas currently just doesn’t have.”

Spears worries that many ducks are going to fly to Arkansas and then be forced to turn northward again or keep driving south.

“The ducks need food so they may go to Louisiana, or Kansas, or Missouri — wherever they can find that food source,” says Spears. “Which is going to leave both public-land duck hunters and even most hunting clubs just completely out of luck.”

Private-land duck-hunting clubs are a popular option for many Arkansas hunters and visiting nonresidents, as even during droughts, most clubs can pump water to create duck habitat and attract birds. The 2026 drought has been so bad, however, that many clubs won’t even have the water to pump.

This is especially troubling to some public-land waterfowl hunters, who worry that the private hunting clubs that can still pump water may end up attracting what few ducks do make it to Arkansas. This could result in a season that benefits the haves over the have-nots.

“I think hunting clubs are the only thing that’s going to make Arkansas appealing for ducks right now,” Spears says. “Most of the smaller rivers, sloughs, and backwaters we have on public land can be walked across in flip-flops right now. So the clubs that have the option to flood fields and create habitat are where the birds are going to be. But with the water table so low, clubs with the ability to pump will be few and far between, so any ducks that do show up during the season are going to have to be babied quite a bit.”

The fact is that if the drought continues in Arkansas, duck hunters on both public and private land alike are going to have to weigh their priorities. Drought conditions are going to be tough on ducks that migrate through Arkansas, and hunting pressure will make surviving the migration harder even for birds that aren’t killed.

This leaves duck hunters with a choice to make.

“It’s going to come down to responsible management on all sides because if we want to maintain the ducks we have, we have to be careful with them,” Birch says. “There are several components to management. It’s not just hunting and the noise of guns, we must be careful disturbing the ducks in any capacity. Your vehicle is an issue because you’re going to bump ducks going in and out of your hunting area, and you’re going to have to be real careful with how many days you hunt and how many hours you hunt in a day, because you’re going to have to let the birds rest.”

With Arkansas’ duck season lasting a total of 51 days with two relatively short splits, hunters looking to limit out consistently are going to be putting serious pressure on what will already be a limited resource.

So instead of hunting hard, both Birch and Spears recommend self-imposed bag limits and time on the water so that the resource can continue to both be conserved and shared.

“My suggestion to any duck hunter in Arkansas is that if you have ducks on your property, take care of them,” says Spears. “With the limited resources, they aren’t going to be able to handle a lot of pressure. You’re going to have to limit how much you hunt and how many birds you shoot, and not be afraid to cut your hunt short. Get a few birds and then leave so the ducks can get back to the water to feed.”

Read Next: Has Hot Cropping Ruined Duck Hunting? Here’s What the Data and Biologists Say About How Flooded Corn Affects Waterfowl Migration

While there is hope that conditions will change, the fact is that the whole of Arkansas’ 2026 duck season may be a nonstarter for many hunters. That short-term pain, however, could help future duck seasons look a little brighter. Spears and Birch are hopeful for a future where water and the waterfowl will eventually return, filling the skies and waterways like flowing veins and once again making Arkansas the beating heart of the Mississippi Flyway itself.

“We need to be good stewards of the resource,” urges Spears. “Hunters should do everything they can to keep [ducks] around and not shoot them off what water we do have.”

Sell on Fiverr if your service can be packaged at a set price, like logo design or voiceovers, because buyers search for it and order without a pitch from you. Fiverr keeps 20% of every order, tips included, so build that cut into each package’s price.

Freelancers with a service they can package and price up front, such as logo design, editing, or voiceovers, get a storefront that buyers already search, and that’s worth the 20% cut. #8444. Old-School Whitetail Wisdom for Filling Your Tag After Opening Day

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 20, 2026 5:30 PM EST

Get everything from whitetail news and opinion pieces, to advanced hunting tactics and cutting-edge gear reviews.

These days, a buck can’t grow to trophy proportions on hard-hunted public lands by folding up under the pressure exerted by the opening-day crush of hunters. A whitetail lives the 3½ years necessary to grow a bragging set of antlers by learning to cope with the annual influx of hunters during the season’s first days. Every opening day that the buck survives increases his chance of surviving the ensuing openers, as well.

Some big bucks live in locations that allow them to avoid the opening weekend crowd by slipping into the sanctuary offered by state parks, game refuges or private posted land. Others crawl into the most inaccessible and gosh-awful cover their “territory” has to offer — the kind of place hunters walk around, rather than through — and stay there until the crowds leave. And on more than one occasion, I have found a bruiser buck in a tiny, secluded patch of isolated cover — the kind of place most hunters never think to look in.

But the whitetail is a homebody at heart, and he is most comfortable on his loosely defined home turf. You can bet that once the steady crack of opening day rifles slackens to only an occasional pop, those big bucks will be right back to business as usual. And that is the precise reason why your best chance for bagging a wall-hanger occurs after the opening day madness has subsided.

Where you begin your search for that after-the-opener buck hinges upon one factor: the rut. Many states plan their firearms seasons to coincide with the rut, offering their hunters every opportunity to harvest the surplus bucks. Other states, bound in tradition, open the season after the main rut has ended. If you are planning to travel out of your home state to hunt whitetails, it makes sense to hunt a state where the season coincides with the rut, all other criteria being equal.

A mature whitetail buck is a different character during the rut than he is after it. A buck’s sole purpose at that time is to procreate, and this he does with obvious enthusiasm and the stamina of a teenager. There are stories abounding in every deer camp in the country of the crazy antics performed by bucks under the spell of the “rutting moon,” such as lovesick bucks strolling across open fields in broad daylight. Others tell tales of bucks putting their noses to does’ tracks and following those tracks, even after being shot at and missed several times. Rut-crazed bucks, while under the influence of a powerful rush of hormones, have even been known to either pick fights with or attempt to mate with assorted farm livestock.

So rampant are the stories that I’m afraid there exists a whole contingent of deer hunters laboring under the false assumption that all a hunter needs do to down one of these crazy buggers is to walk into the woods, lean up against a stump and wait for one of the poor, sex-addled dummies to saunter on by. Although such tactics work just often enough to keep the myth perpetuated, plenty of hunters have been sitting against stumps for more unsuccessful years than they will probably admit, and they’re still waiting for a buck to wander by.

Hunting whitetails during the rut and after the opening weekend of the season isn’t easy. You must employ all of the skill and woods savvy you have. Any breaks you receive because of a buck’s overactive glands should be considered a bonus.

After the opener, I refine my hunting strategy for big bucks by determining what stage the rut is in. This is important because the stage of the rut will determine where I concentrate most of my midweek hunting efforts.

The whitetail buck is ready to breed long before the first doe enters estrus. During this period, the buck runs off excess energy by beating up saplings, sparring with bushes and, on occasion, duking it out with other bucks. In the process of making rubs on bushes and trees, the buck deposits scents that tell the rest of the whitetail community who was there.

Scrapes begin to show up in increasing numbers as the level of testosterone builds in the buck’s system. The buck paws out scrapes and leaves his scent both in the bare earth of the scrapes and on overhanging branches above the scrapes. Again, this is a means of communicating with other whitetails. The message to does is that the buck is now standing at stud, and it tells other bucks that they had best move along if they know what’s good for them.

A buck will paw out most of his scrapes in areas where they are most likely to be seen or smelled by does. Openings in woods, old logging roads and the edges of woodlots are common places to encounter scrapes. A buck may make a dozen or more scrapes, and he’ll check some of them daily, making sure they are free of debris and liberally doused with musk/urine. These are the scrapes to hunt over.

However, once the does begin cycling into heat, the dominant bucks that handle the bulk of the breeding chores are often so busy accompanying, tracking and servicing does that they neither have the time nor the need to freshen their scrapes. But if you find a string of scrapes that have not been freshened for several days, it doesn’t necessarily mean that the rut is over or that the buck that made the scrapes is hanging from someone else’s game pole. It may mean that the buck is out doing his job.

The best way to determine what stage the rut is in is to spend a day or two in the woods prior to the hunt. If fresh scrapes abound, you will be hunting the pre-coital period, and a stand near a scrape line is going to be hard to beat. If, on the other hand, you find that more than half of the scrapes are old and abandoned, it’s a good bet that the big bucks are out taking care of the does, while the lesser bucks are still hanging around their scrapes, waiting.

If you just don’t have time to get into the woods prior to the season, you can get a good idea about the stage of the rut by speaking with area game managers, milk haulers, rural school bus drivers, postal carriers, loggers, trappers, farmers, grouse hunters, bowhunters or others who spend most of their time in deer country. If the bucks are chasing the does, chances are these people will have observed some of the activity.

Why all of the fuss over determining what stage the rut is in? Because it makes a big difference when you have to decide how you want to hunt after the opening weekend of the season.

When the season begins, if the actual breeding season has not yet begun but bucks are busy pawing out new scrapes and freshening old ones, chances are the bucks will curtail this activity during the high-pressure days at the beginning of the season, resuming their rounds once the hunters thin out. I like to have at least a half-dozen scrape lines pinpointed prior to the opener, and I check them after the opening weekend for any sign of activity. I then concentrate my hunting efforts near the “hottest” scrapes.

If your pre-season scouting and snooping indicates that the actual breeding season is in progress, then hunting over scrapes may not be your best option for tagging a really good buck. Remember, it is often the big, dominant bucks in the area that handle the bulk of the breeding chores. Even in an area with an excellent buck-to-doe ratio, a breeding buck can be kept so busy that he has little time or need to tend his scrapes. Often, a buck will spend 24 hours with the same doe, breeding her several times before her cycle ends. At this time, it is the doe, not the buck, that determines where the pair will travel. Though I would not totally rule out hunting in the vicinity of inactive scrapes at this stage of the rut, there are other options that I’ve found give me a better chance at tagging a big buck.

One of my favorite methods during this period is to concentrate my hunting efforts in areas where I have encountered good numbers of does in the past. Does and fawns tend to hang around together, and they routinely congregate in specific areas, often bedding as a loosely knit group in a favorite swale or sunny hillside. I can’t direct you to these “ladies-only bedrooms,” but I’ll bet there is such a place in the chunk of woods you hunt.

You can locate these places that hold special favor with the does by simply noting those areas where you encounter the most doe activity. After a few years of hunting the same ground, a familiar pattern becomes apparent.

On several occasions, I have located a hotbed of doe activity by simply listening to other hunters. When you hear a hunter complain that he sat on his stand and saw 15 does but not a single buck, find out where he was sitting. You can bet that when the time is right, there will be a buck or two sniffing around the vicinity.

A dominant buck ranges well out of his home area during the actual breeding season. I don’t think he goes out of his way looking for does so much as he is drawn out of the territory when following the tracks of a doe that has visited his scrapes or just wandered through the area. A buck engaged in this activity moves with a single-minded purpose, shuffling along, nose to the ground, seldom looking up, intent upon finding the maker of the tracks he is following. I once missed a buck that trailed a doe past my tree stand in this manner, my arrow slicing harmlessly over the buck’s back only to skitter noisily through the carpet of dry oak leaves a few yards beyond. The buck lifted his head and looked in the direction of the commotion. Apparently satisfied that whatever had made the racket was not what he was looking for, he then ambled on his way while I frantically fumbled around trying to nock another arrow.

When a buck finally tracks down a doe, as often as not, she will then lead the buck on a little chase that, in all likelihood, will take the buck still farther from his home base. By the time the buck actually mates with the doe, he may be miles from his original starting point. On the way back to his core area, it is not unlikely that the buck will cut the track of another “hot” doe and repeat the scenario.

All of this rambling makes it impossible to pattern a buck during the height of the breeding season, prompting many knowledgeable whitetail hunters to claim that taking a good buck during the peak of the rut is mostly a matter of luck. I disagree.

Hunting near a known “doe hangout” can help. And you can stack the deck in your favor even more by hunting a funnel area near a concentration of does. A funnel is simply any natural or man-made feature of the terrain that restricts the movement of deer. An hourglass-shaped section of woods is the classic funnel. Deer moving from one wide portion of the hourglass to the other must pass through the narrow waist. In farm country, the funnel may be a brushy fenceline connecting two woodlots. In the rugged country of the West, where whitetails are becoming increasingly common, a jutting jaw of sheer rimrock can force whitetails into a confined passage. Funnels work well because even though a buck with a snootful of “hot” doe scent wouldn’t care if he was standing in the middle of Madison Avenue, the does do not lose their heads. Does will stick to cover when on the move, even when there is a grunting, panting Romeo dogging their every move.

In many whitetail states, hunters are left with no choice but to hunt well after the main rutting period is over. At first, hunting after the opening weekend under these circumstances appears to be a futile endeavor. Without the promise of the rut to keep the bucks on the move, and with the absence of hunters to jar deer loose, what chance does the midweek hunter have of scoring on a decent buck? He has a pretty good one, I would say.

First, although the bulk of the breeding chores are completed in about a two-week period, there is still some activity after the main rut is over. Does that were not impregnated will cycle back into heat 28 days after their first estrus cycle ends. In some states, this is just about the time the rifle season rolls around. In addition, in some of the best whitetail areas, it is not uncommon for female fawns of the year to breed. This often applies to as many as 40 percent of them. Frequently, these young breeders experience their first estrus cycle later than older does. So, don’t strike out the possibility of the rut working in your favor even though the peak has passed. In that part of Minnesota where I live, the bulk of the breeding is completed by mid-November, yet each year, I find active scrapes late into November and even December. Last season, during an especially mild December, I found a pair of bushel-basket-size recently freshened scrapes while hunting grouse on New Year’s Eve day. If you can find these “late scrapes,” concentrate your hunting efforts near them.

But even if you fail to find any of these scrapes later in the year, you still stand a good chance of tagging a buck during the middle of the week if you let the after-effects of the rut work in your favor. During the rut, a buck takes little time out to eat. By the end of the breeding season, a buck that began the rut in peak condition can be drawn and thin, actually haggard looking. Some bucks lose up to 20 percent of their body weight during the course of the rut. Across the Northern states and Canada, where winter-kill is an annual problem, the big, breeding bucks follow the fawns in death each winter simply because they run off all of their reserve fat during the rut and are often unable to replenish it before the onset of winter snows.

Although the largest bucks are often nocturnal in their feeding habits at other times of the year, when the rut is over, dominant bucks cannot afford to limit their foraging to the hours of darkness alone. In order to regain their strength and put on the layer of fat necessary to see them through the winter, they must forage during the day. This gives the after-the-opener hunter the chance he needs to find bucks up and about during shooting hours.

This need to feed heavily does not necessarily mean that a big buck will be found sauntering around an alfalfa field at high noon, scarfing down the last frost-tinged greens of the year. It does mean that rather than tucking himself safely away in a thicket long before the morning sun ever peeks over the ridge, a buck will now tend to linger at the feeding grounds longer in the morning. Does and fawns often feed for an hour after sunrise, and now, bucks will begin to do the same. In the evening, when they normally would not begin feeding until complete darkness had fallen, bucks will now arrive at the feeding sites earlier — often in that last precious minute of shooting light.

Even at midday, the big boys will not be content to simply lay in their beds and chew their cuds. I have noticed that once the rut is over, bucks are much more likely to rise from their beds and spend an hour or two at midday — often between 11 a.m. and 2 p.m. — browsing near their bedding sites.

All of this daylight activity is a big plus for the after-the-opener hunter who must depend upon natural deer movements, rather than other hunters, to put a buck in front of him. The natural inclination is to hunt from a stand near the feeding area, but this is a mistake when you’re after mature bucks. A big buck is constantly alert, using each of his senses to detect the slightest hint of danger. Never is a buck more alert than when he is feeding during shooting light because he knows he is most vulnerable then. The bucks I have observed feeding during the season have been wound-up tighter than a watch spring and ready to snap at the slightest provocation. One miscue on your part, whether it is movement or scent or whatever, will send him running. I try to avoid known feeding areas, and I concentrate my efforts near the bedding areas.

Hunting near the bedding area means that any shot I take will most often be attempted in good light. That’s important for a clean kill. A buck may not arrive back at his bedding area until the sun is an hour high in the morning, and he may leave his bed to begin a dawdling trip to the feeding area in late afternoon. Instead of risking a poor shot at a shadowy form in the gray gloom of dusk or dawn, I take my shot when the light is in my favor.

Also, by concentrating my efforts in the vicinity of the buck’s daytime haunts, I have a better chance of catching him up and about during the midday hours. If I am forced to move into the bedding area and take a stand at mid-morning, I risk detection by the buck. But if I move into my stand in the dark and set up quietly, I double my chances of scoring. If I fail to take the buck as he returns from breakfast, I will be there waiting when he gets up for lunch or dinner.

But you don’t have to confine yourself to a stand. If conditions allow for quiet stillhunting, I like nothing better than to either prowl the edges of a buck’s daytime haunts or simply tread my way along a ridge littered with the acorns of the white oak, moving only a few yards at a time and stopping often to look, listen and feel. Often after the crowds of opening day are gone from the woods for another year, it is just me and the deer — one-on-one. And that’s the way I like it best.

#8443. $656,000 of Frugal Things I Still Love Doing

“Until he got all rich and fancy so that he no longer understands the common person’s plight.

Stash probably doesn’t even practice any of these money-saving things he preaches any more!”

When I read things like this, I can’t help but laugh. Because on the one hand, when you put a bunch of personal life details online like this, being misunderstood is just part of the package. But on the other hand, if the critics could peek in and see our real lives – not just mine but those of all the Mustachians – they would have to give up their conspiracy theories and accept the fact that this stuff just works.

Because really, not much has changed when it comes to the basics. Like many MMM readers over the past twelve years, my total wealth level has increased pretty regularly.  But also like many of us, I haven’t felt the need to change very much about my spending because I was doing my best to live an enjoyable life in the first place.

How have so many people found such great success? I think we Mustachians have something that’s a bit more rare and special than standard financial advice, which is what makes it work so well:

Standard Advice: Slash your spending and make sacrifices until you reach a certain savings percentage, and beyond that it doesn’t matter, it’s all personal choice. More income? Great, that means you don’t have to sacrifice as much! FatFIRE for everyone!

Mustachianism: Cultivate a love of efficiency, creativity, self awareness, and self improvement. Use this knowledge to improve your life in all ways, including those which help you live better even as your monthly expense rate drops over time.

Well, I’ll give you some examples from my own present-day life. Things I do because I happen to enjoy them, which also happen to save a lot of money. Some of these are normal, some are silly and may end up in some future gossip magazine hit piece, but all of them happen to work for me, so the critics can be damned.

As I list each item, I’ll include an estimate of how much the activity saves me per decade, because you should always think at least in terms of decades. To make that calculation yourself, just use the “rule of 172” – take a monthly expense and multiply it by 172 to estimate how much it would compound into over ten years, if invested.

1) Fixing my own House (and everybody else’s too)

I’m a big believer in self-sufficiency, and working to build up the skills to manage the most important parts of your own life without depending on too many things (or people) that are outside of your control. In other words, one giant recipe for a happy life is simply to Become a Producer of the Things You Most Enjoy Consuming.

And in my case, I happen to love houses. I like living in beautiful, functional spaces and sharing them with friends. But most houses are ugly and poorly designed when you buy them, so I realized that I also love solving problems and redesigning old buildings to become new again. I enjoy this process so much that I spend most of my free time doing it – on both my own properties and the homes of friends.

And I love teaching other people to gain power over their own houses too. It’s amazing how great people feel as they lose their fear and dependence on outside contractors, and gain the ability to fix and maintain things with their own two hands.

Savings: An average of $20,000 per year = $287,000 per decade

You know what’s great? Having so much money that you can buy whatever you want – high quality things which get delivered to your front door the very next day.

You know what’s even better? Not buying some of those new things, and instead finding ways to share, repurpose and buy equally high quality items from other people who don’t need them any more. All while building up your own community and creating new friendships in the process.

Craigslist, Facebook Marketplace, and even NextDoor all have Buy Nothing groups for most areas. In the MMM-HQ community, we run a Discord server with about 200 local people, who chat around the clock on a wide range of subjects. They help each other with major projects in one channel called #diyhowto, and give away and sell things on #forsale and #buynothing.

Although our private Discord group is my favorite, I also use Craigslist regularly, and probably save (and earn) a few thousand every year thanks to the habit:

We all know that Mr. Money Mustache’s biggest contribution to personal finance is to insist that bike transportation is the best way to get around. And I still feel this way. As we learned in The True Cost of Commuting, cars cost at least 50 cents per mile to operate, while bikes are much cheaper, mainly due to reduced depreciation and maintenance costs (which are even bigger than the gas savings).

I do still use bikes (or walking) for at least 95% of my local trips these days, but because I live in the center of a small city, my life is pretty local. So this still only adds up to about 2000 miles per year, a savings of “only” $14,000 per decade.

But when you choose active transportation, there’s much more to the picture than just cutting your car expenses. You’re changing everything about your physical and mental health picture for the better, which brings us to the next point of…

Although I’m no competitive athlete, whenever I see an option to make my body work a bit harder, I usually take it. Stairs instead of elevators, running the golf course instead of using a golf cart, moving my own furniture and appliances instead of calling a mover, shoveling snow and raking leaves instead of using a machine.

When I face a decision like this, I simply ask myself the question: “Well, Mustache. Do you want MORE health and fitness, or LESS?” Putting it in that context makes the answer obvious.  Every bit helps, because when it comes to your body, the rule is pretty much use it or lose it.

But how much money does this save? There’s no real way to calculate it exactly, but I like to think of it this way: The US average health care spending is about $13,000 per person per year. My lifetime costs due to illness or medication so far have been just about zero, plus I know I’ve had more energy and greater productivity due to being healthy. Let’s just put it very conservatively and set the estimated savings and benefits at $10k per year which means

5) Saving Energy by Running my home like a Glamping Retreat

Here’s where things get a bit silly, but my level of joy is actually at its greatest.

My personality type is probably a weird combination of an engineer, a carpenter, an artsy hippie, and a mad scientist. Oh, and a devoted homebody too. Because of this, my favorite activity most days is to just run around my house taking care of things and trying new little experiments and improvements.

Sometimes I’ll cut a few big holes on on the South side of the house and install sliding doors and big windows to allow nice sunbeams and passive solar energy to get into my house and give me free heat in the winters. Other times it’s just smaller things to save energy and live more at at one with the seasons of my area:

Even taken all together, these things are pretty small – the average combined gas and electric bill for my area is about $250 per month, while my usage adds up to about $75. So while we’re only saving about $30,000 per decade for what sounds like a lot of work to most people, I consider this to be the biggest win because I enjoy living in “MMM’s Energy Efficiency Playground” so much.

“Hey, we’re having a big back yard pool party next weekend to celebrate Amy’s graduation from kindergarten, can you make it?”

“OH NOOOO!!! We will be off in at Disneyland that whole week! We planned the trip months ago, I wish we could make it!

As I type this in the height of the summer season, I really feel this effect at its fullest: almost all of my friends are off on trips, and my guest suite here at home is almost constantly full. People are traveling a lot, and many of them sound like they wish they could spend a few more of their precious summer weeks and weekends at home.

I’ll let you in on a little secret: you can! The trick is saying, “no thanks” more often to plans that involve you being away, and “yes please” to things that let you stay at home. The benefits are numerous:

Estimated Savings: Even if you replace just two weeks of travel for a family of four, with equivalent time at home you might save $5,000 per year in direct costs and a further $5,000 per year in incidental benefits like the health and local friendships. This would work out to a shocking $143,000 per decade of wealth increase!

Of course, travel is generally a good thing for broadening the life experience of you and your kids. It’s worth spending on, lavishly at times. But the key is to balance it out and be discerning, keeping the most enriching trips and pruning a few off the bottom of the list. And remembering that home time is valuable and healthy too.

And Whoa! We’ve already built up a huge list and I feel like I was just getting started.

Taken all together, we’ve already detailed things that compound to $656,000 every decade, which already more than double the median wealth that most American seniors have as they cruise nervously into their retirement years – after over 40 years of work!

And now that I’ve been writing this blog for over ten years myself, I can safely say that over $656,000 of even my most recent worth increases are directly attributable to these simple habits. The same ones many of us have been enjoying and preaching about all along, both before and after our retirement dates.

If money is in genuinely short supply, you could go a lot further than the examples in this article. And indeed, there’s a lot more laid out in this blog or the MMM Boot Camp email series.

But one of the points of Mustachianism is that you usually don’t have to try all that hard. Just tweaking your lifestyle to be slightly less ridiculous and more efficient than average is usually all it takes.

In the comments: what are your quirks and frugal indulgences? The things you do now to save money, or things you still do even after it’s no longer about the money? I often wonder how widespread this frugality-just-for-fun is. But since we Humans are a naturally curious and problem solving species in our natural state, I suspect there are many more of us out there.

This piece really resonated with me – great to see MMM still posting after all these years.

I think his first point “Fixing my own House” is invaluable advice for any homeowner in HCOL areas. I live in a very HCOL city (a conscious decision that currently is worth the tradeoff for me) and bought a modest “fixer upper” for well below my neighborhoods average home price during COVID.

Boy did I quickly hit the “find out” part of that decision. I’d never touched renovations or building or fixing a home / apartment beyond mounting bike racks on my rented apartments walls. I received insane quotes for electrical, plumbing, HVAC, and all the drywall repairs required for that kind of work. I did the math out for many of these projects based on the number of people and days the companies told me it would take and in many cases these companies were pulling in $300 per man-hour.

So I didn’t hire any of them. I spent an entire year learning the plumbing and electrical code for my city / state / country. I bothered the hell out of my city inspectors with questions. Made dozens of trips (sadly mostly via car) to the big box stores – eventually even started accounts with supply houses and lumber yards for better variety and deals.

In the two years I spent renovating the house, I’ve saved myself more than $300,000 (estimating the value of my time at $50/hour).

If anybody on here is considering buying a home, but isn’t willing to learn to do this stuff themselves, I think renting might be the more Mustachian decision if the alternative is paying for somebody else to do this work. I also don’t think there’s anything wrong with that.

Thanks for the post MMM! Like those above, I resonated with your article. A lot of these were things I have “always just done” (like hang dry clothes) so a few more that “I just have always done”

(1) My grad school room mate and I loved new clothes but really couldn’t afford them. So we would challenge ourselves to keep our apartment as cold as we could tolerate in Ann Arbor, Michigan and “reward” ourselves in cost savings from our heating bill by buying a new sweater to keep us warm. That $50/month difference meant we were stoked by our new sweater and usually pocketed the savings the other months.

(2) Buy wool clothing. It’s more durable, needs to be washed less, and you can have a smaller wardrobe (which takes up less space, saving you money in storage/heating costs). Even better buy used wool clothing.

(3) Books. I love reading and go through upwards of 50+ books a year. Buying those new at a bookstore would be $30-$50 a month! Instead, I use Libby through my library and constantly have a multitude of books on hold. So yes, I need to wait, but honestly, it’s not that bad if you just had a great book come up that you’ve been waiting for. Slow gratification :)

(4) Shampoo / Conditioner. I’ve experimented a lot with this over the years. Especially for women, there is an expectation to have clean, styled, long hair. There just is. I have finally settled on washing hair 2-3x a week, using tiny amounts of shampoo and conditioner only when necessary means I can save 5 bottles of each a year.

(5) Buying the clearance veggies and cooking them that day. I’m also vegetarian. Both of these things save a TON of money, especially eating out (it’s about 10-15% less to be a vegetarian consistently when ordering out).

My last thought to add to your post is to be adaptable. My partner and I are throwing a large wedding in a month. Weddings are crazy expensive if you let them be. But instead, we’ve found “opportunity” in many unexpected objects left on the side of the road (like an old ladder that became a wine shelf rack) or sold at a huge discount (like silverware from another wedding for $20 for 50 people when it cost $1.25 to rent a single fork!!!) .

It may not be planned and perfectly coordinated, but we’ve created a wedding we’re proud of – both financially and visually. Most of it comes in, as you said, finding joy in the opportunities, not being frustrated with “what we don’t have”. We know we “could” have it, but honestly, that doesn’t bring me joy. Fixing up the old ladder and hearing people gasp when they see the before and after pictures does :)

Putting numbers on how much one saves by acting a certain way is hard, I find. My lifestyle has been very different than most. I’d like to think it’s inspiring, but, yet, most people can’t relate or don’t see themselves doing it, despite the many savings and rewards.

I’ve been a nomad in sailboats and RVs for two decades, being fully self-contained, fixing most everything ourselves, and working as a freelancer. In those 20+ years, I saved heaps of money – on rent, utilities, restaurant meals, … and I never owned more than our current home on wheels or hulls and what’s inside.

We wild camp/boondock for free, have solar panels and a Lithium battery my husband built, use a “composting toilet”, and we have Starlink internet for work. So, the only things we depend on others for is fuel and drinking water. We hate depending on other people, so these two things are still the “sticky points.” But, we have converted our camper to be independent and off grid in nature for up to two weeks.

Our financial approach is different from yours, because we don’t put those savings in the bank. Our approach is “”The less you spent, the less you have to earn.” So, we feel free, travel the world (our truck camper is currently in South America), and work just as much as we need to maintain our lifestyle. Without having to touch our savings. We will never be rich and I don’t even know if we will ever retire. But, we’ve been living our lives internationally and to the fullest, on a budget, and on our own terms “forever.” :)

Take out a Navy Federal home equity loan or line if you’re a member who needs to borrow most of your equity, since Navy Federal pays the closing costs and lends up to all of it. With a top credit score and plenty of equity, get a quote from a bank too before you choose.

Navy Federal Credit Union pays the closing costs on its fixed-rate home equity loan and home equity line of credit (HELOC), and charges no application or origination fee, but only members can borrow. Membership is open to service members, veterans, Defense Department civilians, and their family and household members.

#8437. Climber Falls to Death on Ama Dablam

Search teams have found the body of Wolfgang Waschiczek, 57, of Germany, who went missing after he reached Camp 3 on his way down from the summit. Evidence shows he fell 1,700m to his death.

Waschiczek was one among over 200 climbers who lined up toward the summit of Ama Dablam this past weekend. He reached the top on October 25 with guide Sonam Sherpa, but for some reason the two of them stopped descending at a rather high point on the mountain.

“The pair decided to stay at Camp 3 overnight after borrowing a sleeping bag and other gear from other climbers,” his expedition outfitter, Real Himalaya Nepal, told The Tourism Times.

Climbers above Camp 3 on Ama Dablam. Photo: Dorjee Gyalzen Sherpa

According to the outfitter, the climbers prepared to continue down this morning. Lama asked his client to stay in place while he returned the sleeping bag to the tent where he had borrowed it. When the Sherpa returned, Waschiczek was nowhere to be found, but his crampons were still there, which suggested a freak fall. A search helicopter was called, and the remains of the climber were found this afternoon at around 4,500m.

Waschiczek is the first fatality on Ama Dablam this season.

Together with Manaslu, Ama Dablam is the most popular fall mountain in Nepal. The latest update from Nepal’s Department of Tourism on October 17 showed that over 300 foreign climbers had applied for a climbing permit. That day, the rope-fixing team opened the route to the top, and a massive summit wave started a couple of days later.

Virtually all foreign climbers are guided by one or two Sherpas, so the summit rates and numbers are remarkable. Local media estimate that over 200 climbers, among locals and foreigners, have topped out so far this season. Further teams should join them over the rest of October and November. However, no matter how tamed with ropes and anchors Ama Dablam gets, a fall from its steep slopes is usually lethal.

The upper part of Ama Dablam at sunset. Photo: 8K Expeditions

#8435. New Cyclone Approaches Nepal

For the second time in just over a month, a violent storm is approaching Nepal and threatening two meters of fresh snow on already overloaded mountains. This new setback comes at the height of the trekking season and also affects several climbing teams, including those engaged in alpine-style expeditions in remote areas.

The first storm hit Nepal toward the end of September and abruptly ended the climbing season on Manaslu. Worst of all, it caused an avalanche that killed 16 Base Camp staff on Himlung. The mountain remained open to commercial expeditions despite the accident, and several guided teams are currently launching their summit pushes.

Manaslu Base Camp tents buried under the snow after the September storm in Nepal. Photo: Shiddi Ghising

A low-pressure front that formed in the Bay of Bengal has now developed into a deep depression and will turn into a full cyclone tomorrow. It is expected to hit Nepal on Wednesday or Thursday through the end of the week.

The Nepal National Mountain Guides Association, in association with Senior Meteorologist Krishna Bhakta Manandhar, has put out a detailed forecast. They note that clouds spreading out from this system will hit Nepal’s mountains on October 28, especially above 6,500-7,000m in the eastern part of Nepal, including the Khumbu and Kanchenjunga regions. This will spread over the next two days, causing heavy rains throughout Nepal and snow at higher altitudes.

Authorities and local media have urged trekkers and climbers to modify their plans and avoid river areas and high passes. The main concern is for those currently in remote areas without InReach, Starlink, or satphones.

Trekkers should check with local agencies, especially those heading for the Annapurna and Manaslu regions. Several passes there were already cut or in poor condition after the previous storm and subsequent floods.

A Russian team in the Kangchenjunga region is acclimatizing to climb 7,710m Jannu. According to their latest report, they plan to touch 7,000m before attempting their main goal.

Fellow Russians attempting the West Ridge of Everest have retreated to Kathmandu to rest and recover, so they should not be affected. Andrei Vasiliev, Serguey Kondrashkin, and Vitaly Shipilov, all climbing without supplemental oxygen, are enduring some lung problems. They returned to Base Camp from their second foray up the mountain last Friday, without reaching 7,500m, as they’d hoped.

After climbing in the Cholu range, Jost Kobusch of Germany and his small team moved to the Manaslu area for the second stage of his acclimatization before attempting Everest solo in winter, also without oxygen and via the West Ridge. However, the poor state of the trails after the recent floods and the approaching cyclone have thwarted his plans.

“The flood cut our planned path and, according to forecasts, the incoming cyclone will leave up to two meters of snow,” Kobusch told ExplorersWeb from Samagaon, where the team is pondering their options.

#8433. Gifting Your House Costs Your Family the Tax Break They’d Get by Inheriting It

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Giving your house to a child or grandchild while you’re alive hands them your cost basis, the figure their capital gain is measured from, so selling it can cost them tax on years of growth. If its value has climbed, leave it to them instead, since an heir who sells owes tax only on growth after your death.

Signing the house over to family looks simple, until they sell.

Your cost basis is what you paid for the house plus improvements. Say a mother paid $90,000 for her house and gives it to her son, who sells it at today’s $490,000 value. He takes her $90,000 basis, so the sale leaves him a $400,000 taxable gain. If he owns and lives in it two of the five years before selling, the home sale tax exclusion shelters up to $250,000 of it ($500,000 on a joint return). She’d also file a gift tax return, but owe gift tax only after using up a lifetime exemption in the millions.

If he inherits it at that value instead, his basis steps up to $490,000, and he owes nothing on the sale.

So if your house has gained value, leave it at your death through a will, a living trust you can change, or a transfer-on-death deed where your state allows one. If it must change hands sooner, sell it at market value, lending the buyer the money through seller financing if needed, so their basis is the price paid. Or give only part of it, and the share you keep steps up at your death.

A gift during your life carries other costs too:

Before anyone signs a deed, have an estate planning attorney in your state draw it up.

#8432. Here’s Proof That You Don’t Need to Break the Bank for a Hardside Deer Hunting Blind

Early Black Friday deals are here — Shop hunting gear, fishing tackle, optics, and more!

Published Nov 21, 2026 10:00 AM EST

We may earn revenue from the products available on this page and participate in affiliate programs. Learn More ›

Get the hottest outdoor news from Outdoor Life.

Growing up, I never really hunted out of a blind. Here in the Northeast, we traditionally hunt from treestands or just pick a good spot on the ground with natural cover. Sure, I watched plenty of hunting shows where they sat in a hardsided blind over a food plot, but that just wasn’t an option for me. That is, until recently, when I started planting my own food plots here in Pennsylvania.

Once I figured out the planting cycle, I knew it was time to get my hands on a hardsided blind. But the absurd prices of some of the higher-end models really turned my stomach. Then, I heard about the Maverick XL-V and knew it’d be a great fit for my new food plot.

This six-panel blind provides a near 360 degree view with large, vertical windows that are perfect for archery hunting. It’s also quite spacious, easily allowing two people to sit and hunt comfortably. But the best part is, it’s a fraction of the price that you’d pay for some of the competition out there. Here’s what you need to know about this versatile hunting blind.

After tending to my food plot for the better part of the summer, the clover was flourishing and my Maverick XL-V had arrived just in time to build it a month or so ahead of the season. This allowed the deer to get used to the blind’s presence prior to the season getting underway in October.

The first true test of the blind was setting it up. Maverick talked up its six-panel lock-in system, and I was excited to see how it all came together. Unfortunately, the first shipment I received was missing the door panel. After a quick call to customer support, the missing door panel arrived about a week later, but that panel was missing the window. Rather than wait any longer, I opted to simply replace the window with a piece of plexiglass cut to fit.

The good news is that the lock-in system works flawlessly. The panels all fit together quickly and seamlessly, making it easy to get the blind placed on our homemade platform with just two people. (For some of the bigger, spendier hard-sided blinds, you need a tractor or forklift.) Once it was set up, all that was left was to wait for our archery season to open.

On the opening weekend of archery, my girlfriend and I had an amazing first evening sitting in the XL-V blind. With several does and a few small bucks under 20 yards away, they never had any idea we were there. It was spacious enough for two blind chairs, our hunting packs, and our bows to fit with plenty of room to spare.

Since then, I’ve spent several weeks in and out of the blind, with deer in the plot almost every time. I have yet to see a target buck arrive in daylight, but I have a feeling the skunk will be knocked out of the blind in no time.

After spending several weeks in the XL-V, I can say I’ve grown quite fond of this blind. The windows offer a great view and operate on friction hinges, with three easy-to-use latches to keep them shut. Thus far, the windows open and close silently, which is obviously incredibly important to avoid spooking any deer in range.

The door offers two easy-to-use handles, too, and is large enough to fit through without having to contort my body to squeeze into the blind. Aside from the missing components with delivery, the set up was easy and straightforward. The panels with the lock-in system were intuitive and functioned as expected. I honestly expected to struggle getting it set up on our homemade platform, but was pleasantly surprised to be proven wrong.

Obviously, the issues I experienced with the missing door and then the missing window were not ideal. It’s hard to say if that’s a one-off and I simply got unlucky, or if there’s a larger issue at play there. Aside from that, there are a few other areas I think the XL-V could improve.

First, the near-360 degree view is great, but it leaves you backlit on sunny days. I’d love to see included covers for the windows behind you to avoid the backlighting issue. On top of that, this blind is not airtight, meaning you need to be aware of where your scent will be going just like hunting from a treestand.

While the XL-V might have some room for improvements, it’s worth keeping in mind how affordable this hardsided blind is compared to others on the market. It might lack some of the high-end features those blinds offer, but it still gets the job done for a fraction of the price.

Once getting it set up and deployed in the plot, I’ve thoroughly enjoyed every sit. It’s provided me with some incredible hunts, plenty of room to stretch my legs throughout some long sits, and ensure I have all of the gear I need. If you’re in the market for a budget hunting blind, don’t overlook the Maverick XL-V hunting blind.

#8430. Mont Blanc Has Grown Almost Two Meters — But Not in the Way You Think

These days, topographic surveys typically show that a mountain’s altitude is decreasing due to shrinking snowcaps. But strangely, Mont Blanc, the highest peak in the Alps, has grown significantly since its latest measurement in 2023.

Mont Blanc is now 1.88 meters taller than it was three years ago, according to a recent report by France’s IGN (National Geographic Institute). The new official altitude is now 4,807.47 meters (15,772.5 feet) above sea level.

However, it may be wise to wait before changing the figure in climbing guides. Measurements are carried out every two years, and each time the registered altitude varies:

Graphic showing the results of the last few measurements on Mont Blanc, by LaChangingMeteo

Mont Blanc’s “summit is constantly shifting,” Jean des Garets, chief geometer in the Haute-Savoie department, told Le Monde.  “Each individual measurement is not significant in itself.”

So, what’s with the yearly differences? Obviously, it’s the variation in the thick but ever-changing snowcap that covers the summit.

The mountain’s rocky summit measures around 4,792m above sea level. The snow cover varies with the seasons. The difference from the previous measurement shows that 2023 was much drier at summit altitude.

The survey team on itsir way to the summit of Mont Blanc.. Photo: ING

A team from the Order of Chartered Surveyors (Ordre des géomètres-experts) acclimatized first by climbing Bishorn (4,153m). They then spent some days measuring several points around the mountain. Finally, they climbed Mont Blanc via the normal route on September 15-16.

Once on top, they pinpointed the highest point using a GNSS (Global Navigation Satellite System) pole, which measures altitude in real time.

The recent survey featured an interesting novelty. In addition to altitude, the survey also measured Mont Blanc’s gravity by installing a gravimeter on the summit for the first time ever. This measured the force with which the Earth attracts the device. In so doing, they wanted to determine whether the summit has sunk, regardless of ice cover.

The gravimeter on the summit of Mont Blanc, September 16. Photo: ING France

“When the height of Mont Blanc changes, we can’t know for sure whether the ground or the rock has moved or if the ice has melted,” explains Olivier Jamet.

Gravity provides the missing information: mass. If the ice has melted, there is less material under the instrument, but the rock has moved closer to it. Distinguishing these two effects requires a model of the ice cap and the massif, and above all, repeated measurements at the same location. And the effort is worthwhile, especially now that the effects of climate change on Alpine glaciers are becoming increasingly apparent.

The gravimeter on the top of Mont Blanc measured the gravity at 9.7944689 m/s².

“For comparison, this value is 9.81 m/s² in Marseille (located at sea level) and 9.8043046 m/s² in Saint-Gervais-Le Fayet (580m above sea level),” ING reports. “This difference in value, even if it seems small, allows for the detection of changes in mass, particularly in the mass of the ice. Repeated over time, these gravity measurements will thus contribute to improving the determination of the altitude of the highest peak in Western Europe.”

#8429. Interest-Free Credit From Suppliers – Ask for Longer Terms and Pay on the Due Date

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

Supplier payment terms are credit that charges no interest, and every extra day you get keeps cash in your business. Once you’ve paid a supplier on time for a few months, ask for 30 to 60 days to pay. Then pay each bill on its due date, not early, unless the supplier offers a discount for paying sooner.

Paying suppliers on delivery, or paying each invoice the day it arrives, hands over cash that terms would let you keep for weeks. That cash could be covering payroll, rent, or the next order.

Terms like net 30 give you 30 days after the invoice date to pay the full bill, with no interest. Take a gift shop that buys about $12,000 a month from its two biggest suppliers and pays on delivery. Moving both to net 45 means it pays for each order a month and a half later, so about $18,000 more stays in its account going into the holiday season.

Ask for longer terms after a few months of paying a supplier on time, since that record is your best argument. Go from paying on delivery to net 30, or from net 30 to net 45 or net 60. Better still, ask for terms that match how long your own customers take to pay you, so their payments come in by the time your bills come due.

Then pay on the due date, not before and never after, with each payment scheduled in your bank’s bill pay to arrive that day. Many suppliers report how you pay to Dun & Bradstreet, whose PAYDEX business credit score tracks how promptly you pay them. A late payment can pull that score down, and it gives a supplier reason to shorten your terms, not lengthen them.

The exception is a discount for paying early. Terms of 2/10 net 30 take 2% off a bill paid within 10 days and otherwise give you 30 days to pay it in full. Saving 2% for paying 20 days sooner is like earning about 37% a year on that money, far more than a savings account pays, so take the discount whenever you have the cash to spare. Offering your own customers an early-payment discount turns that 37% into a cost you pay.

Start with the supplier you pay the most, since every extra 30 days of terms keeps about one month’s worth of its bills in your account.

#8427. Walking and Canoeing from Kansas to the Gulf of Mexico

In April, Robert Cowden, 52, set off on foot from New Haven, Kansas, on a two-stage journey across the United States. First, he planned to walk nearly 2,000km to Pittsburgh, then canoe 3,200km downriver to the Gulf of Mexico. With him is his dog, Enzo, a pointer-mix.

Robert Cowden and Enzo. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition

When he left New Haven with Enzo, Cowden was at a low point. His battle with alcohol addiction had cost him his job, car, and home. Entering a residential treatment program would leave Enzo with no place to go. Now sober and with housing waiting for him after the end of his journey, Cowden sees his expedition as part of the larger effort to rebuild his life.

During the walking stage, Cowden towed his camping gear and supplies in a cart, which Enzo could ride in to take a break from walking. Setting out with very little, Cowden has relied on the kindness of strangers, both online and on the trail, to continue his expedition.

“The number one warning you’re going to get on a walk across America is, ‘Be careful, there’s creepy people and bad people,'” Cowden recalled, speaking to a local KOMU 8 reporter while passing through Missouri. Instead, he’s been overwhelmingly met with generosity and helpfulness.

Cowden shows the wear on his trail shoes, as Enzo looks on. Photo: Enzo The Great: An American Expedition

Cowden completed the walking stage in September. Now, he’s on the Ohio River and hopes to reach the Gulf by the end of 2026. While the second stage lets him and Enzo get off their feet, it has its own challenges. They launched the canoe into the Allegheny River at Pittsburgh. It soon joined the Ohio, and lengthy stretches of slow water pushed Cowden to paddle continuously.

It’s 1,579km down the Ohio to its confluence with the Mississippi in Illinois, which Cowden and Enzo aim to complete in under 40 days. They’re currently on pace, averaging about 20km a day.

Cowden posts regular updates on Facebook and on the expedition’s webpage.
