My millenial co-workers used to snicker at my frugal ways, sadly. They should start teaching finance in middle school!

> “In the Comments: Where are you at on this spectrum of stinginess versus abundance mentality, and fulfilment versus longing in life?”

I’m definitely trying to operate more with an abundance mindset these days (thanks to the likes of you, Carl @ 1500 days, and ChooseFI). However, it is difficult to communicate accurately to my wife why I think spending $250 instead of $90 for a flight with more convenient times is fine but spending $15 on McDonald’s is a total waste. > “A Temporary Note about Teslas and other electric cars: Rumor has it that the $7500 EV tax credit might be disappearing when our new president takes over next week, so this might be the cheapest chance to buy what I feel are the best cars on the market: The Model Y, or Model 3.”

I’ve benefited from the EV tax credit, but at the same time I don’t like the federal government distorting the market, but then also at the same time the federal government already does that in so many areas with ridiculous Byzantine regulations, so the EV tax credit could be seen as a form of “un-distortion”. Either way, if the tax credit disappears I am quite confident that the market will find a new equilibrium all on its own.

I’ve heard that “subsidy/distorted market” argument about EVs so many times over the past few years, and yet I find it mostly irrelevant. I think most people don’t know that the combustion engine vehicles industry has been heavily subsidized for decades, either through tax breaks, direct investments from the government, direct subsidies to oil companies and, in a more subtle way, by very lax environmental regulations that have allowed the production of these vehicles (or oil) at a distorted cost. The only difference is that when buying EVs, consumers receive the tax credit directly instead of getting a hidden discount on a combustion engine vehicle that was subsidized on the production line. So yes, in the end, everything is subsidized in one way or another!

MMM (or others), can you elaborate on the comment, “(plus the usual hidden subsidy of a paid-off house)”….exactly what is that? I think I am fairly informed in the world of finance (have been FIREd since 2014 @ age of 40) but not exactly sure what this is. Thank you!

It is a “subsidy” in the sense that it reduces monthly/yearly cash requirements by the amount of principal+interest (and in the case of MMM, insurance since he chooses to self-insure). If you have a mortgage then you have a requirement to pay the mortgage every month (PITI), but in MMM’s case he only pays the ‘T’ part or taxes.

If he had a mortgage, then his $30k/year spend would probably be closer to $60k/year (or something, depending on the amount financed, interest rates, insurance, etc.). So the subsidy is the reduction in annual spending because of not having the mortgage. But he got that by working at paying off the mortgage earlier in life, which he acknowledges is a trade off.

#8407. Solo Trekker Flouts Khumbu Rules, Evacuated After Cliff Fall

A 26-year-old Australian solo trekker who fell from a cliff near Lobuche in the Everest region has been evacuated by helicopter to Kathmandu. He is recovering in intensive care. By law, all foreign trekkers are supposed to have a guide in the Khumbu.

Joshua Patrick Cherubino sustained severe head injuries after falling at Kongma La Pass. He was first taken to Lobuche, then flown out on October 27, according to The Tourism Times.

Kongma La, at about 5,535m, is the highest of the trio of high passes on the classic Everest Three Passes circuit. It links the Chhukung side of the Imja Valley with Lobuche over rocky, non-glaciated moraine. The crossing is long and remote; the descent toward Lobuche is often loose underfoot and comes after hours already spent at altitude.

The case has again drawn attention to Nepal’s rules in the Khumbu. Since 2023, the Nepal Tourism Board has required that all foreign trekkers be accompanied by a licensed guide within national parks, including Sagarmatha.

In practice, the local Khumbu Pasang Lhamu Rural Municipality has continued to issue its own permits and has not strictly enforced the national guide requirement. Thus, independent trekking remains common on the main Everest routes. Officials quoted by The Tourism Times described unguided travel in the region as a violation of the mandatory rule and a source of preventable rescues.

Cherubino was traveling alone when he was found. No further details on the circumstances of the fall or his condition have been released beyond the hospital’s assessment that he is recovering.

#8406. Family or Friend Won’t Repay a Loan? Get a Payment Plan in Writing First

Many or all of the credit card, banking, and other offers on this site are from companies that pay us. For example, we may be paid when you click a link, are approved for a product, or open an account. Compensation may influence which products we cover and how, where, and in what order they appear. It doesn’t influence our editorial evaluations, ratings, or opinions, which are ours alone. We don’t include every bank, credit card company, or offer available in the marketplace.

If a relative or friend has stopped repaying money you lent them, ask privately for a payment plan they can afford, with a set amount and start date. Confirm it in a text they answer. Save a demand letter or small claims court for a broken plan, or forgive the rest and say so.

Without a set payment or due date, repaying a loan is easy to put off, and every month of silence makes the subject harder to raise.

So skip the hints and make one specific request. Call or meet in private. A text is easy to ignore, and with others listening, embarrassment can turn into an argument. Propose an amount and a schedule they can actually meet. A sister owed $2,400 might ask her brother for $100 a month starting next payday, which clears the debt in two years.

Afterward, text them a short summary of the plan and ask them to confirm it. Their reply is a written record that they owe the money and agreed to repay it, which matters if the plan falls apart.

If payments don’t start, or start and then stop, put the request in writing. Send a short letter or email that states what they owe, the payments they missed, a deadline to pay, and that you’ll file in small claims court if they don’t. Keep a copy. California’s courts require you to ask for the money before you file, and your copy shows the judge you did.

Once the deadline passes, file in small claims court. It takes claims up to a cap your state sets, from $2,500 in Kentucky to $25,000 in Delaware and Tennessee. Filing is cheap. California’s fee for a $2,400 claim is $50. For the hearing, bring the bank or payment app record of the transfer and every message in which they agreed to repay you.

Suing a relative or friend can cost you the relationship, win or lose. When the relationship matters more than the money, forgive the rest on purpose and tell them it’s now a gift, which settles the debt for both of you. Then stop lending to that person. For anyone else, lend only money you could afford to give away.

The 101 money moves that matter most, from the foundations to protecting what you’ve built.
